en: Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-sandarbha [There are several different editions of the Kṛṣṇa-sandarbha.
The Bengali edition appears to be earlier than the Vṛndāvana edition published by Haridās.]
Shastri (1983). The additions found in the Vṛ edition are likely authentic,
as there is clear evidence that Jīva Gosvāmī made extensive corrections and emendations in some of his books after they were sent to Bengal along with Srinivasa.
In order to satisfy the two saintly ones, Śrīla Rūpa and Sanātana,
this is once again analyzed by the southern Bhaṭṭa, Thakur, in the 1570s. ||o||

Having thoroughly examined the first manuscript of that work— which was disordered, missing, and fragmentary— and having arranged it in its proper sequence, Jīvaka writes it down. [1] Now, regarding that which has been established as supreme over all by means of the three preceding compositions, of that glorious—
This composition is undertaken for the purpose of determining the meaning of the Blessed One.
Regarding that, they say, starting from "In the second [chapter] of the first [book]" (BhP 1.2.11), and so forth. [Vṛ. adds:]...
Because they appear in various forms, those statements are cited for the purpose of determining the ultimate reality:
[as stated in the *Vṛtti*] "that reality is indeed one."
It has been stated that [the reality] is designated as "Brahmā" and so forth;
now, that very triad beginning with Brahmā is analyzed as the third [category]. Here, however, "Brahman" refers to—
"When both existence and non-existence have been negated here by one's own self-awareness,
and [these two] are understood as having been produced in the Self through ignorance— that is the vision of Brahman.
By such statements, even though [the Self] is distinct therein, [it is so described].
Because there is no doubt due to the manifestation of a single form, it is not useful; therefore, that statement should not be cited as an example.
However, this is not the case for the venerable Bhagavān and the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
It is illustrated as follows:

therein, it was previously determined that there is no such thing as a formless Īśvara, and by the term "Supreme Self" (paramātman), the Person who is the inner controller of all is intended; [this applies] to those very [entities].
In the textual compositions;
and that being so, starting from the third chapter, it should be presented as follows:
"Now, was it not previously stated that reality is one and of only three kinds, namely as Brahmā and the others?"

In this regard, what is the definition of Brahman, or of the Blessed One (Bhagavān) and the Supreme Self (Paramātman)? Is there any distinction between them? Furthermore, since there are many forms such as the venerable Īśvara and others, which form corresponds to the name "Śrī-Bhagavān"?

Anticipating the question of Śrī Śaunaka and others as to whether the Supreme Self (paramātman) is indeed those two [the Lord and the individual soul], and what their essential nature and so forth may be, Śrī Sūta spoke, first determining the identities of the Blessed Lord and the Supreme Self:
"The Blessed One assumed a human form through the great elements and other principles."
In the beginning, with the desire to create the world, He assumed a form consisting of the sixteen digits (*kalās*) that had come into being,
prior to the manifestation of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the creation of the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest.
He manifested it.
For what reason?
Out of a desire to create the world.
The meaning is: for the purpose of the manifestation of the collective and individual souls of the worlds, as well as their respective presiding deities;
for indeed, those [deities] reside within Him.
"They were dissolved," it is said;
therefore, their manifestation in the third [creation] is described by means of that very [process]. "The Blessed One alone was here... [BhP]
In this context, beginning with [BhP 3.5.23], it is said:
"But by means of the function of time, the powerful Adhokṣaja infused his seed into Māyā, who consists of the guṇas, through the Puruṣa who is his own self" (BhP 3.5.26).
In that regard, he explains their actual existence [as follows]: "produced by" means joined together with the Great Principle (mahat) and the others;
the meaning is that the principles beginning with the Great Principle are contained within it. That [Self] has the subtle elements of the material beings placed within its body.
Thus, from the third [chapter] itself:
the root *bhū* preceded by the prefix *sam-* is well-known in the sense of "conjunction," as in [Māgha’s Śiśupālavadha 2.100]:
"The great [river] today goes to the ocean together with the mountain-rivers. Etc.

Thus, regarding the statement "Viṣṇu indeed has three forms" and so forth, there is first the form known as Puruṣa, which is heard [in scripture] as the creator of the Mahat-tattva; and there is that which is heard in the Brahma-saṃhitā and other texts as Saṅkarṣaṇa, reclining upon the causal ocean.
It has been established that he grasped that very [power] by virtue of being the agent of the creation and other functions of the universe; furthermore,
for the sake of conceiving his supreme sovereignty beyond even that, it says "sixteen"—
The meaning is that "kala" refers to being endowed with all powers in their entirety.
Here, "entirety" (pūrṇatva) is relative;
for although He is a treasure-house of His own essential power (svarūpa-śakti), by His very presence, He is the agent of the creation and so forth of the universe through the functions of māyā.
It has been stated that He possesses a portion of the Blessed One and is the sole manifestation of His own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*).

Having thus described the Blessed One and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) in general, he now defines the Supreme Self through three verses by means of various distinctions regarding His abodes, activities, essential nature, and forms.
From the lotus in the lake of whose navel there arose Brahmā, the lord of the creators of the universe, as he lay upon the waters extending his yogic sleep; [he who was thus lying] upon the waters—
the *garbhodaka* at the time of dissolution— of that form of the Supreme Person.
[Regarding the difference between *ādau* and *śayānasya sataḥ* in the Vṛ. edition:
He is the Blessed Lord who was previously described as possessing the six perfections of sovereignty (*ṣaḍ-aiśvarya*).
That very [form] is designated as the "human form" by virtue of being human;
that same form he assumed at the beginning, at the start of creation, which was primordial (prākṛta).
He has accepted that which was dissolved during these dissolutions (pralayas) by making it manifest.
For what purpose? To this he says:
"Out of a desire to create the world."
The meaning is: for the purpose of manifesting, through the desire to create, the collective and individual souls of the worlds that were dissolved in that very [state].
Of what nature is that [desire]?
That form was dissolved therein; regarding this, he says: "produced by the Great One (mahat) and the others" means joined together, with the principles beginning with the Great One contained within;
having merged into the ocean.
In the verse, "The Great One now approaches the mountain" (*abhyeti mahān adyā nagāpāga*), the root *sam-bhū* has the sense of "merging.
For in that context, the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the others were merged (*līna*).
Thus, in passages such as "Viṣṇu indeed has three forms," he is first [described] by way of being the creator of the Great Principle.
It is established that He assumed that very form which is known as Puruṣa and which is heard of in the *Brahma-saṃhitā* and other texts as Saṅkarṣaṇa reclining upon the causal ocean. Furthermore—
Of what nature is that form? To this he says: "consisting of sixteen parts," which means it possesses the full powers necessary for that creation. Thus, the Blessed One is he who assumed that form.
That which was grasped by him, however,
is established as the Supreme Self (paramātman) because it serves as the substratum for his own emanations;
such is that [Self] which has the form of the Person (puruṣa).
To establish that [the world] has its origin in the emission [of sound], he says in two and a half verses:
"From the lotus in the lake of the navel of Him who was reclining upon the waters, spreading His yogic sleep, there arose Brahmā, the lord of the creators of the universe."
"The expansion of the world is imagined through the configurations of His limbs"—

this should be connected with the passage beginning, "of Him who, having entered the cosmic egg as a second manifestation of His personal form (*pauruṣa-rūpa*), was lying upon the waters in the *garbhodaka*."

And for one who lies there in such a state, the expansion of the world— the Virāṭ form, the phenomenal manifestation— is imagined through the configurations of the limbs as the actual arrangement of the feet of Śrī and so forth.
"Just as the arrangement of His limbs is, so too is Pātāla the base of His feet"— by such statements, this was proclaimed for the sake of stabilizing the minds of new devotees.
But the meaning is not that, in reality, that very thing is its form; rather, as the Śruti states,
beginning with "The moon was born from the mind" and continuing, "From his feet came the earth, from his ears the directions,
and thus he fashioned the worlds" (Ṛgveda 10.90.13–14), the expansion of the worlds was constructed by those [elements] acting as causes.
This is the meaning.
And likewise, in the *Bhārata*, in the *Mokṣadharma* section of the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "That which is my fourth form created the imperishable Śeṣa."
For he is declared to be Saṃkarṣaṇa, and he also begot Pradyumna.
From Pradyumna I am Aniruddha; my creation occurs again and again.
From Aniruddha likewise comes Brahmā, who is born from the primordial lotus therein.
"All moving and stationary beings are from Brahman.
On that very point, Vyāsa says:
"That which people who know Sāṃkhya and Yoga call the Supreme Self (paramātman)..."
That great person receives the designation of "Great Man" through his own karma.
Therefore, the wise know that the unmanifest Pradhāna was produced from Him;
from the Unmanifest, the manifest world arose for the purpose of creation through the Lord.
"For Aniruddha is indeed called the Great Self among the worlds;
he, having attained manifestation, created the Grandfather (Pitāmaha). Thus it is said.
[The Vṛtti adds here: Having thus described the majesty of Saṅkarṣaṇa, he now speaks also of Aniruddha.
Regarding the phrase "for Aniruddha":
in the worlds, that is, in each individual cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), he is the Great Self, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
"Manifestation" (*vyaktatva*) means becoming evident; the words "from Pradyumna" are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
However, because the intention was not to express a distinction from the *sūtra*, Pradyumna is not mentioned separately, just as one says "the three forms of Viṣṇu.
This is the method [of exposition].
In the sixth verse of the second chapter, in the verse beginning with "sa eṣa ādyaḥ puruṣaḥ" (BhP 2.9.39), the commentary states:
"This is that primordial Lord who, being the incarnation as Puruṣa, performs the creation and so forth. This is the meaning.
Regarding the verse, "Thus the first incarnation is the Person of the Supreme" (BhP 2.6.42), the commentary states:

"The first incarnation is that playful form of the Supreme—the Infinite—who is the Person that sets Prakṛti in motion, as described in the passage beginning with 'Thousand-headed' (Ṛg Veda 10.90.1). This is the meaning.
Likewise, regarding the third [chapter],
the section beginning with "By the Lord" (BhP 3.20.12) and ending with "He followed" (so 'nu), along with its commentary, should be consulted here as the relevant context.
Therefore, its form has not been explained as being that of Virāṭ. And from this it follows that the Blessed Lord, who occupies the position of Vāsudeva, is indeed distinct from Puruṣa.
Now, he describes the essential nature of those two forms in their general unity: "That indeed..."

"The form of the Blessed One is pure, and His being is exalted" (BhP 1.3.3). That is the personal form of the Blessed Lord, well-known as "pure" because it is manifested by exalted *sattva*, and as "power" (*śakti*)— because it is the manifestation of power.

And because there is no difference between their own natures (*svarūpa*), the meaning is that it is indeed of that very form. And regarding the second manifestation of the Person (*puruṣavyūha*), the nature of that form has been stated: "There is nothing higher than this, O Supreme One."
Regarding the phrase "its own nature" (*svarūpam*) in BhP 3.9.3:
it is pure, being devoid even of a trace of insentience, because it exists as a function of its own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*).

It is "ūrjitam," powerful in every respect, because its nature is supreme bliss—as the Śruti declares: "For who indeed could inhale, and who could exhale, if this bliss did not exist in space? (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7.1).
Therefore, since it is the direct form of the Blessed Lord, the point is established all the more emphatically by implication.

Thus, having described the two-fold state and activity of the Person, he now states that its form, like its essential nature, is of a single kind: "The Seers see this" (see paragraph 4). [End of Vṛtti addition.]
Therefore, even though there is an internal distinction here, by accepting non-difference, the statement regarding the two-fold manifestation (*dvi-vyūha*) is the specific point;
thus it follows that the Lord who occupies the position of Vāsudeva is indeed distinct from him.
Likewise, in the eleventh [chapter]:
When, having fashioned the radiant city out of the five elements created by himself, he entered therein—
Regarding the passage, "Nārāyaṇa, the primordial God, entered with a portion of himself and received the designation 'Puruṣa'," this has been explained by those very same [commentators].

First, he describes the incarnation as Puruṣa with the words "by the elements" (bhūtaiḥ): when, having fashioned the city— the Virāj, the cosmic egg— out of the elements created by Himself, He entered it sportively, and not as an enjoyer.
Because the living being possessing abundant merit is the enjoyer therein;
thus, the meaning is seen to be exactly the same in the two subsequent verses as well,
and likewise for the second.

And regarding the verse beginning with "sa eṣa ādyaḥ puruṣaḥ" (BhP 2.6.39) in the sixth canto, the commentary states: "This very one is the primordial Lord, who, being the incarnation as Puruṣa, performs creation and so forth. Likewise, the commentary on the verse "evam ādyo 'vatāraḥ puruṣaḥ parasya" (BhP 2.6.42) has already been shown. Similarly...
In this regard, the section beginning with "By fate" (BhP 3.20.12) and ending with "He followed" (BhP 3.20.17),
along with its commentary, should be consulted here.
Therefore, His form is that of Virāṭ.
It has not been explained.
Here, the statement is made precisely through the non-difference between the Great Creator and the Person who has entered the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). [3]

Then, He further qualifies that very same reality by means of its external characteristics (*taṭastha-lakṣaṇa*) and its essential characteristics (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*): "That form of the Blessed One, whose limbs and configurations constitute the expansion of the worlds, is indeed pure, powerful, and composed of *sattva*. (BhP 1.3.3)
By means of the configurations of its parts— the direct arrangements of the feet of Śrī and so forth— the expansion of the world, the Virāj-form, was fashioned as a manifold manifestation (prapañca).
Just as those configurations of its parts exist, so too does Pātāla.
For this very reason, by the passage beginning with “the root of his feet” (BhP 2.1.26), [the practice] has been proclaimed for the sake of mental steadiness for the benefit of new devotees;
however, the meaning is not that, in reality, that alone constitutes his limb. That...
The personal form of the Blessed One is indeed well-known as pure and exalted.

The meaning is that because the sentient being (*sattva*) is manifested and because there is no difference between power (*śakti*) and its essential nature (*svarūpa*), it is indeed of that very form.
And the fact that this form is the essential nature was stated in the passage: "There is nothing higher than this supreme form of yours, which is your own essential nature" (BhP 3.9.3).
It is pure, being devoid even of a trace of insentience (*jāḍya*), because it functions as the essential power of the essential nature (*svarūpa-śakti*).
It is exalted and powerful in every respect because its nature is supreme bliss;
for the Śruti declares: "For who indeed could inhale and who could exhale, if this bliss did not exist in space? (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7.1). [4]

Having thus described the locations, the actions, and the essential natures [of the goddesses], he also describes their form: "Behold this form, wondrous with a thousand feet, thighs, arms, and faces, with its many eyes."
He has a thousand heads, ears, eyes, and noses,
and he shines with a thousand crowns, garments, and earrings.
That is the form of the Supreme Person, which is perceived by the "abundant eye" known as devotion;
for it has been said: "That Supreme Person, O Pārtha, is attainable by unswerving devotion alone" (Gītā 8.22).

And His state of having a thousand feet and so forth was indicated by the venerable Maitreya in the eighth chapter of the third book [of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa]: "He whose arms, thighs, feet, and limbs are like flutes... (BhP 3.8.24).
"Having a thousand arms as its branches" (BhP 3.8.29),
and "having a thousand golden crests like a crown" (BhP 3.8.30);
likewise, of the ninth [chapter]:
In the fourteenth [chapter], Śrī Śuka says:
"From the lotus born from the lake-like navel of the thousand-headed Puruṣa, there was a son of Dhātṛ named Atri, who was equal to his father in virtues. [BhP 9.14.2] [5]
He explains his very fullness:

[B. reads here: "In that regard, in order to clearly elucidate the Blessed Lord, he explains the manifestation of the second Person, the Vyūha, who resides within the *garbhodaka*, as taking various incarnations"—end of Vṛ.]
This is the inexhaustible seed, the treasury of His various incarnations,
by a mere fraction of a fraction of which gods, animals, humans, and others are created. (BhP 1.3.5)
This refers to that which resides within the cosmic egg;
it is a treasury of lakes, like the ocean, and a constant refuge for its own rays, like the sun.
Therefore, it is "immutable" (avyaya), meaning without decay. It is the "seed," the source of emergence.
He says "of whom" to show that it is not only the seed of the incarnations, but also of the entire world. [6]

Now, describing His incarnations by way of their predominance and with the intention of expressing their essential unity, He enumerates even the relationship between the part and the whole through twenty [verses], beginning: "That very Lord, first resorting to the Kaumāra creation..."
Brahmā practiced difficult and unbroken celibacy (*brahmacarya*).

He who lies upon the waters and he who possesses forms such as the thousand-footed one—he is indeed the deity named Puruṣa; for this is confirmed by the concluding statement: "And these are the portions and fractions of the Supreme Person" (BhP 1.3.28). [The period of] Kaumāra...
Having assumed the form of the four-faced Brahmā, he became Brahmā himself;
secondly, for his own existence, he took the earth situated in the Rasātala realm.
Intending to uplift this universe, the Lord of Sacrifice assumed the body of a boar; indeed,
for the sake of the emergence of this world,
He took on the third creation of the sages, having attained the state of a divine seer (*devarṣi*).

He taught the Sātvata-tantra, because therein lies the cessation of karmic action through action itself. Having entered the lineage of the sages (*ṛṣi-sarga*), and having attained the status of a divine sage (*devarṣi*) known as Nārada,
he taught the Sātvata— that is, the Vaiṣṇava— tantra, which is the Pañcarātra scripture.

The remainder of the sense is that, because of these tantras of the illustrious Bhagavān’s teachings—which exist even in the form of ritual action—*naiṣkarmya* (the state of being beyond action) is perceived as emerging from actions by virtue of its liberating one from the bondage of karma; that is, it is understood to be distinct from them. [9]
In the fourth creation, that of the elements of dharma, the two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa, having come into being, performed difficult penance endowed with self-peace.
This is clear. [10]
The fifth, the lord of perfected beings named Kapila, spoke the Sāṅkhya—which determines the collection of principles—to Āsuri, whose knowledge had been obscured by time.
[BhP 1.3.10] To the brahmin named Āsuri. [11]
The sixth [chapter] describes how he was chosen and obtained as a son by Anasūyā from Atri;
it relates how he taught *ānvīkṣikī* (philosophical inquiry) to Alarka, Prahlāda, and others.
In the fourth chapter and those following, it is shown that Atri merely requested the manifestation of a son similar to himself.
The intention [of this statement] is that,
through these words, it is understood— without any malice— that at some time, the very status of being the son of the glorious Lord himself was chosen directly.
And it is said in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, in the narrative of the devoted wife (*pativratopākhyāna*):
Anasūyā, having bowed to the gods Brahmā, Īśa, and Keśava, spoke. (Page 6)
"If you are pleased with me, or if I am worthy of a boon, then,
being inclined toward grace, you shall become my sons.
[He taught] *ānvīkṣikī*, the science of the self.
This is indeed an incarnation of Śrī Viṣṇu himself.
From him, in the seventh [manvantara], Yajña was born from Ruci and Ākūti;
he protected the period of Svāyambhuva Manu along with the hosts of gods beginning with the Yāmas.
The meaning is that at that time, he himself became the sacrifice (Yajña) and Indra.
[13] In the eighth [manvantara], Urukrama was born to Nābhi from Merudevī, demonstrating for the wise the path honored by all stages of life (āśramas). [BhP 1.3.13]
Urukrama was born as the Bull (Ṛṣabha);
entreated by the sages, he assumed a ninth earthly form.
By him, O wise ones, these herbs were milked; therefore, he is most beloved.
He assumed the form of a fish during the dissolution of the Cākṣuṣa ocean; he was the earthly one, possessing a vast royal body, most desirable and most beautiful.
[15] He assumed the form of a fish during the deluge of the Cākṣuṣa ocean.
Having placed him upon a boat made of earth,
he caused Vaivasvata Manu to descend from it during that deluge of the ocean which occurred in the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara; the term "Vaivasvata" refers to the future [Manu].
This is the name of Satyavrata.

It is heard that even at the conclusion of each *manvantara*, there is a dissolution (*pralaya*). In the first section of the *Śrī-Viṣṇudharmottara*: "O twice-born one, when a *manvantara* has been exhausted, what kind of state arises?"
Thus, in the *Śrī-Vajrapraśna*, following the reply given by Mārkaṇḍeya beginning with "When the Manvantara has perished," it is said:
"The one garlanded with waves, possessing great velocity, stands encompassing everything."
Then, O Yādava, everything residing in the world of Bhūr perishes.
"O Indra among kings, the renowned mountain-clans do not perish;
rather, the Great Goddess becomes a boat," and so forth.
Likewise, the section beginning with "In this very way, there is dissolution during the Manvantaras" is found in the *Śrī-Harivaṃśa*.
And this is clearly stated in the commentaries (*ṭīkā*).
Therefore, the phrase "the son of Vivasvat in the sight" (*akṣuṣe vaivasvatam*) is merely an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).
[16] While the gods and demons were churning the ocean with Mount Mandara as the churning stick...
In the eleventh [incarnation], the Lord assumed the form of a tortoise and supported [the mountain] upon his back.
This is clear.
The twelfth was Dhānvantara, and the thirteenth likewise.
He caused other gods to drink wine, deluding them with the woman Mohinī;
the connection with the word "bearing" (bibhrat) occurs with the following verse.
He was bearing the twelfth form, that of Dhānvantara.

Bearing the thirteenth form, that of Mohinī, He caused the gods to drink nectar—the word "sudhām" (nectar) being understood from the context. In what form? The meaning is: in the form of the woman Mohinī.
What was he doing? The ellipsis is: "deluding the other gods and bringing forth the nectar (sudhā) in the form of Dhanvantari.
These are the incarnations of the Unconquered One (Ajitasya).
These three;
and the fourteenth, assuming the form of Narasiṃha, he tore apart the powerful lord of the Daityas with his claws,
as one who makes a mat cuts an erakā-grass upon his lap.
Assuming the form of Narasiṃha, and having taken the fifteenth incarnation as Vāmana, He went to the sacrifice of Bali,
requesting three paces of land while desiring to reclaim the triple heaven.
Having manifested his incarnation in the sixteenth [age], seeing kings who were enemies of Brahman,
he became enraged and thrice seven times made the earth devoid of Kṣatriyas. (BhP 1.3.20)
In the incarnation known as Śrī Paraśurāma, this is clear.
Then, in the seventeenth [incarnation], he was born to Satyavatī from Parāśara; seeing that men were of small intellect, he made branches for the tree of the Veda. [BhP 1.3.21–22]
Having attained the state of a god among men (nara-devatva) with the desire to perform the work of the gods,
he thereafter performed heroic deeds such as the subduing of the ocean.
"The state of a god among men" refers to his form as Śrī Rāghava.
Beyond this, in the eighteenth [chapter]:
"This is indeed the manifest Person himself; in the Śrī-Rāma-gītā of the Skanda-purāṇa, [it describes] his Brahman-nature as he reveals his universal form (viśva-rūpa)."
From hearing the hymns of praise offered by Viṣṇu and Rudra:
"In his nineteenth and twentieth births among the Vṛṣṇis, the Blessed Lord took birth as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa and removed the burden of the earth. [BhP 1.3.23]
The term "Bhagavān" is used for the purpose of conveying the distinction that this is a direct manifestation of the Blessed One himself, and not of Aniruddha who bears the name "Puruṣa";
for in that case, it is his own direct form.

Since He is His own partial expansion in the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the removal of the burden in the form of Rāma also belongs to the Lord alone; thus, it is indeed a pun that "the Lord removed the burden" in both instances.
Therefore, this applies to Rāma as well.
The fact that Aniruddha has not descended [into this world] has been personally refuted;
moreover, since Śrī Kṛṣṇa is Vāsudeva and Śrī Rāma is Saṅkarṣaṇa, that [refutation] is indeed logical. [24]

Then, when the Kali age has begun, for the purpose of deluding the enemies of the gods, one named Buddha, the son of Añjana, will appear among the Kīkaṭas. [24] "Among the Kīkaṭas" means in the region of Gayā. [25]

Then, at the junction of the ages (*yuga-sandhyā*), when kings consist mostly of bandits, the Lord of the World, Kalki by name, will be born as the son of Viṣṇuyaśas. [25] "At the junction of the ages" means at the end of the Kali age. [26]

Now, for the purpose of summarizing those [names] not previously mentioned— such as Śrī-Hayagrīva, Hari, Haṃsa, Pṛśnigarbha, Vibhu, Satyasena, Vaikuṇṭha, Ajita, Sārvabhauma, Viśvaksena, Dharmasetu, Sudhāman, Yogeśvara, Bṛhadbhānu, and others, including Śukla and so forth— he says:
"O twice-born ones, the incarnations of Hari, the treasure-house of goodness (*sattva*), are indeed innumerable;
they are like the thousands of small channels that flow from a great lake.
The reason for their being innumerable is that he is a "treasure-house of goodness," meaning he is a repository of the power (*śakti*) of goodness (*sattva*) to manifest itself.
Of form (*rūpa*). In this very regard, there is an illustration: "just as" (*yathā*) from a lake that does not dry up, which is empty of depletion. [The Vṛtti adds:]
Canals, springs of that same nature, and inexhaustible waterfalls arise by the thousands.
[The addition from the Vṛtti ends here. In this regard, concerning those partial incarnations (*aṃśāvatāra*), this is the distinction:

It should be understood that among the authorized beings such as the venerable Kumāra, Nārada, and others, there is an infusion of portions of the powers of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) and devotion (*bhakti-śakti*);
while among the venerable Pṛthu and others, there is an infusion of a portion of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
In some cases, there is a direct descent [of power] upon them, as indicated by their statement, "I am the Blessed One himself.
This refers, for example, to the venerable Matsyadeva and others.
It is indeed direct partiality (*sākṣād-aṃśatvam*). In this context, "partiality" means that although He is directly the Lord Himself,
by virtue of His unerring will of that kind, His powers are manifested at all times as being only in one part.
It should be understood that this refers to being the "first" (ādikatva).
This will be illustrated accordingly in the passage: "Abiding in the forms of Rāma and others according to the rule of the *kalās*" (BrahmaS 5.50). [27]
Then he describes the manifestations:
"The sages, the Manus, the gods, the sons of Manu, and those of great power— all these,
along with the Prajāpatis, are known as but portions of Hari."

The *kalās* are manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*). The distinction is that for one of limited power they are manifestations through illumination, whereas for one of great power they are states of possession (*āveśa*). [28]

Thus, having determined the Supreme Self along with His limbs, he now determines the Blessed Lord by way of His form, following the restatement of what has been said: "These are but partial expansions of the Person, but Kṛṣṇa is the Lord Himself" (BhP 1.3.28).
These are those previously mentioned; by the word "and" (ca), those not mentioned are also included, [all belonging] to the person first enumerated.
The portions and fractions of the Puruṣa:
some portions are themselves [primary] portions; they are twofold, being either direct portions or portions of portions.
Some are called "parts" (aṃśa) because they are entered by a portion [of the Lord], while others are manifestations of His powers (kalā-vibhūti).
As for Kṛṣṇa, he is described here as the twentieth incarnation.

"Bhagavān" means that He who is the Bhagavān is indeed the one who descended as a human being; this is the meaning. Here, because of the rule stating that "one should not state the predicate (vidheya) without first restating the subject (anuvāda)," once it is established that Kṛṣṇa alone possesses the attributes characterized by the nature of the Bhagavān, His status as the original source of descent (mūlāvatāritva) is thereby established, and not otherwise.
The state of having become manifest;
this very point he clarifies with the word "himself" (svayam).
And in that context, it is by himself alone.

The meaning is that [he is] the Blessed One, but not by virtue of having appeared as the Blessed One, nor by way of superimposing the state of being the Blessed One. Nor is there any doubt because it is recited even in the section concerning the descent [of the Buddha]. Regarding the sequence of what precedes and what follows, the former—

This is because of the principle that "weakness [is determined] by its nature," as in the Vedic scripture regarding the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice: "If the Udgātṛ should fail, one should sacrifice without a sacrificial fee; if the Pratihartṛ should fail, one should sacrifice with all one's possessions as the fee. And of those two...

Just as in some cases, when a conflict arises between two contradictory penances and their simultaneous performance (samuccaya) is impossible, the later penance alone is established as the rule, so it is here as well;
or else, because the context is set aside by the scriptural statement, "But Kṛṣṇa... (kṛṣṇas tu).

As it is stated in Śaṅkara’s *Śārīrakabhāṣya* on the sūtra [3.3.50]: "And because of the superior authority of the Śruti and other means, there is no sublation," [it is explained that] the Śruti passage, "These indeed are piled by knowledge alone," [sublates] the mental fires (*manaś-cid-ādi*) which have been introduced by the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Even in the section on the entry into action (*kriyānupraveśa-prakaraṇa*), he did not use the word "Lord" (*bhagavat*) anywhere else, but instead used the phrase,
"Right there the Lord took up the burden" (*tatraiva bhagavān aharad bharam*,
BhP 1.3.23). Consequently, because He is counted among the incarnations (*avatāra*), even though He is the Supreme Lord Himself, He remains established in His own essential nature (*svarūpa-stha*).

It follows that He manifests as visible to the entire world only with the intention of nourishing a certain sweetness— through His pastimes such as His own birth— in order to produce a particular wonder of bliss for the multitude of His own attendants.
As it is said in the Brahma-saṃhitā:
"Abiding in the forms of Rāma and others according to the regulation of His portions (kalās), He manifested various incarnations in the worlds; however—"

Kṛṣṇa himself became the Supreme Person; I worship that Govinda, the primordial Person (ādi-puruṣa). And regarding the incarnations, it is said in the *Prākṛta-vaibhava*: "An incarnation (avataraṇa)..."
By virtue of his association with Śrī Kṛṣṇa, it should be understood that even Śrī Rāma’s status as a partial plenary portion (puruṣāṃśa) is transcended;
here, however, the word "tu" [indicates] from among the portions and digits of the Supreme Person.
And this indicates a distinction from the Blessed One;
or rather, by this word "tu," it is understood that this scriptural statement is restrictive.

Therefore, by the principle that "a scriptural statement with a restrictive particle is more powerful," the very fact that other deities such as Mahānārāyaṇa and others are themselves the Blessed Lord— even though it is heard in scripture— is rendered subordinate by that very same scriptural authority.

Thus, by means of that very word which was mentioned alongside them, [the author] causes one to remember that these two are indeed those same two words—namely "of the person" (*puṃsaḥ*) and "the Blessed One" (*bhagavān*)—which were first introduced at the outset; for there is a recognition of identity between the initial mention and the subsequent reference. In order to eliminate the notion of being obscured,
scholars employ either the same word or a word with the same phonemes; for example,
in the section concerning the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, in the passage "One should sacrifice with the Jyotis [sacrifice] every spring," the word *jyotis* is used.
"It pertains to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
Regarding this, the teachers of the Tattvavāda school, however, read the word "sva" (own) in place of the word "ca" (and), and explain it as follows:
"These aforementioned [beings] are the incarnations."
He is the one who possesses the fundamental form himself;
what is his nature?
He is not a mere fraction of his own parts.
But [these] parts are distinct from the individual soul (jīva), as stated in the Vārāha-purāṇa:
"A part is held to be of two kinds: one's own part (svāṃśa) and a distinct part (vibhinnāṃśa)."
Whatever is the capacity of the possessor of parts, whatever its essential nature, and however it exists—
"Therefore, there is not even an atom's worth of difference anywhere between the parts and the whole.

A part that is distinct would have little power; it would be endowed with only a fraction of the capacity [of the whole]. To this, it is replied: the power and other attributes of the parts must be understood as being identical with those of the whole. In that regard:
Just as in the passage beginning with "like a non-drying [river]," their imperishability follows from His imperishability, so too is it because the relationship of part and whole is untenable;
and thus it is in every respect between Śrī Vāsudeva and Aniruddha.
If identity were to follow, then there would occasionally have to be the manifestation of Śrī Vāsudeva even from Aniruddha;
and since that contradicts the Vedas, it is simply not the case.
Therefore, there is indeed a gradation between the one who causes to descend and the one who descends;
for this very reason, it is stated in the third and eighth [chapters]:
To the primordial Lord Saṅkarṣaṇa, the deity of unimpeded being, seated upon the earth, they approached,
desiring to know the reality that lies beyond him.
The sages, headed by Kumāra, questioned him.
"In that which they call Vāsudeva, who highly honors his own very abode," and so forth;
in such passages, the supremacy of Vāsudeva even over Saṅkarṣaṇa is heard.
As for their interpretation in that manner, here the phrase "Kṛṣṇa, however" would be redundant;
[it should rather mean] "the Blessed One himself."

For the intended goal is accomplished by this very [argument]. Furthermore, in the sūtra "Moreover, for them, another [cognition] is not [perceived], just as [the cognition itself is] self-luminous" (Vs 2.3.45), the distinction between part and whole is clearly demonstrated.
Even though He is a partial manifestation (*aṃśa*), the Supreme Lord in the form of the Fish and others is not like this— that is, He is not similar to the individual soul (*jīva*)—
just as the sun, which is a portion of light, is not like a firefly.
And because [the difference] is not of a single kind, as stated by the words "and not of one type," etc.,
therefore, since the difference is established, it is rightly explained that "Kṛṣṇa, however, is the Blessed Lord himself."
In that case, the half-verse beginning with "indrārī" does not connect [with the rest],
because the sentence is divided by the word "tu," and because the expectancy is fulfilled by that much alone.
If, however, there were a single syntactical unity (*eka-vākyatva*), the word "ca" (and) alone would have been used.
Consequently, in the phrase "indrāryaḥ," it follows by implication that those very ones previously mentioned are the ones who grant bliss (*mṛḍayanti*).
Śrī Sūta said: 2.28 [29]
Thus, it has been established that the Blessed Śrī Kṛṣṇa, as the Puruṣa, is indeed the Supreme Self (Paramātman) because He is the inner controller (antaryāmin) of all.
In this regard, an objection is raised: "But is this not merely a single statement intended to establish His status as the possessor of parts (aṃśin)?"
In the face of contradiction with many statements establishing [the Lord's] being a partial incarnation (aṃśatva), it would be a figurative statement (guṇavāda).
To this it is replied: Are those [statements] from the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam or from the works of others?

Indeed, this first chapter, the "Secret of Birth," is the aphorism for all the statements concerning the incarnations of the Blessed Lord, because it indicates them through its initial recitation and because they serve as its subsequent elaboration.
And in that regard, there is the technical definition that "these [others] are portions and fractions of the Person (puruṣa).
Thus, one should understand other individuals mentioned in the accounts of descents (avatāra) as being portions of the Person;
however, Kṛṣṇa is the Person himself.

"By way of being the Blessed One" means by way of making a formal proposition (*pratijñākāreṇa*), because it determines the meaning of the text. As it has been said: "A technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is that which establishes a restriction where there was none.
Now, a technical rule is recited only once in a treatise, not through repetition. [The Vṛtti adds:]
Just as in the case of a negation, the subsequent [rule] takes effect;
and consequently, even the entire range of sentences would have to be taught by this one alone. Thus, rather than being a figurative statement (*guṇavāda*), this [is not so].

The scholarly proficiency regarding those things that appear contradictory is precisely for the sake of making them consistent; nor should that usage be understood as restricted solely to that specific treatise because it is technical terminology—
it is not "secondary" (gauṇa) in every respect.
This is to be expected, because the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavata* is devoted to the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-vastu*) (page 10),
and because that technical definition is also implied therein.
Furthermore, various [interpretations] of the mere statement of the proposition (*pratijñā-vākya*) are observed elsewhere as well.
It consists in the sublation of other statements;

for example, the scriptural teaching of the non-origination of space and the scriptural teaching regarding the vital breaths (prāṇas) are mutually contradictory, as is any other scripture stating that "when the Self is known, all this is known."
"This entire world is what this Self is" (BAU 2.4.6), and so forth, [the world] is sublated;
for this very reason, even by Svāmī and others, this very same statement is applied to each respective [case].
In order to dispel contradictions, this very point has been demonstrated again and again;
thus, since the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavata* is established in its own system as possessing the greatest authority— because it is understood in the first section to be the sublater of all other scriptures.
Furthermore, because they are about to enter upon this very path, it is observed by learned people that even those belonging to others are in conformity with this;
for just as it is so for a king, so too it is for his followers.
In this regard, the statements from the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam* are presented as being consistent with that meaning.
Regarding the phrase "of him who has descended in part" (*BhP* 10.1.2), the meaning is "together with Baladeva, who is his partial expansion.
Regarding the phrase "the two parts of Hari" (*BhP* 10.20.48), the earth is a part (*kalā*) of Hari.
"By these two, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa"— [he said]—
"'by good fortune, O Mother, the Supreme Person has entered your womb.'"

Regarding the verse, "May the Lord himself appear before us as a partial incarnation for our welfare" (BhP 10.2.41): O Mother, He who previously appeared for our welfare through partial incarnations such as the Fish and others, He is now present within your womb as the Lord Himself in person.
Regarding the phrase "then the auspiciousness of the world, a portion of Acyuta," this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the locative case denotes a different referent (*saptamy-anya-padārtha*).
This is because it will be explained that when that whole (the possessor of the parts) descends, those parts also enter therein.
It has been stated there that, by virtue of being complete, [the Lord] is the self of all and has become their very self. And likewise, in the words of those who are not overly learned:
"These two are indeed directly from the Blessed Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa."

"In these two, who have descended here by a portion (*aṃśa*) into the house of Vasudeva"—here too, the meaning is that they have come "by a portion" together with their "entire portion" (*sarvāṃśa*), as they were impelled by Sarasvatī. It is exactly so:
"These two indeed have come here as portions of the Blessed Lord Hari."
Regarding the verse, "And for the removal of the earth's burden, the two Kṛṣṇas, the best of the Yadus and Kurus,
arrived" (BhP 4.1.59), here the suffix *niṣṭhā* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) in the word *āgatau*,
while the accusative case is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*) in the word *kṛṣṇau*. And thus...

Of the Blessed One Hari, the Supreme Person, who is the seed of various incarnations, these two known as Nara and Nārāyaṇa have come as His instrumental portions (aṃśau) acting as agents, while Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna have come as His objective portions (karma-bhūtau); the meaning is that they have entered into those two.
Of what nature were the two Kṛṣṇas? For the removal of the earth's burden; and by the word "ca" (and), for the sake of various other pastimes that bestow happiness upon their devotees.
The meaning is that the two leaders of the Yadu and Kuru lineages have descended into the families of Yadu and Kuru;
however, in Arjuna there is an entry of a human being, whereas Kṛṣṇa is Nārāyaṇa himself.
Such is the scriptural statement regarding the venerable Arjuna with respect to his entry into a human body;
however, as for Nārāyaṇa himself, who is not established by anything else, [it is said]: "You are indeed Nārāyaṇa, yet you are not [the same as] Nārāyaṇa for all embodied beings" (BhP 10.14.14).

This has been shown by such passages as the above. Furthermore, that [state] is to be understood as "dark" (kṛṣṇa) in relation to other objects, according to the principle expressed in [BhP 10.60.15]: "For those two alone there is equality and reversal," and so forth.
Likewise, in the Viṣṇudharma:
"He who knows you knows me; he who follows you follows me.
O son of Pāṇḍu, I know you as non-different from myself."

In that regard, according to the words of the Blessed Lord, because Arjuna is also a friend of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, his entry there is entirely appropriate, as he is more complete than a human being who is merely a friend of Nārāyaṇa.
Furthermore, in certain places, there are terms such as "partial incarnation" (aṃśa) and so forth.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: according to the direction of the Śrī Gītā Upaniṣad, "I am not manifest to everyone, being veiled by my own yoga-māyā" (Gītā 7.15), even though He is complete, there is a manifestation of only a partial portion to ordinary people;
therefore, it should be understood that in His perception by them, He appears as if He were merely a part, even though He is the whole. (Page 11)
Even in the passage, "Equal to Nārāyaṇa in qualities" (BhP 10.8.19), Garga’s intention is that he is one for whom Nārāyaṇa— the Lord of the Supreme Abode— is equal in qualities.
Thus, even in the narrative of Mahākālapura, one should apply this declarative statement.
Furthermore, a treatise (śāstra) is indeed characterized by its nature of instruction (śāsana).
And the teaching is the instruction;
it is twofold: direct and by means of another thing.
Direct instruction, however, is revelation (śruti).
It is explained that "directness" (sākṣāttva) here refers to independence;
thus it has been said: "independent..."
"Direct assertion is the hearing [of the word].

And this being so, it is stated in the *Jaiminī-sūtra*: "In the case of a conflict between direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyā*), each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding because of its remoteness from the purpose."

In accordance with what was stated [in 3.3.14], if the final word were intended to convey distance from the preceding one, then Śrī Sūta’s direct instruction to Śrī Śaunaka— namely, "But Kṛṣṇa is the Lord Himself"— would contradict the instruction given by way of the Itihāsa.

Nor should it be said that the Lord of Mahākālapura himself directly instructed Śrī Kṛṣṇa, as in the verse, "And [the two of them] have descended into my [lineage] as Kalāvatī... For Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s omniscience is never subject to deviation; therefore, [such an instruction] would necessarily involve the relationship of speaker and listener.
"By the occasion of the *saṅgama*, my daughter, desiring to see you both..."—
and by the observation of the intent toward another matter;
and of this *Mahāpurāṇa*.

This is because, like the Sūta and others who instruct in the principles [of the Purāṇas], there is no intention (tātparya) regarding that instruction, and because the words are connected in proximity only to another meaning which will be explained later.
Furthermore, even if— let it be so according to the logic of "let him be pleased"— Śrī Kṛṣṇa were incomplete in relation to him;

Nevertheless, because all incarnations are shown to be eternally established in their own natural state (*svastha*), and because according to some views they remain independent even when manifesting as human beings (*puruṣatva*);
The statements, "You two are the sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa" (BhP 10.89.59) and "Hasten near to me" (BhP 10.89.59), would be contradicted if they were intended for those respective purposes.
Let there be, for now, some other news for us; nor is it narrated anywhere that this Mahākāla has descended in part in various forms.
Furthermore, this would entail the postulation of something unestablished;
for in that very case, there would be two separate injunctions: "Hasten to him who is near me," and "May you two, the sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa, practice dharma."
The mutual contradiction is indeed evident.

Therefore, this too is an additional [argument].
On the contrary, by virtue of being His power (*śakti*), fullness itself is logically established.

Even so, as for Arjuna’s eyes being struck by that light and his state of being overcome with awe born from seeing it— that was [intended] by the Blessed One Himself as a means for the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of those respective divine pastimes (*līlā*).
There is no contradiction, because while one power is manifested, another, though present, is blunted;
and it is observed that even for oneself, defeat and the like may occur at times by an ordinary opponent in battle,
as in this very case.
Thus, even for horses that have come directly from Vaikuṇṭha themselves, their path is lost through the influence of material darkness;
such indeed is the power of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s burden of devotion toward him.
It should not be thought otherwise even by seeing [the texts],
because it is seen to be so in the *Śrī-rudra* and other such works, as well as in the *Śrī-nārada* and others.
Thus, whether here or elsewhere, there is no prima facie objection (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding His pastimes, because they constitute His own natural activity (*svarācaraṇa*).
Therefore, His intended meaning (*tātparya*)— [page 12]...

The two meanings arising from the word are seen in this very way. That which arises from its purport is as follows: although Śrī Kṛṣṇa is himself the Supreme Lord, for the sake of the wonderful amazement of the assembly of cowherds during the pastime of the Govardhana sacrifice, he [manifested] a certain aspect of Himself...
Displaying his divine form, he bowed to himself by means of those very forms;

likewise, for the sake of Arjuna’s wonder and curiosity, having caused the sons of the twice-born to be carried away by himself in the form of Mahākāla, and having manifested various miracles along the way, [he appeared] in the city of Mahākāla.
And having revealed to her that certain divine form of his own known as Mahākāla, he bowed down to himself in that form together with him;
likewise, he bowed to himself in that very form along with Arjuna.

And He spoke: as it is said, "He paid homage to Him with His own self along with the people of Vraja" (BhP 10.24.36); and here too, "The Infallible One bound Himself, who is infinite" (BhP 10.89.31). For this very reason, in the *Harivaṃśa*, Śrī [Kṛṣṇa], referring to that light in His presence, spoke to Arjuna:
Kṛṣṇa said: "That eternal splendor is mine" (HV 2.114.9).

Now, there is also a meaning arising from the word itself, as in the case of the meaning of the qualifier in the passage: "pointing toward Śrī Mahākāla, the most excellent of the Supreme Persons" (BhP 10.89.54).

The individual soul (jīva) is superior to that [body]; the inner controller (antaryāmī) is superior to that; and superior to that is He, who consists of the power of Mahākāla, which is the form of the Lord’s own majesty.
Now, from the words of Śrī Mahākāla:
"My daughter, born of a brahmin, was brought by me to this earth out of a desire for you both to behold her, for the protection of Dharma."
"Having descended with your portions (kalā) and having slain the demons who burdened the earth, come here again and hasten toward me.
Thus, O sons of a brahmin, desiring to see you both, I have brought you here to my abode on earth.
"Upanītā" and "ānītā" constitute one sentence.

He states another sentence: "O you two who have descended for the protection of Dharma," [the compound] "kalāvatīrṇau" means "endowed with parts (kalāḥ = aṃśāḥ), having descended"; this is a case of the elision of the middle term (madhyama-pada-lopī).

A summary: Or rather, they have descended into the illusory manifestation (māyika-prapañca), which is a portion or a characteristic part of the totality, according to the Vedic revelation: "A foot of Him are all beings" (Rg Veda 10.90.3).
Furthermore, they have descended again from the earth, being without distinction.
"Having slain the Bhārāsuras, urge both of you to hasten— hasten— to come into my presence, near me;

Because liberation is established for those who have attained that state;

And because of the statement in the *Śrī-Harivaṃśa*: "That great, divine, and effulgent [form] which you have seen" (*tejomayaṃ divyaṃ mahad yad dṛṣṭavān asi*);

and the form *tvarayetam* is the optative (*liṅ*) of the causative (*hetu-ṇij-anta*) used in the sense of a request (*prārthanā*), with the elision of the fourth case ending after the indeclinable *anti*.

And there is a fourth [interpretation], based on the grammatical rule *kriyārthopapadasya ca karmaṇi sthāninaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.14), which states that [the dative case is used] for the object of a word that is subordinate to another action, as in the example "he goes for fuel" (*edhobhyo vrajati*).
It is also like the example "having made a mat, he sends it away" (*kaṭaṃ kṛtvā prasthāpayati*), where both [actions] are involved.
The connection [of words] occurs through a single action alone;
therefore, a single meaning becomes clearly and effortlessly established.
However, when another meaning is possible, the division of a single word into separate words is considered a laborious construction.

Even the two Ṛṣabhas, the most excellent among all those who descend through incarnations,
though their desires were already fulfilled, remained for the sake of stability and the protection of the world, in order to sustain the world by means of the propagation of various dharmas therein.

Among those who practice and perform dharma, you two are the sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa; thus, they are designated as "manifestations" (vibhūti) by virtue of possessing only a small portion [of His nature].

Because you are the foremost among the righteous, you will certainly come for the sake of the son of the twice-born; it was for this very reason that I made such a resolve.

Regarding the rule *mune* [Pāṇini 5.2.59], the Mahābhārata [1.189.31–32] states:
"And Hari plucked out two hairs, one white and the other black."
Those two hairs entered the wombs of Rohiṇī and Devakī among the women of the Yadu clan;
of those two, one became Balabhadra.
That which was white was the hair (*keśa*) of that god;
the second, Kṛṣṇa, became Keśava—the hair which, by its color, is said to be black. Thus.
Regarding this, the intended meaning has been explained by the masters as follows in the verse beginning with *bhūmeḥ suretara-varūtha* (BhP 2.7.26):
in the phrase "one whose hair is white and black," the state of having white and black hair is merely for the sake of beauty.
However, that which was caused by the transformation of age is [not a true change] because of his immutability;
and as for the statement "he plucked out his own hair" and so forth,
that does not intend to refer to an incarnation consisting merely of hair, but rather to the task in the form of relieving the earth's burden.

It is understood that the lifting of the hair was intended to demonstrate that even his own hair alone was capable of performing that task, and also to indicate the respective complexions of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa;
for Kṛṣṇa is indeed the Blessed Lord.
"By oneself" and "because of contradiction"—this [explanation] is also possible as the intended meaning here. [Objection:
But for what purpose are you being seized by you all, O gods, in order to rescue me alone?

Of me— who am known as Aniruddha, the manifestation of the Supreme Person, whose abode is the White Island in the Ocean of Milk— those two who are like my own hair, to be borne upon their respective heads by [my devotees], namely Śrī Vāsudeva and Saṅkarṣaṇa, shall themselves descend.
Consequently, the removal of the burden of the earth was indeed easy for them both;
thus, the meaning of the very words "then he plucked out his own two hairs" is also established.
In the *Muktāphala-ṭīkā*, it is said that Keśava, the Lord of Bliss, being white, extracted [the hair] from his own body;
for in the *Harivaṃśa*, the Blessed One, having deposited his own form in a certain mountain cave, [sent] Garuḍa...
And it has been stated that he himself came here after having established him there;
thus it was said: "Having given leave to the gods," and so forth.
However, those who have explained this exactly as they heard it have not grasped it correctly; for even a mere god is well-known to be subject to decay.
Since the Blessed One is untouched by time, the emergence of old age is impossible, and consequently, the whiteness of his hair cannot logically occur. Nor does he...
There is authoritative evidence that hair is naturally white or black;
for this very reason, in the *Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa*, in the context of the Kṛṣṇa incarnation, the word *śakti* alone is employed and not the word *keśa*. To illustrate:
"And descending from Vasudeva into Devakī in the family of Yadu,
my two powers, Śita and Kṛṣṇa, will cause Kaṃsa and the others to be slain" (NṛsiṃhaP 53.30–31),
and so forth. Let it be, then, that the word *keśa* indicates a portion [of the Lord].
No,
because [He] can be ascertained as the Primordial Person (*ādi-puruṣa*) by virtue of His possessing all powers unimpaired and being Kṛṣṇa-Viṣṇu.
Because the word "etcetera" (ādi) implies no distinction and because synonyms are understood [from it],
the birth day of no other incarnation or any other person whatsoever is as renowned by the name "Jayantī" as this one.
Therefore it is said in the Bhārata:
"And here the Lord Vāsudeva is celebrated as the eternal,
the supreme, everlasting Brahman, the stainless object of meditation for yogis."

Regarding its being fashioned by time, in the speech of the venerable Queen Devakī beginning with, "O friend of the unmanifest, they say that this which is called 'time' is Your activity" (BhP 10.3.26),
she says: "O Lord, we bow always to Your lotus feet."
It is worshipped by Viriñci, Vairiñca, and the lords of the gods;
it is the supreme refuge for those desiring security here,
where Time, the supreme lord, has no power.
This is well known from such passages as the speech of the residents of Śrī-Dvārakā;
therefore, that which is shown in the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa regarding the hair being merely "childlike" (bāla) is simply a demonstration of whiteness characterized by the graying caused by time.

Because it falls within a section dedicated to establishing the white detachment (*śukla-vairāgya*) of embodied beings, and because it is well-known as referring only to gods and non-liberated beings (*nirjara*), its meaning is not primary; therefore,
it lacks authority regarding its own literal sense.
Beginning with "By whom Brahmā... and so forth:
"By whom Viṣṇu was cast into great peril during the undertaking of his ten incarnations;
by whom Rudra, skull-in-hand, was made to wander for alms on all sides. [GarP 1.113.15]
"In passages such as this, [the phrase] 'homage to that action' is [said] because of the words of Garuḍa;
however, this is merely a deceptive statement based on a verbal similarity for the purpose of establishing that [point]. For example:"
"Aha! Who could possibly describe the wickedness of gold?
For despite its identical name, this [gold] causes intoxication even when it has been thoroughly rubbed away.
Furthermore, because it belongs to the Śiva scriptures, there is no use here for that which contradicts the Vaiṣṇava tenets; for...
It was stated by Śrī Śiva himself to Ṣaṇmukha in the Skanda Purāṇa: "Even in the Śiva-śāstra, that which is consistent with the Bhagavat-śāstra should be accepted.
This is because [the former] lacks intrinsic authority there, as its primary intent lies elsewhere.
And this is logical, as in the verse beginning, "Just as mud [is cleansed] by muddy water" (BhP 1.8.52).
Furthermore, in the *Pādmottara-khaṇḍa*, even those Purāṇas that propound Śiva are shown to be purely tāmasa;
likewise, in the *Mātsya*, it is stated that they consist of the narratives of the tāmasa kalpas. And this is appropriate for that [text], as it is ancient.

The speech arising from an incorrect understanding of the reality of the Blessed Lord by one who has not studied the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam* of Sūta and who disregards Śrī Baladeva is spoken of as follows: "O royal sage, some sages endowed with wisdom say...

and so forth, [the claim] of the vacana, "We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal" (RgV 8.48.3), and so forth, is sublated.
It should be understood as being like a contradiction;
here too, because of the presence of reasoning, it is seen that "whatever contradicts your own words, they surely do not remember that" (BhP 10.77.30).
In that very passage, doubt regarding the self was indeed suggested by that charioteer:
"Those entities which are truly inconceivable, one should not [speculate about them]..."
By the passage beginning with "one should apply [this] through reasoning," and furthermore,
because in that very subsequent section— where the cause for the occurrence of the blemish is stated in the context of the descent of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—
it is explicitly said, "He is Viṣṇu himself," there is a contradiction with his own words. Therefore, it is not [so].

Even though the word *keśa* refers to hair, its intended meaning here is "hairiness" (*bālatva*), either by way of a pun (*chala*) or due to ignorance of the true nature of the Blessed One (*bhagavat-tattva*). Therefore,
the literal meaning of the verses of the Vaiṣṇavas and others is as follows:
"Behold— those rays which shine forth are designated as my hair (keśa).
Therefore, O best of sages, they call me Keśava because I am all-knowing."
Thus, from the statement in the *Bhārata* as cited in the commentary on the *Sahasranāma*, the word "hair" (*keśa*) denotes a ray of light;
for in that context, no term other than "hair" is used anywhere, and it is well known in the *Mokṣadharma* that Śrī Nārada (p. 15) beheld rays of various colors.

Thus, since their status as rays has been established, and since those two rays are specified as indicating the incarnations of Vāsudeva and Saṅkarṣaṇa, it is understood that they must belong to those two alone.
The manifestation of those two within Aniruddha is indeed logical, because the descent (avatāra) is included within the light that has been brought down.
In this very way, [the qualities] sattva, rajas, and tamas [are explained]. (BhP 1.2.23)

Thus, Bhava’s status as an incarnation of the person named Aniruddha, as established by the verse in the first book (*skandha*) beginning with [BhP 5.17.16], and his status as an incarnation of Saṅkarṣaṇa, as established by the prose passage in the fifth book (*skandha*), are both consistent.
And thus, the meaning of the phrase "he drew forth" (ujjahāra) is this:
from his own self, he drew forth—that is, extracted and manifested—two hairs (*keśau*), which were portions (*aṃśau*) of Śrī Vāsudeva and Saṅkarṣaṇa. This is the meaning.

In this context, just as the term "Sumeru" refers to the entire undivided mountain by the mention of only a single part, so too, by the mention of that [one aspect], the manifestation of the whole should be understood.

and by the word "also" (*ca*) in the phrase "those two also," there is an inclusion of what was not explicitly stated, signifying that the Blessed Lord and Saṅkarṣaṇa themselves entered [them].
It indicates that subsequently, those two entered into identity with that [object];

thus Keśava is renowned in Śrī Mathurā as the sovereign of the great yoga-pīṭha known as Keśavasthāna.

The scriptural statement,
"Kṛṣṇa is Nārāyaṇa himself," refers to the entry of Nara into Arjuna, whereas [the statement] regarding Kṛṣṇa refers to the entry of Nārāyaṇa into Kṛṣṇa.
But as for Nārāyaṇa, who is established as being otherwise [than Kṛṣṇa] by himself— as shown in such passages as "You are not Nārāyaṇa, for you are not among all embodied beings"—
he must be understood as Kṛṣṇa only in relation to another referent. For this very reason:
Even the statement from the *Śrī Hari-vaṃśa* regarding the arrival of Puruṣa-Nārāyaṇa was spoken with the intention of describing the extraction of His splendor;

"I have been asked by you about the welfare of the world;

Only the capacity to denote [the Lord] is obtained.

thus, "the Blessed One" refers to this very person, and these [beings] are but partial manifestations (*aṃśa-kalā*) of that Supreme Person, while Kṛṣṇa is [the Lord himself].

In this context, it should be understood that the conclusion is "the Blessed One himself. For example, regarding the mantras known as *ādhvaras*, such as "May Agni, knowing [the way], lead the sacrifice," and so forth, [the conclusion pertains to] the *ādhvaryava* [priesthood].

In the dialogue with Nārada;

and in the table of contents of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, this occurs increasingly more frequently throughout the later sections.

This scripture is named *Bhāgavata* because it is its expositor;
moreover, it is not merely indicated here and there, but rather more than half of the entire work is devoted to its practice.

therefore, it was rightly said: "And these shoulders..."
"Kṛṣṇa, however, is the Lord himself, the source of all parts (kalās) of the Supreme Person.

as it has been said: "In the house of Vasudeva, the Supreme Person, the Blessed Lord himself [was born]" (BhP 10.1.23).

Or as in: "O, what fortune! O, what fortune! and so forth (BhP 10.14.32).

10.14 // Śrī-Brahmā said to the Blessed One: // 75 // [76] Therefore—
You Yourself, O Lord of the three worlds, are without equal and beyond all excellence.
Having attained all desires through the splendor of sovereign self-rule,
the soles of his feet were massaged by the tips of the crowns of the long-enduring world-protectors as they brought him tribute.

The meaning is that for Him there is neither equality nor superiority, such that in relation to Him no other thing possesses either equality or superiority. The reasons for this are: He is the Lord of the Three (tryadhīśa), being the sovereign even over the three [expansions]—Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha; because He is the part-whole of all, He is therefore endowed with the Sovereignty-Lakṣmī, which is the supreme bliss exceeding all else.
Having obtained all enjoyments through the very perfection of his own nature,
he was gazed upon by the world-protectors, who for long had been offering him worship in the form of tribute consisting of compliance with his will.
In comparison, Brahmā and the others are but short-lived world-protectors due to their impermanence; therefore,
he is one whose footstool is praised and lauded by the tips of the crowns of those long-enduring world-protectors who are the inner controllers (antaryāmin) within infinite universes.
The meaning is "supremely excellent" by means of *atyantatiraskṛtavācyadhvani* (suggestion where the expressed meaning is completely set aside),
even when the entire verse is recited (page 29).
This is the very same meaning;
by the term "Śrī-Kṛṣṇa," he reveals his own status as the Supreme Lord (Bhagavān), just as in the phrase "Kṛṣṇa, however, is the Bhagavān himself."
// 3.2 // The illustrious Uddhava to Vidura // 76 // [77] This very fullness has also been demonstrated by means of an illustration:
"In Devakī, who was of divine form, Viṣṇu, who dwells in the cave of all hearts..."

the meaning is that he appeared exactly as he is, in his own true nature.

Just as Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Yadus, surrounded by the circle of the Vṛṣṇis, [dwells] on earth—this is clear. 10.20. Śrī Śuka said: 78.
[79] Likewise, because this Mahāpurāṇa is the very form of the representative of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, it is Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself.
He also said that this is the primary subject matter:
"Now this sun of the Purāṇas has risen for those whose vision is lost in the Kali age, when Kṛṣṇa had departed to his own abode along with dharma, knowledge, and the rest. [BhP 1.3.43]
This is clear. 1.3. Śrī Sūta: 79.
[80] Thus, in this way, the fact that Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the Supreme Lord Himself has been demonstrated;
and that is so even by the commonality of their destination.
It is obtained; as it is said in the Mahābhārata:
"All the Vedas, all branches of knowledge, all scriptures, all sacrifices, and all objects of worship are Kṛṣṇa."
"O King, for those Brahmins who know Kṛṣṇa according to reality, all ignorance is completely ended.
In this passage, because of the establishment of the harmony of all [scriptures], perfection itself is obtained.

Likewise, in the Śrī Bhagavad-upaniṣad: "By all the Vedas, I alone am to be known; I am indeed the author of the Vedanta and the knower of the Vedas" (BhG 15.15), and also: "For I am the foundation of Brahman" (BhG 14.27), and so forth.

In the *Brahma-saṃhitā* (5.29), beginning with the words: "While he protects the Surabhis in palaces made of heaps of wish-fulfilling gems, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of desire-trees," and continuing:
"Taking as his support the duration of even a single exhalation of his..."
"The lords of the cosmic eggs live by the hair-pores of that Great Viṣṇu, of whom Govinda, the primordial Person, is a specific manifestation; him I worship. [BrahmaS 5.30]

Now, it might be argued that in the *Pādmottara-khaṇḍa* and other texts, it is heard that Nārāyaṇa alone is the sovereign of the supreme realm (*para-vyoman*) and the source of all incarnations; whereas in the *Pañcarātra* and other scriptures, it is Vāsudeva who is mentioned, and it cannot be said that he is none other than Kṛṣṇa. To this, we reply: that is indeed so.
Because of the differences in location, retinue, name, and form,
how then can Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone possess the status of being all incarnations or the status of being the Self-Bhagavān?
Regarding this, it is said that the sovereignty of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam over all scriptures was demonstrated by a single section in the first compendium;
it was revealed by the venerable Vedavyāsa immediately after the manifestation of complete knowledge.
And it is well-known in that very context;
moreover, its capacity to supersede other treatises is clearly seen in this work.
Thus some explain this, having forgotten what was previously cited:
"In the abode of the sage’s dwelling, how could the sight of an ill omen be possible? (BhP 10.57.31), and so forth;
and they speak thus: "O royal sage" (BhP 10.77.30), and so forth.
Therefore, it is also stated in the Ninth Canto:
"Leaving behind his own disciples, Paila and the others, the blessed Bādarāyaṇa proclaimed this supreme secret to me, his peaceful son" (BhP 9.22.22).
Thus, it is established that [the title "Bhagavān"] is applied metaphorically to all scriptures;
therein, the status of Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone as the self-manifested Bhagavān is determined.
Moreover, it is observed that through the excellence of the praiser, there is also the excellence of the praised;
just as, for example, by virtue of being the most supreme in both the village headman’s assembly and the royal court.
Two specific objects being praised enter into a state of relative gradation.
Thus, even though those other praiseworthy things exist elsewhere, [the praise] of the Śrī-Bhāgavata—being praised [here]—is [superior]. Śrī...
The supreme supremacy of Kṛṣṇa alone is established;
therefore, it was correctly explained previously that the scriptural statement "Kṛṣṇa, however, is the Lord Himself," which contains a restrictive particle (*tu*), sublates other scriptural passages.
Moreover, therefore, those such as Nārāyaṇa and Vāsudeva, the lords of the supreme ether, must be specific manifestations of Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, being addressed as "You are Nārāyaṇa" and so forth,
becomes Mahānārāyaṇa, who is renowned in Dvārakā and elsewhere as Mahāvāsudeva; consequently,
he alone is clearly manifested in the Nārāyaṇa and Vāsudeva Upaniṣads.
"He is the friend of Brahman, the son of Devakī" (NāU 4),
and "May the delighter of Devakī gladden everything"—
it is precisely in this way that he [should be understood].
He also explicitly states that Vāsudeva himself is non-different from the divine manifestations (vibhūti), clearly saying: "Vāsudeva is the foremost among the Blessed Lords" (BhP 11.19.29).
Likewise—
"I am the supreme primordial form of the nine forms of the Sātvatas," [BhP 11.19.32].

And the commentary states: "Of the Sātvatas, that is, the Bhāgavatas, in the worship of the nine-fold manifestation (navavyūha), they are Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Nārāyaṇa, Hayagrīva, Varāha, Nṛsiṃha, and Brahmā."

Among those nine forms, the one called Vāsudeva is this [central form]. For this very reason, even in the ritual manuals for the worship of Vyāsa followed by renunciants who profess non-dualism (advaitavādin),
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is seen occupying the central throne, while Vāsudeva and the others, as well as Vyāsa and the rest, occupy the surrounding positions.
Regarding the status of being a deity:
for this very reason, in the *Kramadīpikā*, within the chapter on the eight-syllable mantra, Vāsudeva and the others are mentioned as belonging to that [central deity's] enclosure (*āvaraṇa*).
As for the statement in the Bhagavad-upaniṣad, "Among the Vṛṣṇis, I am Vāsudeva" (Gītā 10.37),
there the word *vāsudeva* is used in the sense of being the offspring of Vasudeva, [referring to] Śrī-...
Baladeva alone is spoken of;

and thus [he describes] his own vibhūti.
He says: even in that case, the attribution of such a manifestation is not tenable,
because the hearers perceive it as something entirely distinct from the speaker.

Therefore, when the primary meaning is sublated, such an interpretation is indeed appropriate. Consequently, it has been correctly explained: "Vāsudeva is the foremost among the Blessed Ones," and so forth. [BhP 11.19.29] // 11.19 // Śrī Bhagavān // 80–81 // [82]

Since his excellence is thus supreme in every respect, for that very reason the greatness of his name and other attributes is also superior compared to others; and another commonality of destiny is thereby obtained.
In this regard, as for the name, it is as follows:

In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, within the *Śrī-Kṛṣṇāṣṭottara-śata-nāmāmṛta-stotra*: "Whatever fruit is obtained by reciting the thousand meritorious names three times, a single name of Kṛṣṇa bestows that very same fruit with a single recitation. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, the superiority of the fruit of Kṛṣṇa’s name is made manifest in the Pātāla-khaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa,
within the Śrī-Mathurā-māhātmya, in the very words of Śrī Mahādeva: "Liberation arises from Tāraka, but loving devotion (prema-bhakti) arises from Pāraka."

Previously, in this context, the names Rāma and Kṛṣṇa were designated as "the Savior" (tāraka) and "the Deliverer" (pāraka) respectively, on account of their being the liberator and the giver of love;
and therein, regarding the name Rāma—

The meaning is that while the power of liberation alone is predominant in the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the power of bestowing the bliss of love— which eclipses even the happiness of liberation— is even more predominant.
Thus it has been stated in the Viṣṇu...
In the *Dharmottara*:
"O tiger among men, that which is called 'capacity' (śakti) is that which effects [an action] upon that very object, whether the objects be gentle or cruel."
Furthermore, the greatness of the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is heard even by mere recitation in the Prabhāsa Purāṇa,
within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Kuśadhvaja, in the words of the Blessed Lord: "O scorcher of foes, the name called Kṛṣṇa is the most preeminent among My names."
Thus, by way of the commonality of their destination and through the greatness of His name, the excellence of His greatness has been established;
likewise, [the same applies to] His qualities, form, pastimes, Mathurā, and so forth.
He should also be sought after even in those places whose greatness is proclaimed in various scriptures as being supreme;
however, they are not cited here for fear of prolixity.
