Immediately following this is the section on the commonality of destinies (*gati-sāmānya-prakaraṇa*), concerning the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa— ]
The passage beginning with "In the *Māhātmya* of the Thousand Names" and so forth, from the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*, should be explained immediately after [the previous section]. As it is said:
"Of the God of gods, the Wielder of the Discus, who is endowed with the power for all purposes..."
And whatever name is pleasing, one should employ it in all matters.

Thus, according to the perspective of the *Viṣṇu-dharma*, since all names of the Blessed One possess unrestrained majesty, the recitation of them even when collected together is not redundant; because it serves as a cause for the accumulation of purificatory impressions (*saṃskāra*), it is like the accumulation of recitations for a single [name]. This has been accepted by the authors of the *Nāma-kaumudī*.

Likewise, by the power of reciting the thousand names three times as previously collected, one must consider the utterance of Kṛṣṇa’s name to be necessarily effective. Regarding this, some explain that one should employ whichever name of the God of gods is desired and dear for all purposes.

"Just as [the demons] were instantly slain by Hari's beloved one under the name Govinda"— surely, this refers to the Goddess who was constantly reciting the *Bṛhat-sahasra-nāma-stotra*. Regarding her thousand [names]:

By such reasoning as "O fair-faced one, the name 'Rāma' is equal to those [other names]," Śrī Mahādeva, demonstrating that the fruit of the Thousand Names is obtained through the name 'Rāma' alone, further indicates that even the names of Kṛṣṇa included within that Thousand Names are secondary (gauṇa).
In that case, how is the statement regarding the Brahmāṇḍa not contradictory?
It is said: [it refers to] the present Bṛhatsahasra...

The proficiency regarding the name of Rāma is that the fruit which results from even a single recitation of the *Nāma-stotra* is attained; however, because two cows are possible for the name of Kṛṣṇa and because of the plural usage in the phrase "of the thousand names," the fruit that results from three recitations of many such *Sahasra-nāma-stotras* [is different].
That it becomes the fruit [of all other rites] is a sign of even greater maturity;
for this very reason, it is there said to bestow the fruits of all recitations and sacrifices and to destroy sins.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the one hundred and eight names.
Having said this, the fruit of other recitations mentioned in the Vedas and elsewhere is also included [within the fruit of this one].

Consequently, since the latter is stronger than the former due to its superior excellence (*prauḍhi*), the greatness of the former must be explained as being entirely non-contradictory to that [latter].

For at that time, although the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa— just like Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself— is the whole of all names due to its being entirely full of power, nevertheless, the fruit may still arise through the commonality of the parts.
Just as even for the giver of direct liberation, Śrī Viṣṇu, when he is employed as the recipient of an offering (*ādhāna*) performed as a constituent part of a sacrifice, he bestows only heaven.
Or, for example, even by reciting the Veda along with the mantra of the Lord contained within it, one does not obtain a fruit superior to that of the world of Brahmā;
just as in this very case, the name of Rāma alone [is sufficient].
Even for one who recites it only once, the fruit of the *Bṛhatsahasranāma* is fully attained, as the *Ekonasahasranāma* (the Thousand minus One) of Rāma is inherently included within it.
Furthermore, for one reciting even the *Bṛhatsahasranāma*, the *Bṛhatsahasra-* [fruit is attained].
The fruit of the names is not merely additional; rather, it is the fruit of the nine hundred and ninety-nine names.

For this very reason, even in the case of common names such as Keśava and others, which are not perceived through their distinctiveness as belonging to Him alone, they should be understood to yield only the fruit common to the names of other incarnations.
In the *Nāma-kaumudī*, however,

it is only the destruction of all misfortunes that is negated as a distinction between knowledge and ignorance, and not the gradation in the fruits such as love (*prema*) and so forth. Thus, while the name of Kṛṣṇa grants common fruits, [the following applies] to a thousandfold—
It is rightly said that the name "Rāma" is equal to other names, O fair-faced one;
yet in reality,
the fruit of the name Śrī Kṛṣṇa is itself superior to all those who descend through various incarnations.
Because he is the Blessed One (Bhagavat).

If it is argued that— just as in passages such as "by means of the *pūrṇāhuti*, which is an ancillary (*aṅga*) of the New- and Full-Moon sacrifices, one obtains all desires," these are merely explanatory statements (*arthavāda*), so too will they be in both cases here— that is not so.

For after reciting the *Bṛhatsahasranāmastotra*, having uttered the name of Rāma even once toward the Goddess who was about to eat, and being one who has fulfilled her purpose, she was invited by Śrī Mahādeva himself to eat with him, saying, "Eat with me."
In the case of the name "Kṛṣṇa," however, the status of being a figurative expression (artha-vāda) is utterly dismissed.

because the exalted majesty of Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone is incomparable, He Himself,
toward the illustrious Arjuna— who was beloved by the Blessed Lord who is worshipped by the entire host of devotees— revealed all...

In the concluding statement of the Śrī Gītā, which constitutes the essence of the meaning of the entire scripture, the worship of one's own [form] alone is taught as the most secret of all secrets, surpassing the worship of all other manifestations.
As it is said: "That which you do not wish to do out of delusion, you shall do even against your will" (Gītā 18.60).
Immediately following: "O Arjuna, the Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings,
causing all beings to revolve by His power of illusion, as if they were mounted on a machine."
Go to Him alone for refuge with your whole being, O Bhārata;
by His grace you shall attain supreme peace and the eternal abode.
Thus has this knowledge, more secret than the secret, been declared to you by me;
having reflected upon it in its entirety, act as you wish.
Listen further to my supreme word, the most secret of all secrets;
because you are dearly beloved to Me, I shall therefore speak what is for your benefit.
Fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me;
you shall come to Me alone—this I promise you in truth, for you are dear to Me.
"Abandoning all duties, take refuge in Me alone;

I shall liberate you from all sins; do not grieve. (Gītā 18.66) The meaning of these [verses] is as follows: the passage beginning with "You have mourned for those who should not be mourned" (Gītā 2.11) is not...
Since [the previous statement] beginning with "to do" was a designation for battle, this [present statement] is indeed a designation for the ultimate truth;
therefore, he says: "In that regard as well, hear what is more secret, even the most secret of all."
"Īśvara," and so forth:

He who is the one Lord, the inner controller of all, he alone, causing all beings mounted upon the machinery of saṃsāra to wander by means of Māyā, abides within the very region of their hearts as the Puruṣa in his entirety.

"All this indeed" (ŚvetU 3.15)—by means of such contemplation, through the turning of all the senses [toward Him], one attains supreme peace and His highest devotion. As it is said: "Peace is the steadiness of the intellect fixed upon Me" (BhP 11.19.36). His abode is His own realm, more secret even than the secret knowledge of Brahman.

The suffix *tarap* is used to express excellence between two things. Now, considering that even this [instruction] was not sufficient for that supreme devotee who was exclusively devoted to Him alone,
the Blessed Lord, disregarding [the devotee's lack of comprehension], Himself revealed the ultimate secret out of an abundance of great compassion.

Furthermore, having transcended even the stages of devotional practice— which are characterized by a gradation of what is to be worshipped, beginning with Pradyumna, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva, and culminating in the Lord of the Supreme Ether (Paramavyoman)—
He suddenly instructs that which is to be accepted above all else, saying: "Again, I shall declare that which is the most secret of all" (18.64).

Although it follows from the very statement that this is the "most secret" that it is superior even to the "secret" and the "more secret," nevertheless, the use of the word "all" implies that it surpasses other scriptural statements intended for the worship of Paramavyoman, Adhipa, and others, even though those are themselves most secret.
Because it functions according to its full purpose;
the suffix *tamap* is used here to denote excellence among many things;
for this very reason, it is "supreme" (*paramam*).

He states the reason for listening to such beneficial instruction composed by himself: "Because you are very dear to me," [referring to the thought] that such [instruction] comes from me, the supreme trustworthy one.
The meaning is that the sense is: "Your words must necessarily be heard.
He states the reason for revealing such a secret of his own with the word "tataḥ" (therefore), because of such a desire [on his part].
For this very reason, having thus aroused his eagerness, and in response to the expectation of "What is that?",
He says to him— whose hands are joined in reverence and who has tears of affection in his eyes— "Man-manāḥ" (with Me as your mind),
because of My being your friend.
"Be one whose mind is fixed thus upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa while He stands directly before you; likewise,
become My devotee with Me as your sole objective," and so forth— in all such cases, by the repetition of the word "Me" (mad), [the meaning is established].
It is understood that one must perform the practice of worship in various ways directed toward the vessel itself,
but not merely toward the reality of the Lord.
He declares the fruit to be exactly in accordance with the practice when he says, "You shall come to Me alone.
By this very word "alone" (*eva*), his own supreme excellence over all others is indicated.
On the other hand, [the result for] another...
"What need is there to speak of me?"—
this very point will also be made clear by Śrī Parīkṣit regarding Kali.
Since you, when Kṛṣṇa has gone far away with the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow,
are grieving in private for those who are not to be grieved for, you are indeed pitiable.
"Striking me, you deserve death.
By the words "It is true for you," he demonstrated a special degree of affection, saying, "In this matter, I swear by you alone.
Furthermore, out of great compassion, he spoke the words beginning with "The most secret of all secrets" for the sake of strengthening the meaning of the statements.
He says, "I promise.
[The opponent objects: "But for me, whose mind is distracted by various obstacles, how could even your 'manas-ness' and so forth be established? To this he replies, "All... and so on.
By the word "all" (sarva), all phenomena up to and including the eternal are intended;
by the prefix "completely" (pari), their abandonment even in terms of their own intrinsic nature is established; and "sins" (pāpa) refers to obstacles.
Because no sin arises from abandoning [the body] by his command;
he confirms this very point through a negative argument with the words "do not grieve.
In that regard—
You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for, yet you speak words of wisdom regarding both the dead and the living.

In the opening statement, "The wise do not grieve" (Gītā 2.11), his lack of wisdom is revealed; the intended meaning is that, by abandoning grief, you should simply accept the instruction given by me.

And therefore, although he has taught in many ways for the sake of understanding the relative gradation [of teachings], having pointed out the supremacy of this very instruction situated in the great concluding statement, [the Lord] says to the two of them: "Abandoning grief, you must grasp this very instruction."
The fact that these two statements refer to the same subject matter is also clear.
*Sarva-saṃvādinī*: Now, regarding the six verses of the *Śrī Gītā* beginning with "The Lord is the Master of all beings," another interpretation must indeed be explained.
For instance, in this regard, someone says:
"In passages such as 'God [is] the Lord of all beings,' the worship performed with the thought that 'everything indeed is God' involves a touch of the aspect of knowledge."
But here, in the passage beginning with "Fix your mind on Me," pure devotion alone is taught; for this very reason, it possesses the nature of the secret of all secrets.
Or rather, what need is there for the previous statement?

Since another person has pointed out that very same Lord—who was previously indicated only as being beyond perception—as being directly perceived, there is no need for me to say anything further. As I have stated before:
"Fix your mind on Me, be My devotee..."
Sacrifice to me, bow down to me;
thus, with your self disciplined and making me your supreme goal, you shall come to me alone. [9.34]
This is because [the Lord] has been described as the object of worship for those who are pure by such statements;
nevertheless, He has also been described as the inner controller (antaryāmin) in passages such as, "I alone am the sacrifice here in this body, O best of embodied beings" (Gītā 8.4).
There is no inconsistency in [the text] being both the most secret of all secrets and more secret than the secret,
because whatever was previously stated in general terms is precisely what is specified in detail at the end.
It is said: first of all, there is no gradation in the vessels;
for even if a gradation in the objects of veneration were possible here, [the distinction between] the secondary and the primary—
For it is by logical necessity that the meaning is indeed understood from the suffix;
and its primacy is established by the principle stated as: "And its status as the primary meaning follows from the fact that the result [of the action] arises from it" (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.29).

Specifically, however, because there exists a distinction between the statement "He Himself is not of that nature" expressed by the word *tat* (that), and "He Himself is of this nature" expressed by the word *mat* (my/mine), one perceives incompleteness through the signs of indifference and non-penetration in both types of instruction.

Because the very meaning [of that verse] is strengthened by the mention of the distinction of fruits and by the word "only" (eva), the gradation of the object of veneration is perceived quite directly; however,
in reality, this refers to the phrase "with one's whole being" (sarva-bhāvena).
The meaning is precisely "by being inclined toward all the senses.

For, according to the principle of the secondary and the primary, the sense of the object— consisting of worship characterized by the meditation on the state of being the self of all, which is mixed with knowledge— is sublated.
"You shall attain the eternal state," because it is precisely the attainment of a specific excellence in the world that has been indicated; therefore,
there is no room for a gradation in the degree of devotion,
nor indeed for a gradation in the object of devotion itself.
There is a distinction between the two descriptions based on whether they are indirect or direct;
at that very moment,
this contraction of activity must be conceived through both that former and this present process of movement.
If no state higher than that of the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) were heard of in scripture, yet in the scripture a state higher than that state is indeed heard of;
And beyond even that, it exists everywhere;
as in this very context, for instance, in the passage beginning: "Those who know Me as existing in the elements (adhibhūta), in the divine (adhidaiva), and as the sacrifice (adhiyajña)" (Gītā 7.30).
Because of the designation of difference;

for in that context, by the traditional rule (smaraṇa) "when joined with 'saha,' the subordinate element [takes the third case]" (Pāṇini 2.3.17), the inner controller (antar-yāmin) associated with the sacrifice is understood as being in a compound with a word ending in the third case expressing the sense of "together with" (sahārtha).
Since it is stated that the *pada* (the individual soul) is subordinate to its own self, the supremacy of Śrī Kṛṣṇa beyond that is manifest indeed.
This very same point is revealed in passages such as "I alone am the sacrifice here" (Gītā 8.4),
just as in the statement, "This Blessed Lord Droṇa exists in the form of progeny" (BhP 1.7.45).
Therefore, it is established that the gradation of the teachings is intended precisely to express the gradation of the worthiness of those to be honored.
But he who speaks otherwise speaks excessively.

Just as in the passage, "He speaks surpassing all by means of truth" (ChāU 7.16.1), the meaning is that he who speaks by means of the Truth—which is Brahman itself, serving as the object to be realized—speaks surpassing every disputant; that is to say, he alone speaks having surpassed everything.
Such being the meaning, just as in that case the name and so forth are understood through the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the excellence of the discourse, [so too here].

Just as in that context, although all things up to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) are taught with each subsequent one being greater than the last, it is established that Brahman alone possesses the quality of plenitude (*bhūman*); likewise here too, the superiority of the subject matter is demonstrated by the superiority of the instruction.
Therefore, it has been stated even at the conclusion that the supremacy belongs to Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone; this is the general direction.
[End of Sarva-saṃvādinī]
Therefore, the superiority of Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone is established.

For this very reason, according to the maxim: "If it be argued that [the Lord is not the Supreme] because of designations as non-existent, we say no, because of another attribute [indicated] by the remainder of the sentence" (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.17).
Since the meaning of the entire scripture consists precisely of the conclusion and the purpose of the introduction, the universal form mentioned therein is dependent upon that [conclusion] alone;
and this is logical.
Because it has been demonstrated by that very [text]: "And there—
having spoken thus to Arjuna, Vāsudeva showed his own form once again" (Gītā 11.50).
Thus, because he refers to the human-form four-armed appearance itself as his own,
it is clear that this universal form (viśvarūpa) is not his actual essential nature (svarūpa).
Therefore, even for Arjuna, the supreme devotee, that was not his desired object; rather, it was His own original form that he desired.
"I am thrilled at seeing what has never been seen before, and my mind is distressed with fear" (Gītā 11.45).
Because of such statements, by the sign of granting divine vision to Arjuna for the purpose of that very sight, it is He alone...
"His majesty," however, is merely the clamor of the ignorant;
for it has been said: "The Supreme Brahman in human form—He remains as that immeasurable, non-dual Brahman" (BhP 10.14.18).
"Thou art the supreme friend, the ultimate bliss" (BhP 10.14.32);
"He alone has dispelled Māyā through the direct experience of the eternal self-bliss" (BhP 10.12.39);
and "How is it, O All-pervading Lord, that Thou art perceived here within the range of the senses? (BhP 10.14.32).
Likewise, [it is said]: "For I am the foundation of Brahman" (Gītā 14.27),
and "I am not manifest to everyone" (Gītā 7.25).

Because for one whose vision has been perfected through hearing, even that [vision] is not the instrument; rather, it is only the vision conjoined with a specific power of the Blessed One that serves as the instrument there.
Consequently, the divinity and the bestowal of that vision [are established].

This [divine form] is the cause for the vision of the Supreme Brahman in human form; it is distinct from that natural vision [of the Absolute], being considered solely as the cause for the vision of the divine body.
And that [form] is the Supreme [Brahman] in human shape—
It has been said that Brahman is difficult to perceive even for those with divine vision:
"This form of mine which you have seen is very difficult to behold;
even the gods are constantly longing for a sight of this form."
By such passages as [Gītā 11.52], it is stated that "only through devotion is He well-seen"; for it is said:
"But by unswerving devotion alone, O Arjuna, may I, who am of such a nature, be known."
To know it, to see it in its true essence, and to enter into it, O scorcher of the foe.
[By the passage beginning with Gītā 11.54: "Thus, etc.";
and the passage beginning with "extremely difficult to see" (p. 33) refers to the Universal Form (*viśvarūpa*). Having seen this...

Because the passage beginning with "mānuṣaṃ rūpam" (Gītā 11.51) was stated immediately prior, and because the section on the Universal Form (viśva-rūpa) is separated from that by an interval; thus, in the eleventh chapter, for all the gods and others—
"In his arrival, they gazed with insatiable eyes at Kṛṣṇa of wondrous appearance" (BhP 11.6.5);
likewise elsewhere in that same book, "protected by the arm of Govinda" (BhP 11.2.1), and so forth;
and in the seventh [book], "you..."

and in the third [chapter], "and the astonishing of oneself" (vismāpanaṃ svasya ca).
Therefore, in accordance with the conclusion and by the intended meaning of his own statement, this section also [concerns] Śrī...
It is precisely the state of being centered on Kṛṣṇa.
Therefore, in the Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Gītās as well, the status of Śrī-Kṛṣṇa alone as the Supreme Lord (svayaṃ bhagavān) is established. Thus it has been said:
There is but one scripture: that sung by the Son of Devakī;
there is but one God: the Son of Devakī himself; and there is but one duty: service to the Son of Devakī.
"Even the mantra is one, namely the name 'Son of Devakī'.
Likewise, in the *Śrī-Gopāla-pūrvatāpanī-śruti*, the sages indeed said to Brahmā:
"Who is the supreme deity? [GTU 1.2], and immediately after this, the Brāhmaṇa spoke as follows.
"Kṛṣṇa is indeed the supreme deity," and so forth; and in the conclusion: "Therefore, Kṛṣṇa alone is the supreme god; one should meditate upon him, taste him, and worship him—Om Tat Sat. (GTU 1.49)

What need is there for much? It is heard from three chapters of the *Padma-purāṇa* that the seals (*mudrā*) of the Great Blessed One (*Mahābhagavat*), which are distinct from all incarnations (*avatāra*), actually reside there in person;
such is the case with some of them.
Verses.
Brahmā said:
Listen, Nārada, I shall describe the characteristics of the marks on the feet.
For the form of the Blessed One Kṛṣṇa is indeed a single mass of bliss.
O sinless one, I have indeed described to you my innumerable incarnations;
now I shall correctly declare the supreme truth: Kṛṣṇa is the Blessed Lord himself.
For the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods and likewise that of the sages,
the Blessed One has manifested out of a desire to do what is pleasing to his own kin.
I alone know those by whom the Lord, the Blessed One, who is affectionate toward His devotees, is known; there is no other. This which I have spoken is the truth.
Indeed, sixteen marks were seen by me at that site:
eight marks on the right side and seven on the other.
The banner, the lotus, the thunderbolt, the goad, and the barley grain;
the svastika, the upward line, and likewise the eight-cornered [figure].
O best of Vaiṣṇavas, I shall now describe seven others:
the rainbow, the triangle, the pitcher, and the half-moon.
The garment, the fish-sign, and the cow’s footprint—these are recorded as the seventh;
O wise one, whenever these marks are seen, [they portend the end].
The Supreme Brahman known as Kṛṣṇa has undoubtedly been born on earth;
he is either two-fold, or three-fold, or four-fold, or even five-fold.
"O best of Vaiṣṇavas, they are indeed seen in some way during an incarnation," and so forth;
and ending with: "O seventh among the celestial rishis, hear likewise of the sixteenth mark, which is seen wherever it may be, having the shape of a jambū fruit."
*Sarva-saṃvādinī*:

Now listen, O Nārada; I shall explain [this], beginning with the words "I shall explain," up to the *Pādma* statement that establishes the foot-marks (*caraṇa-cihna*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), these verses also are to be understood.
In the center, the banner is to be known; the lotus is three finger-breadths in height.
The vajra is indeed on the right side, and the goad is at its front.
Even a barley grain may be at the base of the thumb; wherever there is a svastika, it begins from the forefoot and extends as far as the middle of the foot.
Furthermore, O dear child, in that which is called the Padma [mandala], an upward line is indeed described;
it is an eight-cornered figure, and its measurement is eight finger-breadths.
"O best of Vaiṣṇavas, the sages indeed say that these very marks are indicated on the right foot; such are the signs of the foot."
I shall now describe here the positions on the left side [of the hand],
measured at four finger-breadths from the vicinity of the fingers.
One should know that the rainbow exists there; it would not occur anywhere else.
A triangle is indicated in the center wherever the water-pot is located.
O you of excellent vows, that [mark] should be a half-moon, measuring eight finger-breadths in size;
its shape is described as being like a half-moon.
"The *bindu* and the fish-mark (*matsyacihna*) are indeed prescribed at the beginning and the end;
among these, the 'cow's footprint' (*goṣpada*) should be understood as being one *aṅgula* in measure," and so forth. And further on:
"Listen, O best of divine sages, to the sixteenth mark as well:
wherever a mark resembling a *jambū* fruit is seen, that is declared the sixteenth mark; so say the sinless sages. Thus [it is said].
In this context, "O best of Vaiṣṇavas" and so forth is an address to Śrī Nārada. "Yadā kadā" means "at some time or other."
The middle is the equal space between the center of the two heels; there, a banner (dhvaja) [is placed],
measuring three finger-breadths.
The meaning is that one should leave a space measuring three finger-breadths at the tip of the foot;
beneath the verse, it bears a banner that conquers all misfortunes.
It is called "dhvaja" (the banner) according to the *Skanda-saṃvāda*.

In this context, in some places the meaning is "all around. Starting from the joint of the thumb and forefinger up to the middle finger, there is a vertical line established; this is known as the "pādma" (lotus) in the *Purāṇa*.
The meaning is "it has been stated.
Regarding the phrase "the measurement is by eight finger-breadths," the meaning is that one should exclude a measurement of eight finger-breadths starting from the tip of the middle finger.
Because of its extensive nature, there is no room for it within this commentary;
for this very reason, it was also explained in that manner previously.
The same should be understood for what follows as well. The rainbow, the triangle, and the half-moons are situated progressively lower and lower;
"elsewhere" refers to this.
The meaning is "other than Śrī Kṛṣṇa. A drop is the sky; at the beginning, He placed a drop near the toe of His foot.
In this context, it should be understood that the fish-mark and the sixteen-mark are present on both [feet] at the region of the heels,
because it has been stated without restriction as to whether they begin from the right or the left.
According to the Skanda Purāṇa, there is a discus below the right thumb and a conch and a lotus below the left thumb;
for these are indeed heard of in relation to Śrī Kṛṣṇa as well as elsewhere.
As it is stated in the *Ādivārāha-purāṇa*, in the section on the greatness of the Mathurā region:
"Where Kṛṣṇa sported in full company and played according to his pleasure."
"By him, whose feet are marked with wheels, in that auspicious place consisting of Brahman.
Thus it is said in the *Śrī-Gopāla-tāpanī*: "And his two feet are marked with the conch, the banner, and the parasol. This parasol is to be understood as being beneath the wheel.
Because of the preeminence of the right [hand],
and because its placement occurs in that very [position],
it is only as long as the measure of a finger.
It should be known that from its width, it is one-fourteenth part;
elsewhere, it is one-sixth part in length.
Because it is well known to have a measurement of fourteen *aṅgulas* in length and six *aṅgulas* in width;
therefore, the state of being the Blessed One belongs to Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone.
And so, in the *Brahmavaivarta-purāṇa*, in the context of the incarnations of the Blessed One, there is this statement of Sūta: "Indeed,
the incarnations of those whose nature is pure goodness (*sattva*) have been innumerable."
Having heard twenty of those which are the principal among them, one may be liberated from great sin.
Having thus enumerated those [Purāṇas], such as the Śrī-Bhāgavata, and others like the Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Saṃhitā, he speaks again:
"The Nara-Siṃha and other [Saṃhitās] are also destroyers of all sins."
Whatever is born upon this earth adorned with a particular excellence of power should be understood as arising from a portion of a portion of Kṛṣṇa.

Having thus considered all this, he applies the very verse of great import— just as the etymology of the word *bhagavat* occurs in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa*— directly as a designation for Śrī Kṛṣṇa as well.
"From whom the birth, etc., of this [proceed]" (BhP 1.1.1).
"The Supreme Brahman in human form" (Vṛ. reads here: ...).
From the Purāṇa section,
and from the Gopāla-tāpanī Śruti which states, "Therefore, Kṛṣṇa alone is the supreme deity," we meditate upon the supreme Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
He states the definition of his essential nature with the word "truth" (satyam),
because it is heard in such passages as: "His vow is truth, he is devoted to truth, he is the triple truth" (BhP 10.2.26).
[Vṛ. reads here:
"O Satyabhāmā, Kṛṣṇa is established in truth; truth is established in him.
Govinda is the truth beyond truth; therefore he is truly named 'Satya' (Truth). — Mahābhārata 5.68.12]
This is because it is so heard in the *Udyoga-parvan* and in the *Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-nāma-nirukti* composed by Sañjaya. By this,
the non-deviation of that form is demonstrated.
He states the incidental definition (*taṭastha-lakṣaṇa*) by saying "by his own abode" (*dhāmnā svena*); that is,
by his own essential nature (*sva-svarūpa*), which is the abode known as Śrī Mathurā, [the Lord] is eternally free from [all defects].
That by which the world— characterized by the activity of illusion—
is churned, or rather, that by which the entire universe is churned through the knowledge of Brahman.
That which constitutes the very essence of that [city] is what is called Mathurā.
Thus, according to what is well-known from the *Gopāla-uttara-tāpanī*,

he describes the divine play (*līlā*) of that very primordial Lord, who eternally shines forth in Śrī Mathurā, Dvārakā, and Gokula by virtue of being the son of the illustrious Ānakadundubhi, the Lord of Vraja.
This is with regard to His manifestation in the world for a specific purpose;

since His birth was from the illustrious house of Ānakadundubhi, He is [known] by that name, yet because of His lineage, He is also [known] otherwise— in the other place, namely, the house of the illustrious Lord of Vraja as well.

It comes by way of being a son, following after him; the connection is with the word "ya" (who) in the subsequent [verse]. By the word "yataḥ" (since), the word "tasmāt" (therefore) is obtained by itself.
How is it so by way of logical sequence?

To this he says: regarding matters such as the deception of Kaṃsa and others, by those very inhabitants of Śrī Gokula who possess such feelings, that certain indescribable [joy], which is like a mass of clouds for the entire multitude of blisses, [arises].
He is one who is proficient in the definitions of those [pastimes] or in their meanings, such that it is said, "The play is accomplished";
and therefore, being self-sovereign (*svarāṭ*), he shines by means of those very inhabitants of Gokula.
In that regard, although they have fallen under the power of love for Him, it has not been obstructed; He speaks of that sovereignty with the word "tena" (by Him).
He who [bestowed] the Veda upon Brahmā, the first poet.
In order to cause wonder, he expanded his majesty— consisting solely of the essence of Brahman, which is truth, knowledge, infinite, and pure bliss— by mere mental resolve alone;
for from that [majesty], such [a form] arose.
For the sake of the play that is appropriately both mundane and supramundane, the wise devotees of Him become bewildered and attain a state of helplessness through the arising of an excess of love;
this is because the word "yat" (that which) connects with what follows as well. That...

Precisely because through such play (*līlā*) there occurs a transformation (*vinimaya*) of even fire, water, and earth according to their respective natures— wherein the transformation of fire, such as that of the moon and so forth, is an exchange of attributes with objects devoid of light—
since the luster of her glorious face and other features effects the state of being "devoid of light" in the moon and so forth for those situated nearby...
And because it brings about brilliance in an object through its own radiance;
likewise, water becomes liquid and solid, and clay,
stone, and so forth become fluid by means of the sound of a flute.
Since the threefold creation within Śrī Kṛṣṇa—the manifestation of the splendor of Śrī Gokula, Mathurā, and Dvārakā—is not false but is indeed true; thus says Veda-vyāsa. // 1.1 // 82 // [83]
In this way, even the concluding statement, "To whom and by whom was it revealed? and so forth [BhP 12.13.19], is consistent with that very point:
"He who first created Brahmā..."
To him who knows this, Kṛṣṇa causes [the Veda] to be sung;
for one desiring liberation should indeed go for refuge to that God, the light of the intellect of the Self. [GTU 1.26]
Thus it is stated in the Gopāla-pūrvatāpanī Śruti;
and in the second Sandarbha, it has also been explained that He alone is the speaker of the Catuḥślokī.

Thus, [He is] the moon in the ocean of the nectar of Śuka’s words.

"Whatever the nature of the Blessed Lord himself may be, such indeed shall be the greatness of those [incarnations]. Therefore, as for the fact that Śrī Balarāma is an incarnation through partial entry (āveśāvatāra), [it is not contradictory].

yet, through the description of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Rāma as a pair, their equal radiance is seen—[as in BhP 10.8.22]: "The two of them, dragging after them their pair of feet, crawled along. For...

but not so in the case of earth and the other elements;
therefore, this is also their greatness.

Furthermore—The seventh is the abode of Viṣṇu, which they call Ananta (the Infinite). 85. Moreover—
"He became an embryo in Devakī, increasing both joy and sorrow.

Ananta is a portion (kalā) of Vāsudeva; he has a thousand faces and is self-ruling (svarāṭ).
"The Lord will appear before him out of a desire to do what is pleasing to Hari.
Śrī Saṃkarṣaṇa is the first portion, a partial expansion (kalā) of Vāsudeva, the son of Śrī Vasudeva.

Some say that this is because actual attraction is impossible;
and in such a task,

He who is indeed called Śeṣa becomes even thousand-faced,

Thus it was said by the venerable Goddess Yamunā:

"O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one, I do not know your prowess, by a single portion of which this world is supported, O Lord of the universe. Thus [it is said], and the commentary states: "By a single portion known as Śeṣa."

Otherwise, if the meaning were that it consists of a single part or a portion of that single component, then the use of the relative pronoun *yena* (by which) as a designation of the agent (*kartṛtva*) would be appropriate; for if the meaning were that it consists of a single part or a portion of that specific component, then the use of the relative pronoun *yena* as the agent— [would likewise be appropriate].

Only an explicit explanation would be appropriate; for, being the words of a great scholar, it serves to refute the perception of a different meaning by means of defining the entry into those specific portions.

However, by means of the indication of the relationship [between the words], the explanation of the commentary itself becomes even clearer; for it is precisely the primary [meaning] that is intended in each individual part. (Page 36)

must be excluded from all [society] according to the injunctions of the Śruti and Smṛti;

"One should look at the sun, touch a cow, and having consumed ghee, one becomes purified. Thus it is said. Furthermore, in passages such as "Then, as he was removing the burden of the earth" (BhP 1.15.34), it should be understood in this same way.
Here, by the words *tanu*, *rūpa*, and *kalevara*, the intention of the Blessed Lord (*Śrī-Bhagavat*) to remove the burden of the earth is indicated.
And it is precisely the state (*bhāva*) characterized by the desire to protect the gods and others that is expressed;
just as in the twenty-third [verse] of the third [chapter], the very state of Brahman is expressed by various terms.
If it were to be explained in that very same way there, then [the term] would be "Śrī-Bhagavatī" all the more so;
and consequently, the manifestation of that state within the Blessed One—
Because it possesses form (*rūpatva*), the analogy of the thorn is indeed perfectly appropriate;
likewise, duality alone constitutes the equality of the Lord.
That, however, has been explained in the very third section [of the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*]: "the forms such as the Fish and others" (BhP 1.15.35).
In the incarnations such as the Fish and others, he assumes those respective states;
furthermore, in the analogy of the actor, the actor is one who performs a dramatic role to be heard.
And this has been explained in the commentary (ṭīkā).

"By the authors [it is said], 'In the eleventh [chapter] of the first [book], the actor is skilled in the representation of the nine sentiments' (Bhāvārthadīpikā 1.11.21). Therefore, just as an actor in a dramatic work to be heard remains in his own form and attire even while singing the previous events through performance, he assumes the state of the hero, heroine, and so forth.
"He both assumes and abandons [them] in that manner.
For this very reason, in the third [chapter], it is shown:
"To those men whose eyes are never satiated and who have not performed austere penances..."

Regarding the verse, "He who, having taken up his own form, the eye of the world, vanished within," here too, having displayed his own form— his own image— which is the eye of the world, he then took it back and indeed vanished within.

But it was not said by Śrī Sūta that He abandoned them; for immediately after the verse, "the forms such as the Fish and others" (BhP 1.15.35), it was likewise stated: "when the Blessed Mukunda left this earth with His own body" (BhP 1.15.36).
In this context, "renunciation" (tyāga) should be explained as having one's own body as its instrument (*sva-tanu-karaṇaka*), and not as "together with one's own body" (*sva-tanvā saha*);
for this avoids the cumbersome requirement of supplying an unstated word (*adhyāhārya*) and follows the rule for case-endings used with qualifying words (*upapada-vibhakti*).
And because of the maxim that the case-ending denoting the agent (*kāraka-vibhakti*) is more powerful; as it is said:
"Alternatively, I am not manifest to everyone, being veiled by my own yoga-māyā" (Gītā 7.25).
As stated in the words of the Śrī Gītā [7.25]:
"He is seen by yogis through devotion; he is never seen without devotion.
Janārdana cannot be seen through anger or through envy."
Thus, according to the determination of the *Pādmottara-khaṇḍa*,
and by the vision of the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam* in the verse, "He was a thunderbolt to the wrestlers" (*BhP* 10.43.17).

"Free from defects such as hatred, he beheld the Blessed One— the Supreme Brahman, whose nature is imperishable splendor, radiant with the garland of rays from the discus in the Lord's hand, and who exists for his own destruction"— thus Viṣṇu spoke concerning Śiśupāla.
That form which manifests among the Asuras through the prose of the Purāṇas is not his true nature,
but is merely constructed by Māyā.

When one's own true nature is perceived, aversion departs; therefore, He abandoned that body by which He had removed from the earth the burden of the multitude of Asuras who were manifesting among them. The meaning is that He did not bring it back again.
But his body, which is visible through devotion,
is eternally perfected; thus he says, "I am unborn" (Gītā 4.6), in Devakī, who possesses a divine form (BhP).
This is because of such passages as [10.3.8], and because in the verse "And there Kṛṣṇa was being praised by the meters" [BhP 10.28.17], He is designated as the presiding lord of Goloka.
Consequently, the meaning of the phrase "just as the forms of the Fish and so forth" is also this very same point. It is like an actor.
Just as a certain magician assumes the forms of fish and other creatures in order to capture his own prey, such as cranes and the like,
and having brought them under his control, casts them off once they have returned to him; so too [is it in this case].

The meaning is this: although he is unborn, by means of that form which was brought to manifestation through his power of illusion (*māyitva*), he destroyed the host of asuras who constituted the burden of the earth;
and that [form] was a physical body (*kalevara*).
"Aja" means that He abandoned [the body], that is to say, He caused it to disappear; however,
as stated in the verse of the Śrī-Gītā, "enveloped by yoga-māyā" (Gītā 7.25), He was covered by a semblance of a body fashioned by māyā, like a snake shedding its skin.
This is the meaning.
In the prose section of the *Viṣṇu-purāṇa*, the phrase "for the destruction of himself" (*ātma-vināśāya*) means for the destruction of himself, namely Śiśupāla.
It was so that [the earth] might be radiant with the garland of rays from that discus which was hurled down by the Blessed One.
She saw him thus:
because he was one whose defects, such as hatred and the like, had been overcome.
By her, upon seeing him so radiant, [she was moved].

The meaning is that, while [the practitioner] exists in reality, having become free from defects such as hatred and having cast far away the illusory veils of his own nature, he beheld the Blessed One.
Furthermore, according to that system, [he beheld] that which pertains to another eon...

In the narrative, according to the manner of Maitreya and Parāśara’s questions and answers regarding the liberation of the pair beginning with Śiśupāla, there is no connection between the curse and Jaya and Vijaya; therefore, it should be understood that those two were different asuras altogether.
And that is logical.
For it would be improper for those two to suffer the torment of a curse in every single kalpa.
[End of Vṛtti addition.
[Page 47]
Now, the meaning of the verse beginning with "atha sūtī-gṛhe" (BhP 10.85.20) is as follows: in the preceding verses,
he was one whose primary qualities were knowledge of the glory of the Blessed Lord and devotion, and who was composed of pure sattva.

Even regarding his own manifestation, [the Lord] established it as that of an ordinary human through an excess of apparent wretchedness, merely as a human pastime, thereby inducing the notion that he was the child of the Blessed One.
And thus follows the question of the Blessed One: "In that case, how is it that you entertain the notion that he is your child?"
Anticipating the objection that in this matter the weight of his word alone is my authority and not logical derivation (*upapatti*), he says: "In the maternity chamber," etc.;
"in every age" refers to us two.
For this very reason, the Blessed One declared in the birth-chamber, "You have been born," meaning that you have descended [into incarnation].
But surely, even that was born [as a manifestation] solely with regard to the entering and exiting of the bodies of yourself and others?
It has been stated that birth is not to be described solely by the signs of entering and exiting; rather,
it occurs through the form of the Inner Ruler (antaryāmin) as the friend of the individual soul (jīva), whether in the form of the individual totality (vyaṣṭi) or the universal totality (samaṣṭi).
[The Self is] difficult to see, hidden, entered into the secret place, situated in the cave, dwelling in the abyss, and ancient (KaṭhU 1.2.12);
and in such passages as "Having created that, He entered into that very thing" (TaittU 2.6.2), there is that entry and so forth.
Because of the commonality of perception, one should consider that this [latter] is likewise merely metaphorical. To this, he says: "Not so."

Based on such scriptural declarations as, "Entering, as it were, by way of causality into the various self-made wombs" (BhP 10.87.19), You are indeed unattached like the sky; for while entering and assuming various bodies for living beings, You cast them off.
The meaning is that you repeatedly enter and then abandon [them].
Who knows— that is, who highly values— the Māyā of yours which consists of the manifold variety of your manifestations (*vibhūti*) due to such abundance?
The meaning is that there is no one else [who does so]. The intention is that this birth of ours is praised by everyone;
therefore, there is also the respect of the learned.
In this context, it has been indicated that while there may be authoritative means of knowledge [for others], for me, however, that is in no way within the range of the intellect.
Here, the meaning of the root *vid* as "entering" is not untenable;
as it is stated in the *Sahasranāma-bhāṣya*:
"He makes them disciplined and protects them"—
thus a verbal root with a general meaning is seen used in a specific sense,
just as in the case where one says "make the pieces of wood," it is used in the sense of "bring them. So it is here.

Thus, in this way, the self-manifested nature of Śrī Kṛṣṇa as the Supreme Lord has been shown, as well as the fact that He alone, the Supreme Brahman in human form, eternally abides in that very form;
likewise, in the first [chapter], the same was shown regarding the earth.
By the verse beginning with "Truth, purity, compassion, and cleanliness" (BhP 1.16.27), the naturalness and infallibility of His qualities— splendor, endurance, vigor,
and strength— are demonstrated. For this very reason, it is stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:

In the *Aṣṭottara-śata-nāma-stotra*, his human form is described by nature as follows: "He who brings joy to the people of Nanda’s cowherd settlement, whose body is composed of existence, consciousness, and bliss,
whose limbs are smeared with fresh butter, the dancer in fresh butter, the sinless one."
In the Śrī-Gopāla-pūrva-tāpanīya Upaniṣad as well, it is stated in the same way:
"He is the eternal among the eternals, the conscious among the conscious,
the one who bestows the desires of the many."
"The wise who devote themselves to that Pīṭhaga attain eternal perfection, and not others"—thus [it is said].
And likewise: "That one Govinda, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss" (GTU 1.33), and so forth. Therefore...
It is thus established that whether he has four arms or two arms, his nature as Śrī Kṛṣṇa remains invariably the same.
Now, what is that state wherein he dwells? To this it is replied:
Just as those cities dear to the Blessed One exist upon the earth,
so do they exist in Vaikuṇṭha, maintained for the sake of His various pastimes.

According to this statement from the Skanda Purāṇa, it should be understood that whatever place exists in Vaikuṇṭha is precisely that [very place]; and that is located specifically in the uppermost portion of the entire Vaikuṇṭha.
For, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa:

Having described Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself as the ninth in the enumeration of the ten incarnations, and by counting the locations of those ten incarnations in sequence starting from the east as the enclosures (āvaraṇas) of Vaikuṇṭha— known as Paramavyoma— the realm of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is reached in the direction of Brahmā.
It culminates precisely in being situated above all else;

for in the Āgamas and other scriptures, the sequence of directions is observed in that very manner. In this regard, however, because we have heard of it from various sources, the world of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is indeed independent.

This is the established position. However, it should be understood that because he is partial toward the side of the Supreme Ether (parama-vyoman), he has been included among its coverings (āvaraṇas) in the Padmottara-khaṇḍa.
[Page 48] In the Padmottara-khaṇḍa—
The subordinate nature of that which is to be propounded has indeed already been described in comparison with the subject matter of the Śrī-Bhāgavata;

however, in the Svāyambhuva Āgama, its status as being above all others is stated with complete independence. For example, in the dialogue between Īśvara and Devī, in the context of the meditation on the fourteen-syllable mantra, in the eighty-fifth chapter: [text follows]...
There, the pure-souled one should meditate; he should gradually contemplate this entire pervasive Vaikuṇṭha, filled with various wish-fulfilling creepers.
The equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas) below, and primordial nature (prakṛti) as the cause of all;
the causes of nature itself, and the qualities individually and in their proper order.
Then, O lady of excellent complexion, the wise one should remember the world of Brahmā, marked by the Brahman,
above the limit as Virajā, which is without boundary.
This auspicious [lineage] has been brought forth by the waters produced from the sweat of the Vedāṅgas;
and these deities are to be meditated upon in due order within the Virajā.
Immediately after this and others [of its kind]:
"Then one should remember the state of Nirvana of the sages who have drawn up their vital fluids (ūrdhvaretas), the supreme ether where the eternal gods reside."
Then one should meditate upon the world of Aniruddha, followed by that of Pradyumna in due order,
and likewise those of Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva.
"One should recollect the lords of the world... and immediately following that:
"It is strewn with creepers of nectar, frequented by various beings, providing happiness in all seasons, pure, and bringing well-being to all creatures."
Dark as the petals of a blue lotus, gently swayed by the breeze,
and scented with the pollen of Vṛndāvana— she who is the beloved of Kṛṣṇa.
The wise man should recall the Yamunā within its boundary, situated amidst groves on its banks and in the midst of pavilions for the play of women, with golden slopes and lotuses.
It is adorned with eternally fresh flowers and the like, overflowing with bliss,
and consists of the objects of the senses such as sound, which are the excellence of the happiness of the bliss of one's own self.
It was embraced by the sounds of various colorful birds and the like,
and made resonant by the humming of intoxicated bees beautified by various jeweled creepers.
It was bordered by wish-fulfilling gems, filled with networks of moonlight,
enriched with fruits and flowers of every season, and completely adorned with young shoots.
Vṛndāvana, filled with blossoming trees and birds, was repeatedly shaken by the breeze from contact with the waters of the Kālindī.
The wise practitioner should recollect that which is the sole abode of play,
the entire essence of happiness in the three worlds, a well-constructed machine, and the beloved of sport.
There, upon that delightful lion-throne made of various jewels,
pleasant and soft with a sweetness exceeding that of the *sumana* flower, and provided with a comfortable cushion;
It shines with the four pillars known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa,
and is adorned by the crowns of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
Therein is the youthful youth, overwhelmed by the weight of love, clad in yellow garments,
dark as the kalāya flower, and the sole abode of beauty.
He is immersed in the ocean of the bliss of the rasa of divine play, an ocean of happiness;
he possesses the luster of a fresh rain cloud, and his locks of hair are adorned with moonlight.
And so forth. (Page 49) [The Vṛtti here adds:
And in the *Mṛtyusañjīvana-tantra*—O Goddess, above the Egg of Brahmā (*brahmāṇḍa*) is the great abode of Brahmā.]
Above that, O Goddess, are the Viṣṇus; above those are the forms of Rudra.
Above that is Mahāviṣṇu, and above him is Mahādevī;
then are Kāla and Atikāla, followed by Paramānanda and [Parama]tataḥ.
Beyond them is the city of Mahādevī, where Kāla, the bringer of all fear, resides.
Then there is the eternally ever-fresh ocean of the nectar of the jewel of Śrī.
On its further shore is Mahākāla, who assumes the form of all that is perceived;
to the north of that is the radiant Jewel Island, called Śiva.
One should meditate on the rising moon over the ocean of nectar and agitated jewels,
in the midst of which is a golden ground adorned with rubies.
It is endowed with sixteen islands, adorned with skill in the arts,
and graced on all sides by auspicious clusters of Vṛndāvanas.
In its center is the great Nandana garden, which intoxicates with passion, surrounded by groves of trees numbering many millions of kalpas; and so forth—
within that, one should meditate upon a vast pedestal extending for a hundred yojanas.
"Resembling a thousand suns... and so forth;
"Within that [space] is a great seat (mahā-pīṭha) endowed with a great wheel (mahā-cakra);
in its center, one should meditate upon a pavilion (maṇḍapa) pervading the entire circle of the universe (brahmāṇḍa-maṇḍala)," and so forth.
One who is likewise [purified] should meditate there upon the Great Goddess herself,
the goddess who resembles a red lotus and is like the rays of the rising sun, and so forth;
she is clothed in yellow garments, and her lotus-like hands hold a bamboo flute.
Her heart illuminated by the Kaustubha gem, she was adorned with a forest garland.

"The Supreme Goddess, who dwells upon the couch that is the auspicious lap of Kṛṣṇa," and so forth. Having meditated thus and having become [the deity] accordingly, by her very grace and by her command, one attains supreme bliss, enveloped in a digit of bliss.
Listen to that, O Goddess, O sinless one; I shall tell you, O Great Mistress:
within this lies the unsurpassed Śvetadvīpa.
Situated in the midst of the ocean of milk, with celestial trees standing close together,
it has dispelled the mass of darkness by means of the rays of the rising half-moon.
The sky was filled with flocks of peacocks dancing at the sight of clouds resembling dark rain-clouds,
while the three worlds were made resonant by the warbling of swarms of cuckoos.
It was filled with winds carrying the fragrance of various flowers and possessed groves of wish-fulfilling creepers where swarms of bees hummed.
The surface of the sky was resplendent with thousands of delightful dwellings,
and it was beautifully adorned by throngs of thousands of lovely women singing.
It was adorned by the great Govardhana mountain, which provides delightful dwellings,
and by another [object] marked with auspicious signs, like a measuring rod of honor.
The southern, eastern, and northern directions were pervaded by the goddess Yamunā, who extended and increased in length in succession, possessing the beauty of dark clouds and water.
"In its center is a great and wonderful mansion made of crystal," and so forth;
"it is surrounded within by various great kalpa-mandāra trees and other such trees;
in their midst is the resplendent Vṛndāvana, crowded with its many families," and so forth.
"In some places there are palaces of jewels, in others dwellings of crystal," and so forth.
"It is adorned on all sides by countless cows and cowherds;
it is free from sin, delightful, beautiful, and always devoid of the six waves [of worldly existence]," and so forth.
In its center is a pavilion made of jewels, adorned with archways;
in the middle of that is a great jeweled throne borne by Garuḍas, and so forth.
[It is situated] on the summit of a mountain of jewels, resplendent with wish-fulfilling trees.
There, one should meditate upon the supreme bliss, the beautiful object of worship, the supreme light.
"One should remember Kṛṣṇa, the beloved of the cowherd girls, who incessantly infatuates thousands of gopīs in the beautiful Vṛndāvana," and so forth; as well as,
"He whose splendor is like that of a full-blown blue lotus and whose face is like the moon," and so on.
Immediately following this,
when the Goddess asked about the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal in the world, Śrī Śiva said: "O Pārvatī, [this applies] to all the abodes of Brahmā and the others."
In this world, the destruction of all things occurs without the prior existence of those two [cause and effect].
This means: of the aforementioned Śrī Bhagavān and Mahādevī.
[The addition from the *Vṛtti* ends here.
[Page 49]

Therefore, by the principle that "whatever exists on earth [exists elsewhere as well]," it is established that the realm of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, consisting of Dvārakā, Mathurā, and Gokula, exists independently above all else as the very playground of the Supreme Lord Himself.
Therefore, Vṛndāvana, which is Gokula itself, shines supreme above all and is renowned as Goloka.
As stated in the Brahma-saṃhitā: "The Supreme Lord is Kṛṣṇa... and so forth.
Having approached—
that great abode called Gokula, which is a thousand-petaled lotus,
whose pericarp is that very realm, and which arises from an infinite portion of Him—
The great Karṇikāra machine is a six-cornered vajra-pile,
the locus of the six limbs and the six-footed one, by means of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa.
For that which abides in the essence of the bliss of love and great bliss is conjoined with the mantra, the seed-syllable of desire, in the form of light.
Its filaments belong to those [deities], its petals even to the Śrīs.
Surrounding that [ocean] is the wonderful square region called Śvetadvīpa; it is square, fashioned in four ways as the four abodes of the Fourfold Form.
It is surrounded by the four aims of human life and the four causes,
and it is bound with ten spikes in the upward, downward, cardinal, and intermediate directions.
It was graced by the eight treasures and likewise by the eight supernatural powers,
and was surrounded on all sides by the ten guardians of the directions who appeared in the form of Manu.
"It was adorned on all sides by those wondrous spears and by the foremost of attendants, who were dark, fair, red, and white.
(Page 50)
Likewise, in the *Brahmastava*:
"In palaces made of heaps of wish-fulfilling gems, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of kalpa-trees, [he beholds him] being protected by Surabhi."
"I worship that Govinda, the primordial Person, who is served with great zeal by hundreds of thousands of Lakṣmīs.
He provides the explanation: "That lotus which has thousands of petals is made of wish-fulfilling gems (cintāmaṇi)."
The lotus is of that form;
and "that" refers to the great, most excellent station, or the station of the Great Blessed One— meaning Śrī Mahāvaikuṇṭha.
Anticipating the doubt that "it, however, is of various kinds," he determines its specific variety by stating "called Gokula";
"Gokula" is its name.

The meaning is that whatever is well-known possesses a form identical to that of a cow and a cowherd; for, according to the maxim that "conventional usage (rūḍhi) supersedes etymological derivation (yoga)," only that [conventional meaning] is perceived.
Therefore, the subsequent text should also be explained in accordance with this very point:
that the abode (*dhāma*) of that Śrī Kṛṣṇa is His dwelling together with Nanda, Yaśodā, and the others.
The great inner apartment is suitable;
he describes its nature with the word "that" (tad),
referring to the [palace] of Ananta Śrī.
From a portion of Baladeva;
that which has its manifestation as eternal appearance—
likewise, this is also [to be understood] by means of *tantra* (elliptical construction).
It is explained as follows: it is that place where even Śrī Baladeva—in whom infinite portions reside—has his origin and abode;
[it is the seat] of the glorious Great King of Mantras consisting of eighteen syllables, which is served by the entire host of mantras.
He states that the principal seat among the many seats is the *karṇikāra* by means of two [verses]. Regarding the phrase "the great yantra":
it is that which, as a mere representation, is everywhere drawn for the purpose of worship as a yantra.
The meaning: he demonstrates its very nature as a machine.
That which has six corners within it is the vajra-stake (*vajrakīlaka*) in the *karṇikāra* (the form of the seed-syllable).
It is adorned with diamond pegs.
He states the purpose for its being hexagonal:

That which has six limbs is the six-footed mantra consisting of the glorious eighteen syllables; its locus is the primordial nature (prakṛti), and the very essence of the mantra is Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, because He is the causal form.
And that very Puruṣa is the form of those deities;
by them it is established and presided over.
The term "love" (prema) is an adjective qualifying both [the preceding terms].
That which consists of the essence of love— the various stages of maturation of the flavors of bliss (ānanda) and great bliss (mahānanda)— is of that very nature.

Likewise, it exists in the form of light through its own self-luminosity, and as the *manu* in the form of the mantra, namely the *kāma-bīja*; thus, although it is included within the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*), it is mentioned separately in some instances with a view toward its specific distinction.
Having thus described that abode, he speaks of its enclosures with the word "tad" (that).
The meaning is that the filaments (*kiñjalka*) of that *karṇikāra* tree constitute the inner circle attached to it.
The meaning is: "the abode of those who possess a share in that [portion]," namely, those of his own kind;
that is to say, the place called Gokula.
This has indeed been stated; and their belonging to that same species was also declared by Śrī Śukadeva:
"Having thus slain the humped bull while being praised by the twice-born, he, the festival for the eyes of the gopīs, entered the cow-pen together with his companions" (BhP 10.36.15).
The petals of that lotus are the abodes in the form of gardens for the splendors of his beloveds, Śrī Rādhā and the others;
here, the meaning is that the roots of the petals with their raised edges—
The paths at the joints should be known as the cow-pens (goṣṭhas) situated at the foremost joints;
for the unbroken lotus is called Gokula, and because it is likewise contained therein.
Now he describes the enclosures of Gokula with the words "quadrangular" (*caturasram*).
Outside of that [Gokula] is a quadrangle; outside of that Gokula, on all sides, is a place consisting of four corners, which is known as Śvetadvīpa. This is its—
In one part, it is called Gokula because of the absence of any specific name;
however, the square inner maṇḍala should be known as Vṛndāvana, while the outer maṇḍala alone is called Śvetadvīpa, and [the whole] is Goloka.
That which is its synonym is already included here under the name Vṛndāvana, which is so well known as to encompass Gokula, and thus it is not specifically mentioned.
But that which encompasses all of this externally is to be known as his outer circle (*bahir-maṇḍala*), called Goloka and Śvetadvīpa.
[The Vṛtti reads instead of the last two sentences:]...
The meaning is that this is an illustration, including what is called Gokoka; for even in Gokula, the state of being Śvetadvīpa certainly exists. If that is so...
Although it consists of intermediate stages (*avāntara-bhūmi*), it is nevertheless designated by its specific name; thus, it is understood as such, and so it has been stated.
However, even within the square (*caturasra*), there is an inner mandala (*antar-maṇḍala*) [of] Śrī...
It should be known as named Vṛndāvana, because it is seen thus in both the Bṛhad-vāmana and the Svāyambhuva Āgamas.
[End of Vṛtti] "Fourfold" (catuṣkṛtam) means fourfold (caturdhā), pertaining to the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha) of the four forms, namely the quartet beginning with Śrī-Vāsudeva.
The abode is divided into four parts; however, due to divine play (*līlā*), they should be understood as remaining above that, situated in celestial chariots (*vyomayāna*),
by means of causes that accomplish the goals of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*) in the form of Manu, consisting of their respective mantras.

"By Indra and others" means by the four Vedas, beginning with the Śyāma [Sāman]; this is the meaning. For it is stated in the *Śrī-daśama*: "And there, they were greatly amazed to see Kṛṣṇa being praised by the meters (*chandobhiḥ*). [BhP 10.28.18]
"By the Śaktis" means by Śrī Vimalā and the others;
