all regarded that bull among the Sātvatas as the abode of all beings—
him who himself existed as the eternal head of his own clan, the bull of the Sātvatas.
They also considered the Blessed One Bhūtāvāsa to be a partial incarnation of him, the inner controller of all beings; thus, he is my sole deity. (Page 68)
Thus, from the beginning up to the end of the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (6.18), "the abode of all beings," there is the scriptural testimony regarding the Inner Controller (antaryāmin);
and it is also said in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (10.43.27): "He is the supreme deity of the Vṛṣṇis."
3.2: Śrī Uddhava to Śrī Vidura. 128–129.
[130] He whom he had previously requested to dwell with him—“O Keśava, I would not leave Your lotus feet even for half a moment;”
"O Lord, I am unable to abandon it; lead me also to Your own abode.
This means that just as You lead the other Yādavas, so too lead me to Your own abode—Dvārakā—which is a particular manifestation of the light of the phenomenal world.
But if it were a different meaning, the word "api" (also/even) would be redundant.
// 11.6 // The illustrious Uddhava. // 130 // [131]
In the *Pādmottara-khaṇḍa*, within the *Kārttika-māhātmya*, it is stated that the Yādavas are likewise [non-material]:
"Just as Saumitri and Bharata, and just as Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others,
so too are they born from their own world by His will."
"Furthermore, by that very path they go to that supreme, eternal state;
for Vaiṣṇavas, there is no bondage of karma nor rebirth. (Padma Purāṇa 6.229.57–58).
Here, the phrases "from his own world" (*nija-lokāt*) and "that state" (*tat-padam*) refer to the Vaikuṇṭhas of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and so forth, according to the *Pādma-uttara*.
This is the Khaṇḍa-mata,
because it is explicitly stated therein that the various incarnations, such as the illustrious Fish and others, reside individually in Vaikuṇṭha.

And it has been stated by Śrī Vidura that for such beings, as for the Blessed Lord himself, birth and so forth occur solely by the will of the Blessed Lord, for the purpose of destroying the path of error:
"The birth of the Unborn is for the destruction of the wrong path."
"Indeed, actions are for the sake of binding those persons who do not perform them;
otherwise, how could the Supreme, who is beyond the modes of nature, be subject to the bondage of the body through the mechanism of karma? [BhP 3.1.44] Thus it is said.
And the commentary [states]: "Who else indeed?

Thus, when it is established and proven that they are the eternal associates of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the description of Vasudeva and others as being performers of sacrificial rites and so forth in a previous birth is also [accounted for].

Just as in the case of the Blessed One, because they descend by the will of the Blessed One alone for the sake of gathering the world and so forth, it is possible through a partial incarnation or, in some cases, through the entry of another jīva;
and furthermore, when they descend by themselves, [it occurs] through that portion.
However, it should be understood that the description is given as a unity according to the method of the *Praveśa* narrative,
just as was explained in the case of Pradyumna.

Thus, in the third instance, in the Lord’s statement beginning with "I know," the address "O Vasu" to Uddhava should be understood as being made solely with regard to his being a partial incarnation (*aṃśa*) of Vasudeva; likewise, the mention of his "final birth" should be understood as referring to his nature as the *aṃśin* (the whole) who is the ultimate locus for such partial incarnations. Therefore, he says:
"In a previous creation, during the era of Svāyambhuva Manu, you yourself were Pṛśni;
at that time, this sinless Prajāpati was named Sutapā.
[BhP 10.3.32] You were indeed the goddess Śrī Devakī as Pṛśni; it is not that "you became Pṛśni," but rather that you were Pṛśni. Thus...
"Then he too," thus spoke the Blessed Lord Śrī Bhagavān: "They call Vasudeva Ānakadundubhi the abode of Hari. (BhP 10.3.131–132)

Thus, as it is said: "The pure *sattva* denoted by the word Vasudeva, wherein the Person moves unobstructed" (BhP 4.3.23), and so forth; the sages declare that the abode of Hari known as Vasudeva is here called Anakadundubhi.
// 9.24 // Śrī Śuka said:

// 132 // [133] Likewise, this should be explained here as well: that Vasudeva [was born] from Devakī, who possessed a divine form, and she too possessed that same form, being of the nature of the manifestation of pure goodness (śuddha-sattva).
Therefore, in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, in the hymn of praise to her by the gods, there is much more, beginning with: "You are the supreme, subtle primordial nature" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.2.7).
// 10.3 // Śrī Śuka said:
// 133 // [134] Therefore, just as I am, you two—who have eternally existed in the form of my parents within the unmanifest pastimes—are now... (page 69)

He says that you two, having followed after My manifest pastimes, shall again enter My unmanifest pastimes by Your own will: "You two have repeatedly [served] Me with the attitude of sons and with the attitude of Brahman."
Meditating thus and having cultivated affection, you two shall go to my supreme state; that is,
by means of the realization of Brahman— perceiving the one in human form as the Supreme Brahman—
to my highest state, which is distinct from my manifest pastimes.
[He describes] my state, which is my divine play (*līlā*):
even though you two had previously manifested through a portion of me, your devotion was directed toward me alone; thus he says:
"The husband and wife, who did not enjoy vulgar objects and were childless... [135]
"Deluded by my divine power (*deva-māyā*), you two did not seek my liberation.
The meaning is: "by my *māyā*, which consists of the power of affection for my domain"; she thus manifested the *vaiṣṇavī* [power].

This is because it is seen [in scripture] both in reference to the Queen of Vraja: "The Lord [manifested] an illusion consisting of affection for His son" (BhP 10.8.47), and as "my mercy which generates such affection.
Thus, *māyā* refers to deceit or to mercy.
This is according to the *Viśvaprakāśa* lexicon.

For it is heard everywhere that the very love for Him (tat-preman) is the cause of the setting aside of liberation (apavarga); nevertheless, he says "ajuṣṭā" (unloved) to state that there is a cause for the concealment of liberation.
The meaning is that detachment arises because there is no longer any immersion in sense objects.
// 10.3 // The Blessed Lord and His Parents // 134–135 // [136] Now, regarding the fact that Śrī Gopā and the others are also His eternal attendants:
"Victorious is the Abode of Living Beings," and so forth.
This is clearly evident; therefore, he said:
"Therefore, I protect my cow-pen, which has me as its refuge, me as its lord, and me as its protector, through the yoga of my own self; this is the vow I have undertaken. (BhP 10.25.18)
This is clear. 10.25. The Blessed Lord. 136. [137] Likewise:
From that time forth, Nanda’s Vraja became possessed of all prosperity.
"O King, Ramākrīḍa became possessed of all prosperity through the qualities of the Self that is the abode of Hari.

[BhP 10.5.18] That which is the Self who is the abode of Hari—by those very qualities it is endowed with all prosperity; by means of the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) denoting eternal connection, it is eternally endowed with all prosperity.
Then, beginning from that manifestation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Vraja of Śrī Nanda [describes] the pastimes of Ramā—
in dwellings with heaps of wish-fulfilling gems and kalpa-trees— ...
In this context, according to established tradition, [the Lord] is surrounded by millions of fragrant [trees],
served with the agitation of hundreds of thousands of Lakṣmīs,
and is the direct abode of play for the Ramās— the Great Lakṣmīs, the Śrī-Vrajadevīs themselves.

It came to pass: while Śrī Kṛṣṇa was sporting there in a concealed manner within that abode of Hari, they too sported in the same way; however, when he appeared openly, they too appeared openly—this is the meaning.
// 10.5 // Śrī Śuka said: // 137 // [138] He elaborates upon this very point with six verses:
"Oh, what fortune! Oh, what fortune for the cowherd Nanda and the inhabitants of Vraja!"
The true friend is supreme bliss, the eternal, perfect Brahman.
This is an indescribable fortune, a certain grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
it is characterized by his repeated expressions of regard.
It has been stated that [the Self] is entirely indefinable.
Since its eternity is already established by its very nature as Brahman, which is perfect and supreme bliss, the fact that it is mentioned again is solely for the sake of the word "friend" (mitra).
It is obtained as a qualifier; or else, for the sake of understanding a specific quality of the predicate, the subject is mentioned and then qualified,
just as in the case of "this gold, which is beautiful, has become this earring," where it is the earring itself [that is qualified].
The state of being delightful is what is to be established.
Therefore, here too, the two qualifiers characterized by fullness of supreme bliss— which refer to that which is restated, namely the Supreme Brahman known as Śrī Kṛṣṇa— are to be predicated.

Since it accomplishes various states precisely through friendship itself, its eternal nature— which functions for that same purpose— should accomplish those states. Furthermore, in this context, because there is no instruction regarding a connection with a specific time, it refers to time in general.
It partakes [of that state]; and thus, it is clear that this subordinate factor characterized as friendship exists throughout the three periods of time.
However, the non-production of another period of time would be a difficulty.

And here, since the eternality of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is established by the words in the two subsequent meanings, the eternality of His attendants who possess His friendship is also not impossible, as such is seen in the case of Śrī Rukmiṇī and others.
(70) [139] Oh! May it be that these [beings], experiencing the supreme bliss of eternal friendship with Śrī Kṛṣṇa, shall continue to exist in this state.
"Now, something similar has happened to us as well," he says:
"O Acyuta, let alone the greatness of their fortune; for we, alas, are truly the most fortunate ones, being eleven in number."
O Śarva and the other gods, we drink again and again with the cups of our senses this nectar-wine of the honey arising from Your feet;
"one" means that which is indivisible and eternal.
Let alone the greatness of their fortune and the majesty of their destiny; for now, even we—the ten guardians of the directions, beginning with Śarva—are most fortunate.
Because of our supreme devotion and because we are the foremost among them, they are referred to as "beginning with Śarva. [The word] *bhūri-*...

He demonstrates the very nature of being a participant: "By means of the cups of our senses—the drinking vessels characterized by the eyes and so forth—we too shall come here again and again and drink this honeyed nectar of the ambrosia of Your feet, so that it may be directly before us. [The word *caraṇa-*...]
Beauty and the rest, precisely because they are exceedingly captivating, are metaphorically described as honey and so forth in three ways through a collective dvandva compound;
and the word "this" (etad) refers either to that very [subject] or to this qualifying attribute.

In this regard, even according to the maxim "let the wicked man be satisfied," if one holds the view that the residents of Śrī-Vraja possess material bodies, then enjoyment performed by deities through their instruments would not be possible for them, because such [divine] enjoyment is eternal. Thus, here in Śrī-... [the text continues].

And because Śaṅkarācārya has determined that the deity belongs only to the category of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and not to the category of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), and thus established that the self alone is the enjoyer—
therefore, what was previously stated in such passages as "O Lord, may that one of great fortune be mine" (BhP 10.14.30) and so forth [remains valid].
He says that this very thing is what was prayed for:
"That birth in this forest is of immense fortune— some indescribable merit— since even here in Gokula, there is the consecration by the dust of the feet of whichever [divine] calf."
"That entire life which the Blessed Mukunda has granted me— even today, the dust of whose feet is sought only by the Vedas.
By this, he requests from You the abundant reward characterized by service at Your feet, obtained simply through the attainment of birth in Śrī Gokula.
It has been indicated that his portion shall always be successful;
there the Blessed Lord descended, and here, in this [place], is Śrī Mathurā.
In the maṇḍala; even there, in the forest of Aṭavī; even there, in Śrī Vṛndāvana; even there, in Śrī Gokula.
Of what nature was that birth? Among the residents of Gokula, [the birth] of which person—of anyone at all—at the feet...
That [place] in which there is anointment with pollen— [End SS] [141]—
therefore, what can be said of their good fortune?
Oh, by whose devotion even you [are moved]!
He says that they have fallen into a state of constant bewilderment, remaining utterly obstructed by these [thoughts]:
"O Lord, will you grant us [our desires],
or not?"— for our mind, seeking a fruit other than the fruit of the universe, wanders in delusion as to where else it might find such a fruit.
Even Pūtanā, along with her kin, was offered to you by the gods despite her wicked appearance,
because for your sake, they surrendered their abode, wealth, friends, beloved ones, themselves, their sons,
their lives, and their very hopes— just as they would for those of pure heart, such as the nurses and other attendants.
[Vṛ. adds: "He obtained the status appropriate for a nurse" (BhP 3.2.23); because of this statement in the third [skandha], from that beginningless kalpa—]

Because it has come down through tradition and is thus obtained precisely through the descent [of the Lord], and because devotion is established by those very individuals alone, it is rightly said that He is the "eternal friend.
And therefore, His abundance—
The sense is that even such things as "fortune" and so forth are rightly prayed for;
[in this context, *rātā* means the giver, and *tvattaḥ* means from you].
"Go from here to there.
[End] Now, is it not observed that these beings possess passion and so forth, just like other humans?
How then [can they be said to be] themselves...
Regarding the Lord’s state as their eternal retinue, he states there by way of a *kaimutya* (a fortiori) argument:

"O Kṛṣṇa, those people do not possess thieves such as passion and the like, nor a house that is a prison, nor shackles on their feet in the form of delusion, for as long as they have You. [BhP 10.14.36]
Thieves are those who carry off the essence of men;
even for other ordinary people, passion and the like, as well as thieves and so forth, exist only so long as those people do not become yours in every respect.

Out of devotion, they do not surrender their very selves to you; yet, once the self has been surrendered, even their passion and other afflictions become established in you alone. Thus, because passion and the rest lack the quality of being "natural" (prākṛta), they cannot be considered thieves and the like.
On the contrary, the meaning is that it is precisely of the nature of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*);
thus it has been requested.
By Śrī Prahlāda: "May that unswerving affection which the undiscriminating have for sense-objects never depart from my heart as I remember You. [ViP 1.20.19]

Therefore, if such is the state of affairs even for those who are merely practitioners, then what need is there to speak of the noble residents of Śrī Gokula, who possess such belovedness eternally? Thus it is.
Thus it has been said:
"In this way, Nanda and the other cowherds, joyfully recounting the stories of Kṛṣṇa and Rāma and taking delight in them, did not experience the suffering of worldly existence" (BhP 10.11.58).
"Becoming" (*bhava*) refers to phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*), in the sense that "it exists therein.
Although these [sufferings] are manifested among those born into phenomenal proliferation,
nevertheless, they did not experience that feeling associated with it— the cognition of objective suffering and so forth.
This is the meaning. Those who know the lexicons state that *vedanā* means both "knowledge" and "affliction.
[143] If so, how is it that for people there is an appearance like manifold diversity (*prapañca*) in the cowherd settlement (*gokula*)? To this he says:
"Though yourself free from manifoldness, you mimic manifoldness upon the earth."
O Lord, in order to manifest the mass of bliss for the people who have taken refuge in You,
although You transcend all phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*), You imitate the phenomenal world existing upon the earth through Your play of birth and so forth,
by means of the signs of worldly emotion such as "This is my father" and "This is my mother."
By this very form of Gokula presented here, You imitate Yourself;
yet in reality, this is Your own true form as Śrī-Gokula.
The intended meaning is that its own nature (*svarūpa*) appears as if it were the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), yet it is not actually of the nature of the phenomenal world.
To the question of what the purpose of such an appearance is, he says "prapanna" (having surrendered).
[This refers to] such a worldly form—
For indeed, by mere sport (*līlayā*), supreme bliss arises for the multitude of people who have taken refuge; this is the meaning.
Therefore, it was well said: "Oh, what fortune! and so forth.
// 10.14 // Brahmā [addressed] the Blessed Lord. // 138–143 // [144]
Therefore he said:
"O King, for those who constantly cast beautiful glances upon Kṛṣṇa, rebirth arising from ignorance is no longer possible. (BhP 10.6.40)
The worldly existence, the state of being a transmigrating soul, or the materiality of those women of Śrīgopapura is not imagined— that is, it does not actually occur; rather,
the meaning is that only their non-material nature is possible.
Since this arises from ignorance,
of what nature are they?
[They are] characterized by the darkness of ignorance.
That which shines even above the love for the sun-like knowledge, and which exists even above that—
the beautiful glance, the state of being a son, the love known as *vātsalya*— that very love they constantly and eternally, from time immemorial, direct toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

[Vr. here adds: This being the case, for those who are known by the specific name Śrī-Kṛṣṇa—whose name is established as such—and who, through their intimate connection with Śrī-Kṛṣṇa, are the objects of meditation at His great Yoga-pīṭha, and who likewise must be shown to be of that same nature in other pastimes as well, [those] Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-...
But what more need be said regarding the beloveds? [End of the section on Vṛndāvana.
Since the Śrīgopīs and others are thus His eternal associates (*nitya-parikara*),
therefore,
with respect to certain practitioners who possess bodies established through this very context, or alternatively—
This refers to the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "Having entered the inner apartments" (BhP 10.29.9) and ending with "And thus one should not feel astonishment" (BhP 10.29.16).
[Sarva-saṃvādinī]
Some gopīs who had gone inside their houses and were unable to come out remained with their eyes closed, absorbed in meditation upon Kṛṣṇa.
Their impurities shaken off by the intense heat of separation from their beloved Duḥsaha,
and their auspicious merits exhausted through the bliss of embracing Acyuta attained in meditation.
Even by uniting with that very Supreme Self through the thought of Him as a lover,
they immediately cast off their bodies composed of the gunas, their bonds being utterly destroyed.
The King said:
"O Sage, they know Kṛṣṇa as the supreme beloved, but not as Brahman.
How can there be a cessation of the flow of the qualities for those whose intellects are fixed on the qualities?"
Śrī Śuka said:
This was told to you previously—how even the King of Cedi attained perfection while being an enemy of Hṛṣīkeśa; how much more so, then, those who are dear to Adhokṣaja?
O King, for the sake of the supreme welfare of human beings, there is the manifestation of the Blessed One—
who is imperishable, immeasurable, devoid of qualities, yet whose very self consists of the qualities.
Those who constantly direct desire, anger, fear, affection, a sense of identity, and even friendship toward Hari indeed attain absorption in Him.
And you should not feel such astonishment toward the unborn Blessed One,
Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Lords of Yoga, for by him this [world] is liberated.
[End of SS addition.
[Vr. replaces the preceding paragraph with the following:
Thus it was for them, in that very manner, their Śrī-...
Just as with Kṛṣṇa, the association of Śrī Kṛṣṇa with those very bodies of the blissful forms (ānanda-vigrahas) has been declared.
Furthermore, the greatness of their forms has been described in such passages as: "The Lord, the son of Devakī, shone exceedingly resplendent among them" (BhP 10.33.6), and so forth.
And by Śrī Uddhava, while offering obeisances to them,

having first demonstrated that they alone were the supreme bearers of bodies with the verse, "First these [are the foremost], O bearers of bodies" (BhP 10.47.58), he then said in the middle, "Where are these women? (BhP 10.47.59).
Having restated the opponent's view and refuted it with the verse "This is not a limb of Śrī" (BhP 10.47.60),
he demonstrates that they possess a form as the beloveds of Him which is distinct even from Lakṣmī, thereby establishing their supreme eternity; and then,
by the words "and the grace that arose therein," he [establishes] that grace.

Having always remained within them and thus indicated their state as permanent residents, [the Lord] again demonstrated, through the verse beginning with "O, the dust of their feet" (BhP 10.47.61), that the dust of their feet is His own supreme human goal (*parama-puruṣārtha*).
Wherein they took refuge...
By the verse beginning with "mukunda-padavīṃ śrutibhir vimṛgyām" (BhP 10.47.61), that very state which is established as the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha) is indicated;
and by the words "yatra vṛndāvane" and so forth, the nature of Vṛndāvana is likewise established.
Such a state has been established.

To reinforce this through a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), he says that for other [beings] who are adventitious and whose bodies are not yet established, the attainment of union with That occurs only through the abandonment of the physical form.
This is indicated by the passage beginning with "Having entered the inner apartments" (BhP 10.29.9) and ending with "And thus one should not feel astonishment" (BhP 10.29.16).
The meaning here is that "some," as mentioned in this context, are those who, having gone into the inner apartments, serve their husbands;
and a detailed explanation will be shown in the sequence of the composition. (Vṛ.)
[End of section.
Here, the word "antar" (within/between) is quite clear;
it refers to the impurity (*aśubha*) in the attainment of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Obstacles are forms such as heavy fear and the like;
auspiciousness is the contemplation of assistance from friends and others as a means for attaining Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
For it has indeed been stated: "There is no bondage of karma nor rebirth for the Vaiṣṇavas" (Padma Purāṇa 6.229.58).
And that is seen elsewhere as well.
The use of that word (*tat*) in an impossible context occurs, for example, in [BhP 10.89.11]: "The prosperity that has struck away my sins by Your feet shall abide upon my chest.
In that case, just as in the words of the Blessed Lord—
Just as another meaning must be sought for the sake of the true sense [of a passage], so it is here as well.

By the phrase "the Supreme Self" (*paramātmānam*), according to the established doctrinal method extending from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, it is shown that Śrī Kṛṣṇa is by His very nature the object of supreme love. As for the word "lover" (*jāra*), [it is used here].

The intellect is conjoined with that [object] even by means of that alone, but not through direct attainment in the form of a lover (*jāra*). By using the word "lover" (*jāra*), the intensity of worship is indicated by way of that state of being.
By this explanation, having shown the transgression of the worldly laws and conventions, it is demonstrated that such a state is utterly unrestrained;
for bondage is that which opposes the attainment of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
[Their conduct] consisted of dwelling among the common people and so forth.
Regarding the statement that they abandoned their bodies composed of the modes of nature (*guṇa-maya*), there was doubt on the part of the King as to whether they knew Kṛṣṇa [as the Supreme].
O Sage, those women [regarded] Śrī Kṛṣṇa as the supreme, absolute, beloved, and hidden...
They know [the Self] as the Beloved (Vallabha), but not as Brahman.
If that is so, how is the cessation of the flow of their qualities possible?
For one who possesses the realization of Brahman, because that which is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) alone arises therein,
there occurs the cessation of the flow of the previously existing qualities born of māyā; yet, within those very qualities, it exists solely as their object of beauty.

The meaning is: since those qualities arise as belonging solely to Him who transcends the material qualities (*prakṛti-guṇa*) even while they are being cultivated, and because they possess the quality of being connected to His own qualities despite the absence of material qualities, how could there be a cessation of those qualities which are consistent with the supreme goal of man?
Or rather, the sense is: how could the continuous flow of their qualities not be ultimately real, such that you speak of liberation from them?
Through its nature as Brahman,

it demonstrates the distinction from [ordinary] sensation; for those whose minds possess the intellect that perceives qualities, even their intellect— which is fixed upon Brahman— is abandoned by them when directed toward His qualities such as supreme beauty.
Regarding the phrase "therein, the final liberation":
because it is as difficult to understand as the story of Purañjana and so forth, this is an explanation of what was stated by [the author] himself;
for it is thus obtained through the power of the illustration.
And just as the word "Eidya" here includes the Karūṣa as well—
those two being Jaya and Vijaya— and for those inhabitants of the city of Vaikuṇṭha who are devoid of body, senses, and vital breaths:
"You ought to explain this which is connected with the relationship to a body"—
thus, by virtue of Śrī Yudhiṣṭhira’s question, although they both possess imperishable forms by virtue of having non-material (aprākṛta) bodies—
The Blessed One said to the two cowherds, "Go; do not fear; may there be peace!
Although I am capable of destroying the power of Brahmā, I do not wish to do so; this is my resolve," according to the words spoken by the Blessed One.

Thus, according to the prose section of the *Pādma Purāṇa* (Uttara-khaṇḍa), Jaya and Vijaya descended into the cycle of worldly existence solely for the sake of the Lord’s pastimes under the pretext of the curse of Sanaka and others; and likewise, for the amusement of attracting the hearts of His own devotees, He engages in sports such as battle.

By means of that very will, which brings about the impossible through its causal power, he entered three times into another body composed of the qualities and made of earth, [replacing] his own body of supreme light consisting of the *siddhis* such as *aṇimā*.
Therefore, regarding the verse in the seventh book, *kṛṣṇa-cakra-hatāṃhasau* (BhP 7.1.45), the commentary states: "Those two whose sins (*aṃhaḥ*) have been destroyed by Kṛṣṇa’s discus. (page 73)
"Of those two, only the sin was destroyed, but not they"—
this [is the meaning]. Likewise, for that very purpose, by the will of Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone, even here, their non-material (aprākṛta) forms [were preserved].
Thus, at the time of resisting his advance,
the inhabitants of Vraja— deluded by his illusory power— felt no resentment toward Kṛṣṇa,
believing each their own wives to be standing right by their own sides.
As in the expression "it is as if":
entry into that body composed of qualities which is imagined for that moment;
