The sense is that, based on such scriptural passages as *līlākṛṣṭasāraḥ* (BhP 12.12.69), they understand that the experience of such pastimes alone constitutes the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*).
In this context, all three goals are indicated by the word "here" (*iha*).
Even those who possess devotion to the Lord of Śrī-paravyoma and others have turned away [from Him];

and by the qualification "the son of the Gopikā," there is the impossibility of His being their son with respect to the attainment of happiness related to Him for those who were His devotees throughout the three periods of time.
The notions of being other than that and the possibility of separation are excluded;
therefore, by virtue of the reality of the experience of the wise, it is intended that their connection is indeed eternal. (p. 78)

For this very reason, He Himself points directly with His finger, saying, "This is the son of the cowherd woman. Therefore, it has been rightly said that the relationship between the two Lords of Vraja is indeed eternal.
Here, once at home—
The subsequent passage begins with "dāsīṣu" (BhP 10.9.1) and concludes with the two verses beginning with "nemaṃ viriñcaḥ" (BhP 10.9.20).

It was stated precisely as a sublation (*bādhaka*) of the preceding statement beginning with "Droṇa is the foremost of the Vasus," because of the contradiction with the former regarding another attribute.

If it is argued that [the term "non-existent"] does not apply because the previous [position] has been refuted and is illogical, we say no; for it is like the case [in the *Vaiśeṣika-sūtra*]: "Because of the designation of non-existence, [it is] not so, on account of another property, as [stated] in the remainder of the sentence" (Vs 2.1.17).
And in that context, just as with the word "non-existent,"...
An alternative course of action is considered here as well;
and that has already been shown previously in the two preceding chapters by Bādarāyaṇa, who intends this very point through the present section.

// 10.8 // Śrī Śuka // 151-152 // [153] Thus, in accordance with the declarations of the Vedas, Purāṇas, and other scriptures, the eternal manifestation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, His eternal sporting in Dvārakā and other places, and His eternal retinue consisting of the Yādavas and others— [are established].
And this has been demonstrated;
thus, it is well-established that the Lord Kṛṣṇa himself is indeed such. Now, an objection is raised: if the Lord known as Śrī Kṛṣṇa is eternally of such a nature, [then...]
It is heard that He dwells in various places together with His own retinue; however, it is said that by the prayers of Brahmā and others, Śrī Nārāyaṇa expanded Himself to such an extent.
If there is an entry of Him into Śrī Kṛṣṇa, then...
How is it that they abandoned the Lord Himself, who was eternally manifest in Dvārakā and other places, and went to report [the matter] to Him?
Or how is it that He came to Mathurā through the sequence of pastimes such as His birth?
It is said that He abandoned Gokula, Mathurā, and Dvārakā and ascended to Vaikuṇṭha;

to this, it is replied: He who eternally sports in Dvārakā and other places is the Supreme Lord Himself known as Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is higher than the highest and generally remains unmanifest even to Brahmā and the other gods.

It has already been stated that the Supreme Person, who possesses names such as Nārāyaṇa and whose pastimes reside in abodes such as the Ocean of Milk, is indeed Viṣṇu himself; appearing either directly or through his own partial expansion within those [beings], he is the performer of tasks such as the protection of the cosmic egg.
In that regard, even Brahmā and the others who hold authority over the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) ought to report the affairs of the cosmic egg to Him alone;
therefore, at that time as well, [they act] for the sake of removing the burden of the earth from Him alone.
They reported this.
Immediately thereafter, that man himself, by means of the sight of his hair and by such statements as "He, the Lord of lords, who bears the weight of the earth... (BhP 10.1.22), [addressed them].
Having indicated that this was indeed the time for the Blessed One’s own descent, she herself also desired to descend;
and that desire to descend, according to previous reasoning, manifested itself solely for the purpose of entering the Blessed One Himself.
Thus, even this ascent to Vaikuṇṭha and other realms occurs only through His respective portions.
But He Himself sports there in those very places again in a hidden manner;
regarding this, the scriptural passages from the Tantras, the Bhāgavata, and others, as well as from the Vārāha Purāṇa and so forth, have been cited.
And the scriptural statement should also be considered;
for instance, it will be cited: "The Blessed Lord Madhusūdana is eternally present there" (BhP 11.31.24), and so forth.
And this underlying intention is not understood by everyone;
for the sages describe things exactly as they have each perceived them.

Just as the Vedic revelation states that "this wonderful one rises in the morning from the very sight of those standing on the shore of the ocean and enters the waters in the evening," yet this occurs not in reality— so say the ancients.

If, in that case, a different interpretation is made by means of the statement regarding the circumambulation of Mount Sumeru and so forth, then why should it not likewise be made here as well by means of the statements establishing that the Blessed One himself dwells there eternally?
Likewise, statements regarding the abandonment of Mathurā and so forth refer only to the worldly pastimes manifested for common people during an incarnation; however,
those pastimes which are not manifested exist eternally.
Therefore, from the natural consistency of the concordance (*samanvaya*) of those scriptural passages that describe divine play (*līlā*) as being both eternal and consisting of birth and so forth,
this [conclusion] is obtained.
Just as Śrī Kṛṣṇa Himself, who eternally sports in various places while remaining unmanifest, becomes manifest through the pastimes of birth and so forth;
in that regard, Nārāyaṇa and others as well—

"Entering"—thus everything is peaceful. Therefore, in that regard, the pastimes (līlā) of Śrī Kṛṣṇa are of two kinds: unmanifest and manifest, due to their being unmanifest to worldly people and manifest to them respectively.
Among these, the unmanifest [state] is that wherein Kṛṣṇa, concentrated with his three powers, is established.
"The omnipresent Lord, together with Rukmiṇī, Rāmā, Aniruddha, and Pradyumna" (GTU 2.36).

Thus, in the *Śrī-Gopāla-tāpanī* and other texts that establish the reality of Mathurā, it is said: "In houses consisting of wish-fulfilling gems and clusters of desire-granting trees" (BhP 5.40), and so forth; likewise, in the *Brahma-*, which establishes the reality of Vṛndāvana—
And in the *Saṃhitās* and other texts, she is seen as slightly distinct from her manifest pastimes,
unmixed with worldly beings or their material objects.
It is a continuous flow devoid of distinctions such as beginning, middle,
or end, characterized by daily activities such as sitting in great assemblies appropriate for the status of Lord of the Yādavas and Crown Prince of Vraja, as well as pastimes like herding cattle.
Manifest in form like the Śrī-vigraha,

being indeed indefinable by time and other such factors, she— having attained her commencement and completion solely through the power of the Lord’s own essential nature (svarūpa-śakti) consisting of His will— is permeated by the objects of both the mundane and the non-mundane worlds, belonging to Him.
It is characterized by birth and so forth.
In that regard, it is unmanifest and twofold:
consisting of the practice of mantras and natural.
The first [type] is that which has a fixed station and so forth in one or another of those [locations], consisting of meditation on the respective mantra; as, for example,
the introduction to the *Bṛhaddhyānaratnābhiṣeka* and others in the *Kramadīpikā*, or as follows:
Now I shall describe meditation, which destroys all sins:
[one should meditate upon] Kṛṣṇa, who wears yellow garments and has eyes like lotuses.
Thus it is said in the *Gautamīya-tantra*, or as follows:
[He who] sounds the flute, whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals, who wears a peacock feather as a crest, whose body is as beautiful as a dark rain cloud,
and whose extraordinary splendor is more lovely than ten million gods of love—
I worship that Govinda, the primordial Person.
Wearing a forest garland shimmering with restless moonbeams and jeweled armlets, He is dark-complexioned, playful in the arts of amorous sport, graceful in His three-fold bend, and eternally radiant.
I worship that Govinda, the primordial Person.
Thus, in the *Brahma-saṃhitā* (5.39–40):
"Then, for the pleasure of Govinda, the fire-oblation (*homa*) should be performed as before. Immediately following this:
"One should meditate in the mind upon the auspicious Govinda, situated in the midst of cows."
Adorned with a crest of peacock feathers, he was intent upon playing the flute.
Surrounded by the gopīs, He wore forest flowers as His ear-ornaments.
Thus, in the *Bodhāyana-Karmavipāka-Prāyaścitta-Smṛti*,
Hairaṇya said this: [He saw] a cowherd’s attire, cloud-like, youthful, and resting upon the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpa-druma*).
Regarding this, there are these verses:
"The Lord has eyes like a beautiful lotus, the luster of a cloud, and garments of lightning;
he has two arms, is enriched by the gesture of silence (mauna-mudrā), and wears a garland of forest flowers."
Surrounded by cowherds, cowherdesses, and cattle, seated beneath a celestial wish-fulfilling tree,
adorned with divine ornaments, and situated in the midst of a red lotus.
Meditating in one's mind upon Kṛṣṇa, who is served by the breezes touching the waves of the waters of the Kālindī, one becomes liberated from the cycle of worldly existence.
Thus, in the *Śrī-Gopāla-tāpanī* [1.11–15]: "Govinda, the joy of Gokula, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss" (GTU 1.37), and so forth.
Furthermore, that which consists of various applications characterized by specific desires—taking forms such as the slaying of Pūtanā and others—whatever it may be...
"O You of wide renown, by their intellect they manifest Your various forms; You assume those forms for the sake of bestowing grace upon the virtuous.
According to this statement, even today that very worship consisting of mantra-practice sometimes flashes forth within the heart of the practitioner, as if occurring in the present;
yet, although it consists of mantra-worship, it ultimately culminates in its own natural state (svārasikī) through the realization of its transcendence.
Because it is taught everywhere.
Furthermore, the natural state is exactly as illustrated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Mādhava always sports with calves and heifers."
"Accompanied by Rāma and together with the boys, he entered the interior of Vṛndāvana," and so forth.
And there, by the word "ca" (and), Śrī Gopendra and others are included;
by the word "Rāma," Rohiṇī’s son [Balarāma] is meant.

Moreover, by the words "plays in that very same way" and so forth, even the pastimes such as visiting the cowherd settlement (*vraja*) and sleeping there are included. Since the word *krīḍā* (play) has the sense of *vihāra* (wandering or sport), and since *vihāra* consists of moving through various locations, this [pastime] is distinct from the worship consisting of mantra-recitation which is fixed to a single place.
Spontaneous and consisting of various desires according to the occasion;
thus it is said in the Brahma-saṃhitā:
In palaces made of heaps of wish-fulfilling gems, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of *kalpa* trees,
he was being attended with the bustling reverence of hundreds of thousands of goddesses of fortune (*lakṣmī*).
"I worship that Govinda, the primordial Person" (BrahmaS 5.28).
In this regard, the singing of stories, drama, and even the flute should be understood as referred to in BrahmaS 5.52.
In this regard, the natural [devotion] is like the Gaṅgā, consisting of a continuous flow of various divine pastimes (*līlā*).

However, that which consists of the worship of mantras should be understood as being like a series of lakes from which those [pastimes] have emerged, insofar as it takes the form of each individual pastime. Furthermore, even in the case of devotion consisting of mantra-worship, a connection with the King of Vraja and others is heard in scripture.
How much more so in the case of that which is natural? Thus, one should not imagine its absence anywhere;
all of this is also seen in the root authority (*mūla-pramāṇa*).
In that regard, the manifest form is indeed clearly evident.
Now, he speaks of the unmanifest form consisting of the worship of mantras:
"May Keśava protect me with his mace in the morning."
"Govinda, having taken up his flute at dawn," it is said.

By the specific epithet "having taken up his flute," Govinda is celebrated together with those two places— Śrī Vṛndāvana and Mathurā— which are renowned as great seats of yoga (*yoga-pīṭha*) by their very names.

And those two, appearing there in various places in the form of glorious images from the perspective of worldly people, are described as being actually present in person in the midst of the multitude of forms from the perspective of their own kinsmen.

And therefore, as the deity to be worshipped by the mantra known as the Nārāyaṇa-varma, [or rather] as the deity to be worshipped by other independent mantras well-known from such texts as the Śrī-Gopāla-tāpanīya.
And this has been declared regarding that [devotion] consisting of the worship of mantras.
// 6.8 // Viśvarūpa [said] to Indra: 153 // [154] Following the intended meaning of the Blessed One which is about to be stated, and because its meaning is clear, he states what is in fact natural—
"Do not grieve, O noble ones; you shall behold Kṛṣṇa nearby.
He dwells within the hearts of all beings, like light within fuel.
O noble ones, O Śrī-Vrajeśvarīs, do not grieve, for Śrī-Kṛṣṇa—
"You shall see it;
for how could that which remains in close proximity ever fail to be perceived?
Thus, because its remaining in close proximity is invariable.
The illustration is as follows: like the light characterized by the Supreme Self within the hearts of living beings, and like the light characterized by fire within fuel.
In that regard, for you, there is only the uninterrupted manifestation of that [light].

The meaning is that this is the authoritative proof (*pramāṇa*). However, in the case of another interpretation, because the status of the second half [of the verse] as a logical reason (*hetu*) is not clear,
and because there is no necessity for seeing [the Lord] even though He resides within the heart in the form of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), [that interpretation is untenable].
10.46 // Uddhava [to] the Queen of Śrī-Vraja // 154 // [155] Thus the Blessed Lord spoke: "My separation from you shall never occur in any way whatsoever."

This separation of yours from me does not exist at all, in every respect and by every manifestation; rather, it exists only by virtue of that single manifestation which shines forth in my manifest pastimes.
Separation; however, in the case of unmanifest pastimes (*aprakaṭa-līlā*), the meaning is that there is indeed union with another manifestation (*prakāśa*).
What is intended here is the *dāmodara-līlā*, beginning with the verse: "Neither within nor without does [He] exist," and so forth.
From the perspective of the *praghaṭṭaka* (the continuous narrative), and through the experience of Śrī Vrajeśvarī and others during the pastimes such as eating clay,
the omnipresence (*vibhutva*) of the Śrī-vigraha is seen to reside precisely within its medium size.
And that pair of mutually contradictory attributes exists together in Him, who possesses inconceivable power of omnipresence.
This has been explained in the section concerning the Blessed One by means of the reasoning: "But [it is] possible according to scripture, because [the Veda] has sound as its source.
Thus, since there is omnipresence (*vibhutva*), for the purpose of presiding over multiple locations simultaneously, there is another form—
Creation has been ground down like flour;
however, by that same inconceivable power which simultaneously manifests both mediocrity and omnipresence, according to His will, the single Śrī-vigraha appears in manifold ways.
It shines like a reflection through transparent limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*);

however, because it exists here solely by virtue of the limiting adjuncts, and due to the absence of direct contact with touch and so forth, as well as the rule that its emergence is contrary [to the original], it is not the actual reflection.
And while reflection (*pratibimba*) consists in being delimited,

here, however, because the Śrī-vigraha manifests through the radiance of His own singular power, through direct contact and so forth, arising according to His will, and by virtue of His omnipresence (*vibhutva*).
The distinction is that it is indeed the state of being a reflection (*bimba*).
In this very way, the Śruti declares the fullness of all manifestations as well:
"Full is that, full is this; from the full, the full arises.
When the full is taken from the full, the full alone remains. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.5.4).
And in that regard, by that very same inconceivable power, those manifestations possess their respective activities and so forth as distinct entities.
Therefore, there is no contradiction in the simultaneous manifestation of activities such as the closing and opening of the eyes, which depend on different modes of illumination.
For this very reason, even for that which is all-pervading (vibhu), [there is no contradiction] with respect to one another—
Even for one who takes recourse in a multitude of contradictory activities, his agency in those respective actions is indeed real.

That this reality exists is described in many places in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata and other texts; however, for the wise, the happiness arising from that [agency] would not be possible [if it were unreal]. Thus, the impossibility of that [happiness] otherwise is the proof here. In this way:
Intending this very point, the venerable Nārada said in the passage beginning with "O, how wonderful! By a single body, simultaneously and separately" (BhP 10.69.1):

although there is oneness of the body, there is a separate manifestation in those manifestations, and within those manifestations, there is the status of being the locus of separate activities and so forth; such power, however, does not exist elsewhere among the sages and others.
It has been stated that it is inherently variegated because it arises as such;
this very luminosity is sometimes referred to by the term "self" (ātman) and sometimes by terms such as "form" (rūpa).

Just as it is said in that very same place: "Indeed, he is not present there with his entire self," and "Having made himself of such a size elsewhere," and "The imperishable one, assuming such a form."
And it is said: "By Kṛṣṇa, whose body is His own will" (BhP 10.30.40).

In that regard, for the sake of nourishing the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of His pastimes (*līlā*), He generally assumes by His own will distinct notions of self-identity (*abhimāna-bheda*) among those manifestations and a lack of mutual awareness, precisely because they serve as the substrates for various activities and so forth.
It is indeed understood;
in this same way, it should be known that because they consist of that power, the same applies to their attendants as well. In those cases too, there is a distinction of manifestation.
As in the case of the marriage of the sixteen thousand maidens to Śrī Devakī and the others,
for it has been stated by the authors of the commentaries: "By this, even the simultaneous gathering of the kinsmen, such as Devakī and the rest, at every single house is indicated."

Among them and in Śrī Kṛṣṇa, there is a difference in their self-conception and activity due to the difference in their manifestations, as seen in the glory of Yogamāyā perceived by Śrī Nārada; for in that very place, in one instance, He was playing with dice, and even there, together with His beloved and Uddhava.
"He was honored with supreme devotion through rising from one's seat, offering a seat, and so forth" (BhP 10.69.20).
And while he was consulting with his ministers, such as Uddhava and others,

on some matter (BhP 10.69.27)— here, by the distinction between "there" and "elsewhere," a difference in the underlying sentiment (*bhāva*) and a resulting difference in self-conception (*abhimāna*) are indicated.
"This very person, in that same state, is I myself here"—
thus, at a certain sixteen-thousand-fold wedding of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
For Devakī, while performing auspicious rites in his presence, there is the bliss of beholding him;
but when he is out of sight, there is the longing to behold him.
It is the same regarding the vision of the majesty of Yoga-māyā.
In some places there is union with Uddhava, and in others separation; such is the variety.
Thus, while there exists a distinction in the manifestations [of the Lord], and while there remains a distinction in the activities of ego-inflation through that state, [the following occurs].

At that time, through the unmanifest manifestation (aprakaṭa-prakāśa) of Śrī Kṛṣṇa residing within the particular manifestation of Vṛndāvana, there occurs a union with those gopīs who are of the nature of unmanifest manifestations; this union is effected by that very manifest manifestation (prakaṭa-prakāśa) which was previously situated in that particular manifestation but has now gone to Mathurā and accepted [the role] in all three locations.

The statement regarding the eternal abiding of Śrī Kṛṣṇa along with His entourage would remain uncontradicted; for even if He, together with His entourage, were to depart at some time from the manifest pastimes to another place, He would continue to abide through another manifestation.
Therefore, it was rightly said by you: "My separation from you... and so forth.
And this state of eternal union is the supreme secret, described here through a metaphorical comparison to the knowledge of Brahman.
It has been taught by being veiled;
moreover, in other instances of secret instruction as well, speech is observed to be expressed while concealed by another meaning.
Just as Vidura did toward the Pāṇḍavas when they were going to the house of lac in the *Mahābhārata*,
or as the venerable Nārada did toward Haryaśva and others in the sixth [chapter],
so too does he instruct once again in that very same manner: [156]—
Just as the elements— ether, air, fire, water, and earth— reside within the elemental beings, so too do I reside as the substratum of the mind, the vital breath, the elements, the senses,
and the qualities. Just as the elements such as ether, which exist in their causal forms, reside within air and the others, which exist in their respective effects.
These [elements] are situated within the beings;
therein, the space resides in the air, the air in the fire, and so forth.
Likewise, the meaning is that although I am not perceived externally, I always abide within these beings.
Of what nature am I? I am the refuge of the minds and other faculties of you ladies, whose sole life-sustenance is me.
The implication is that otherwise, even for a moment, those very faculties would not endure in separation from me.

Alternatively, in response to the inquiry, "In what form do you abide?", he says: "I am indeed in that very form which serves as the locus for the minds and so forth of you ladies—the form of the two-armed, dark-complexioned, beautiful one who delights in the flute. [157]
One might object: "In that case, how could such a variety of manifestations occur, by which separation and union exist simultaneously?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By myself, within myself alone, I create, destroy, and protect myself."
By the power of my own *māyā*, which consists of the elements, the senses, and the *guṇas*, I myself,
by means of myself, manifest within myself— which is composed of infinite light and characterized by the glorious form— the self as a particular manifestation of light.

By what? By the power of His own inconceivable essential energy (*svarūpa-śakti*), which serves as the instrumental cause; that is, He is endowed with His own eternal power known as *māyā*. Thus it is stated in the *Caturveda-tātparya-nirṇaya* cited in the Madhva-bhāṣya.

From the crest-lock. Of what kind? "By that which has the elements, the senses, and the qualities as its self" (bhūtendriya-guṇātmanā); that is, by that which is the illuminator of the elements—which are the ultimate truths that are my senses—and of the qualities, such as form, taste, and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: in the reading "buddhīndriyaiḥ," the word "ātmanā" (by the self) serves as a qualifier. Here, "buddhi" refers to the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and "indriya" refers to the external organs (*bahiḥkaraṇa*).
The qualities are form and so forth; "by that" refers to that in which all of those constitute the self, that is, the essential nature.
Thus, having manifested, I may at some later time strike [it],
and then go elsewhere; for the root *han* signifies both "striking" and "going."
"Perhaps later on, I shall protect you again by coming myself; I will protect those who are distressed by separation from me"—this is the implied meaning.
As for the reason for this, it is because I am indeed yours... [BhP]
This will be explained in the beginning [of the section on verse 10.47.34].
Regarding the root *han* (to strike/kill) in its other senses, although three [factors] may share a single object and agent,
I sometimes cause that very Self to become concealed from manifestation.
Therefore, the meaning is: "Having drawn that light [into myself], I unify the diversity of lights.
In this very way, it was also explained by the Master (Svāmin) in the seventieth chapter of the *Daśamūla*: "Thus..."
"Having emerged individually from all the houses, immediately thereafter, he alone entered Sudharmā" (10.70.17). And as for the statement of Svāmī (?), cited in the Mādhva-bhāṣya (page 83):

"That God, the Supreme Person, who is devoid of qualities and manifold, becomes one again and lies down, the faultless Hari, the original creator. And the Śruti cited in the commentary of Śaṅkara states: "He becomes one-fold."

"He becomes twofold," and so forth; immediately thereafter, the meaning is that he protects that very self once more, and having manifested again, he brings about the bliss arising from play with his own supreme beings.

Thus, although the verb *hanti* is vulgar, there is no reason to suspect a fault, as it is employed here by the speaker himself through a shift in emotional state (*bhāvāntara*) born of compassion for those separated from him: "I would even cut off my own arm if it were to act against you."

"Just as in the verse [BhP 3.16.6], one might object: 'Surely You sport openly in Mathurā; how then can our conviction arise that You are sporting here now as well? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] describes their own experience."
He establishes this through authoritative proof:

"The Self consists of knowledge, is pure, distinct, and unassociated with the qualities; it is perceived through the states of deep sleep, dreaming, and waking, which are functions of *māyā*. [BhP 10.47.31]

Or rather, let alone the report of the absence of separation from Me during the unmanifest pastimes (*aprakaṭa-līlā*); even regarding the manifest pastimes (*prakaṭa-līlā*), let that [absence] be considered. Thus he says, "The self consists of knowledge," and so forth. And this is the meaning: in this context, the word *ātman* refers to the word *asmad* (the first-person pronoun).
And therefore, I, the Self characterized as Śrī Kṛṣṇa, am indeed perceived and experienced by you through the functions of the mind characterized as deep sleep and so forth.
Of what nature? Consisting of knowledge, he is proficient in various branches of learning. He is pure, being free from defects.
Or, he is "distinct" (vyatirikta) because that from which he has departed is excessive, or because he is pre-eminently distinct.
He is the most excellent, endowed with a lineage of virtues, and possessed of all qualities;
therefore, this experience, which is of the nature of a direct manifestation, is sometimes even conceived as occurring through direct perception (sākṣātkāra).
Thus, it should be understood as the cause for kindling [the memory] of those [qualities], even during long periods of separation.
In this context, even regarding deep sleep (*suṣupti*),
the mention of its manifestation has the sole purport of [showing] that "I am always manifest.
Or else, in that state...
It is already established that for them, dreaming and waking do not have distinct functions; for, due to the impossibility of any other state of consciousness,
even in that deep sleep characterized by samādhi upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa, those [states] belonging to dreaming and waking persist in that very same condition.
Because the various fluctuations (*vṛtti*) remain as mere impressions (*anubhāvitā-mātra*) of that [state], there is an entry [into it];
subsequently, just as ordinary people say "I slept happily," one reflects upon it with the thought "I was that [very state].
Thus it has been said.
For it is said in the Gāruḍa:
"Whatever mental modification arises for a yogin established in yoga during the states of waking, dreaming, or deep sleep, that becomes based upon Acyuta. [159]
[The opponent objects: "But even so, for us, separation alone manifests as the all-destroyer;
what can we do? Anticipating this doubt, [the author replies: "Alas! If [you] somehow wish to restrain the mental state that conceives of itself as being separated from me..."
Thinking that the state of eternal union will then emerge of its own accord, he explains the system of the Yoga-śāstra through two verses by means of such instruction:
"By which one might contemplate sense-objects as false, like a person awakened from a dream..."
He should restrain them; remaining wakeful, he attained this state.

Just as a man who has awakened continues to contemplate a dream that was entirely unreal, so too one should contemplate—that is, reflect upon—the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest, even though they have been sublated by that mind.
And meditating,
he should restrain that mind by which he attained— that is, reached— the sense-faculties, remaining wakeful and free from laziness.
Regarding the phrase "he should restrain":
although, as in the case of dreams and the like, the absence of that [world] in those [pastimes] is not superimposed by ignorance—
since that [absence] is not attained in the manifest pastimes because those [pastimes] are established by direct experience— nevertheless...

In order to cause one to contemplate eternal union within the unmanifest pastimes (*aprakaṭa-līlā*), it was appropriately stated by the Lord that instruction regarding Him must be given precisely as such;
even when the union exists in only a single aspect.
Or rather, that there is no separation at all.
He praises that very cessation of the mind: "This is the limit of the sacred tradition; it is Yoga, it is Sāṅkhya for the wise."
Renunciation, austerity, self-control, and truthfulness are like rivers flowing into the ocean.
This refers to that whose fruit is the internal cessation and completion of the mind;
"samāmnāya" means the Veda. That—
The meaning here is that it culminates therein.
Even though there are different paths, the illustration for their converging at a single point is:
"like rivers flowing toward the ocean."

Since the restraint of the mind is praised by all those who are learned in the Vedas and other scriptures, it is implied by these two verses that you too must restrain the mental activity characterized by the conceit of separation from me. [161]
Now, oh! If you, possessing such a compassionate heart, are teaching us the means for attaining yourself because we are so deeply distressed by separation from you,
then why do you not reveal yourself directly?
Thinking, "Since you did not come, this compassion of yours is merely a pretense," he says:
"But that I remain far away from you, though I am dear to your sight, is for the sake of drawing your minds near through the desire to meditate upon me. (BhP 10.47.34)
That I am now far away from your eyes, though I am dear to you,
is for the sake of that mental proximity which arises from your desire to meditate upon me; this is my abode for you.

The meaning is this: when you are standing nearby, my absorption (āveśa) may manifest through your sight; however, when you are far from me, it occurs only in the mind, and thus my proximity would exist there [in the mind]. [162]
He illustrates this very point:

"Just as the mind of women dwells upon their beloved who is far away, having entered into it, their consciousness does not function in such a way toward one who is nearby within the range of their vision. (BhP 10.47.35)
Because of the word "ca" (and), [the rule applies] also to one who is most beloved among women.
Regarding the contact with the mind, he says: "Let it be known that 'I shall be attained very quickly'—what would happen? [163]

"Having fixed your entire mind upon me, with all mental fluctuations— consisting of the longing for separation and its causes— completely abandoned, by constantly remembering me you shall soon attain me.
(BhP 10.47.36) That mind by which all fluctuations in the form of longing for separation and the contemplation of its causes have been abandoned is [fixed] upon me.
Having entered into My form as Kṛṣṇa and remembering Me as that very form of Kṛṣṇa, you shall soon come into My presence— indeed, you shall attain Me in such a way that I am known by no other.

If that is so, why do you not appear there openly? To this he replies: for the sake of attaining Him instantaneously and for the purpose of making known His eternal presence through other pastimes in Vṛndāvana itself, He gives an illustration:
"Those who were staying in Vraja while I was sporting in this forest at night..."
"May the auspicious ones, who have not yet attained the essence [of the rāsa], attain it by contemplating my prowess"—
the meaning is that this was for the purpose of deceiving external obstacles.
For they [were already present] at that night's manifest rāsa.

Even those who have not obtained even a mere fraction [of this], having become untouched by all obstacles right here in Vṛndāvana, have indeed attained Me, the treasury of manifest and diverse pastimes;
and thus it is said in the *Vāsanā-bhāṣya*:

The words of Mārkaṇḍeya: "At that very moment, the leaders of the cowherds attained through meditation the glorious Kṛṣṇa, who is affectionate toward his devotees and the embodiment of supreme bliss."
Even there, O auspicious ladies, you shall be free from all obstacles;
and in another sense, you shall remain with your very bodies. [The Vṛtti adds:
"With your bodies" means that by the casting off of those respective bodies, your attainment of Me would not occur; rather—]
The intention is that the attainment of Me shall occur with this very body.
Furthermore, the intention is that their casting off of the body and so forth is merely illusory (*māyika*).

Therefore, because they were not perceived through their manifestation in Vraja, and according to the words of Mārkaṇḍeya and the upcoming statement, "Thus indeed has devotion toward Me arisen in living beings" (BhP 10.82.44), their desired object—
Since the attainment of my own beauty and charm is already established, there indeed exists within this manifest pastime another distinct pastime;
and in that [other pastime], you also have your place, just as I do.
Let it be resolved:
that very pastime which, in accordance with my repeated promise to come to Vraja,
[shall be performed] immediately from the city of the Yadus, being constrained by love for you.

The meaning is: "Having come together, I shall constantly manifest myself to all the residents of Vraja, after first removing their respective obstacles, in a manner that is entirely consistent with everything. By the use of the word "in this" (*asmin*), He indicates that even at that time, He was situated in Vṛndāvana.
In this context, the following is stated:
for in this matter, the science of inner knowledge (adhyātma-vidyā) does not lead to their welfare.
"Therefore, for the yogi who is endowed with devotion to Me and whose very self is absorbed in Me,
neither knowledge nor detachment generally constitutes the highest good in this world," thus said the Blessed Lord.
For it has been stated by Brahmā that even for ordinary devotees, [knowledge] is not to be adopted, as in: "Having cast aside effort toward knowledge, they live only bowing down" (BhP 10.14.3);
nor is the flame of their separation extinguished by hearing of that [knowledge].
Without that dark-complexioned, heart-stealing one,
even for ordinary devotees— who, as stated in the direction of *BhP* 6.17.18, perceive the same essential purpose in heaven, liberation, and hell— [there would be no such realization].
Or, as stated in such passages as "They do not even reckon with that [divine] grace as ultimate," they experience it solely as something to be abandoned; however,
this is because of their own inherent nature (*svarasa*).
That is indeed utterly contradictory;
for it was previously stated: "First, let the beloved message be heard, which shall bring you happiness" (BhP 10.47.28).
Therefore, it was said by Śrī Svāmī himself when explaining their very intention: "Indeed, why do you entice us, who are not others, with the knowledge of the Self?
We, however, [seek] the most beautiful..."
"We cannot endure separation from you even for a moment, though you are adorned with every ornament.
Therefore, this is merely a deceptive statement on the part of Vidura; thus, the intended meaning becomes manifest as an internal truth.
"And he is accessible only to them, just as he is to Yudhiṣṭhira.
(10.47) Śrī Bhagavān [speaks to] the Goddesses of Vraja.
(155–164) [165] He speaks according to the previous explanation alone:

Having thus heard what was commanded by their beloved, those women of Vraja, filled with joy and having regained their memories through his message, spoke to Uddhava. "Those whose memories had returned by means of his message" refers to those whose recollection took the form of a constant contemplation of union with Him.
Therefore, they are delighted;

for beyond this, if there should ever be an experience of manifest pastimes, their satisfaction would arise from that, whereas from the manifestation of the pastimes itself, there is only separation—thus a duality of moods (bhāva) is observed. [166]
And regarding that contentment, it is said:
"Then, their fever of separation dispelled by Kṛṣṇa’s messages, they honored Uddhava, realizing themselves to be Adhokṣaja. [BhP 10.47.53]
"Thus he was instructed by him; that is to say, having experienced himself in that very way, and having experienced Adhokṣaja."—Śrī Śuka. (10.47) [165–166] [167]
They manifest their own separation:
"Will the descendant of Daśārha come here, tormented by the grief caused by his own actions, reviving us with his limbs as Indra revives the forest with rain-clouds? (BhP 10.47.44)
"Scorched by grief caused by their own [separation from] their kinsmen, will He perhaps come here to revive us with His limbs through the touch of His hands and so forth?"

10.47 // The Goddesses of Śrī-Vraja to Uddhava // 167 // [168] Thus it was instructed by the illustrious Uddhava through his intermediacy, and likewise it was instructed directly by Him himself at Kurukṣetra. (page 86)

[Vṛ. adds: Even during the pilgrimage to Kurukṣetra—do you not remember us, O friends, who went out for a long time out of a desire to accomplish the welfare of our own people, with our minds intent on the destruction of the enemy faction? (BhP 10.82.41)
Having thus informed them of the reason for the delay in his arrival, he spoke again:
"Indeed, devotion toward me leads living beings to immortality;
by good fortune, you have possessed such love for me that it has brought me here. [BhP 10.82.44] (End of Vṛtti)

In this context, the fruit for such [gopīs] is the direct attainment of Him himself, and not merely immortality as it is for others; this follows immediately after the Lord’s words, which were intended to provide them with consolation. [An objection:
"But you always sport in Dvārakā, while we dwell in Vṛndāvana; how [can this be]?"
Fearing that you might think, "We shall attain [him]," he teaches such a Self with two verses, [showing] that "I am indeed eternally united with you.
[The Vṛ had instead of the above paragraph:]

Having thus declared their inevitable attainment of Him, and observing that even then they were unable to endure any delay of time, He Himself— just like the message sent by means of Uddhava as a messenger for the sake of immediate consolation— [proceeded with His own eternal...]
He teaches the union:
"For I am the beginning, the end, the inner, and the outer of all beings—
just as ether, water, earth, air, light, and women are among material things."
For thus these elements are [perceived] within the elements by means of the self within the self; then, behold both of these manifested within Me, the supreme, imperishable One.
Just as I am the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*), the source of the elements, the beginning and end of all elements such as space and the rest—
"Form" (rūpaḥ) means that space and the other elements are indeed included within the ego (ahaṅkāra).
And just as the elemental substances such as space constitute the beginning, end, and intermediate forms of material objects such as bowls and salt; [so it is with the elements].
The meaning is that these are indeed included within the *khādis*.
Thus, these [pastimes], being experienced during the manifest pastimes (*prakaṭa-līlā*), have become objects of your possessive attachment; yet they are the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*).
The entities such as Śrī Vṛndāvana and so forth exist within those ultimate realities which, though they are the objects of the unmanifest pastimes among the elements, remain concealed;
whereas your own self is the locus of the ego that identifies with the manifest pastimes.

And it is pervaded by the Self, which is the locus of "I-ness" (ahantā) conceiving itself as the subject of unmanifest pastimes; thus, that which is both the locus of "this-ness" (idantā) and "I-ness," even while manifest here in this visible world, remains eternally yours within that imperishable realm where He sports in the forest of Vṛndāvana.
"Behold that which appears and shines forth within me, who am of the nature of the locus of attachment.

Therefore, it is solely due to the differentiation of manifestation that there is the designation of the distinctions between this or that object and so forth, as well as the determination of separation and conjunction.
And this is also clearly evident here:
the venerable sage spoke in accordance with the training of the Blessed One— those who were thus instructed by Kṛṣṇa through spiritual instruction are indeed to be protected.

They attained Him by means of the constant remembrance of that which was thus instructed— [an instruction] concerning the Self, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, through spiritual training (*adhyātma-śikṣā*) and His direct teaching (*upadeśa*). By such remembrance, the sheaths of the individual soul (*jīva-kośa*) were destroyed, [revealing] the eternally perfect and unmanifest...

Those [energies] by whom the phenomenal world— the sheath of the individual soul (jīva-koṣa)— which has been destroyed and almost abandoned through the renewed contemplation of Līlā, as well as the attachment to its manifestation therein, have been [removed];
they [are the energies] who themselves taught that which is eternally united.
They perceived Śrī Kṛṣṇa as their very form, having fixed their minds upon Him;
even there, they recalled the statements regarding His eternity found in the Vedas and Purāṇas previously shown, such as: "For devotion to Me indeed... (BhP 10.82.44).
And having considered such statements as "The statement regarding the distinction of fruits is neither knowledge nor detachment" (BhP 11.20.31), which indicate that [the literal sense] is improper,
one should not interpret them as having a different meaning intended for indirect discourse (*parokṣa-vāda*).

The object of knowledge (*prameya*): Now, those who do not accept the manifest meaning (*prakṭārtha*) as being of the nature of cognition, yet accept the secret meaning (*rahasyārtha*) as being of the nature of eternal pastimes (*nitya-līlā*),
nevertheless remain, as before, fearful of separation due to their attachment to the manifest pastimes (*prakaṭa-līlā*).
Thus, they prayed with the utmost dejection; so he says:
"And they said: 'O You whose navel is like a lotus, [we pray for] Your lotus-feet, which are meditated upon in the heart by the masters of yoga possessed of unfathomable wisdom.'"

May that support for crossing over the pit of saṃsāra always arise in the minds of us who dwell in the household, even though we are struck down by ill fortune; let alone the scent or even the report of Your vision, O Lord! He... [BhP 10.82.48]
O Nalinanābha, may your lotus-foot arise within our minds in accordance with your instruction.
Indeed, what is there that is impossible?
Regarding this, they say: "This should be contemplated in the heart by the masters of yoga alone, but not by us, who fall into a swoon at the very commencement of remembering You.
Thus it was said by the Blessed One himself to Uddhava:
"O dear one, while I, the dearest of their beloveds, am staying far away, those women of Gokula, remembering me, faint away, overwhelmed by the longing of separation.
Thus they explain this very point: even when there is direct perception by those of unfathomable wisdom, they remain unperturbed—
[They see] with their intellects—
not, however, like us, whose intellects are agitated by the desire for a vision of you. Furthermore,
the metaphorical identification of your foot as a lotus is such that the cooling of its burning occurs only through contact with you, and not otherwise.
The phrase "in that way, by the remembrance of you" is used for the purpose of making this known.

Now, one might object: "Surely, in the same way, profound meditation (nididhyāsana) itself will remove your pain of separation—just as it removes the suffering of worldly existence for the lords of yoga—and bring about its cessation. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
This is a support for crossing over only for those fallen into the well of saṃsāra, but not for us who are submerged in the ocean of separation;
for at the very commencement of thinking of you, we experience only an increase in our suffering.
This is the intended meaning. [Objection:
"But surely, having just arrived, you have experienced me directly again and again";
to that he says: "the home..."
The meaning is "of those who enjoy the houses of others," that is, of those who are not independent;
or alternatively, "of those who enjoy their own homes. And your association [with me] shall take place in that abode of the pastimes of our former union, which grants all our desires.

The meaning is that, due to a particular personal desire— namely, "May [He] reside only in Gokula, His own home and the natural abode of our love, and not in Dvārakā or elsewhere"— [the phrase] "of those who have affection for Him alone" is used. He who...
Just as in the expression, "He alone is the bridegroom who takes away one's maidenhood," and so forth;
therefore, because we lack the capacity to contemplate Your feet in our minds, and because we lack the power to come of our own accord, and due to a lack of inclination—
Or rather, the sense is that if you come directly to Śrī Vṛndāvana itself, only then will there be deliverance;
[the Vṛ edition adds here:
the Blessed Lord accepted this very sentiment].
As it was said immediately following this:
"Thus questioned and highly honored by the Lord of the World, they, their sins destroyed by the sight of His feet, replied with joyful minds. [BhP 10.83.2] [end Vṛ]
[Addition] // 10.82 // Śrī Śuka // 168–170 // [171] Thus, the spontaneous and manifest pastimes have been shown.
Now, He describes both [pastimes] through their specific purposes, even though they are not manifest: "Of all embodied beings, including the gopīs and their husbands..."
"He who moves within is the overseer; here, by means of play, he assumes a body as one possessing a physical form.

Thus, while remaining unmanifest within the interior of the gopīs, their husbands, and those who considered themselves their masters—acting as one who possesses a body for the sake of play—he appeared to them as the crown prince of Gokula.

And he who moves about as the presiding lord (adhyakṣa) and sports— even while having entered into manifest pastimes— becomes the possessor of a body for play even for all embodied beings dwelling within the universe; thus, being their protector, he moves about as their presiding lord.

Therefore, since from time immemorial they have been accepted as being characterized by play with them, there is in reality no fault of adultery even in union with those who are of the nature of their [divine] powers.
Consequently, they attained the status of being His wives,
according to the manner that will be described in the passage beginning with, "They indeed felt no envy toward Kṛṣṇa" (BhP 10.33.37).

For them and for those women, it is merely a matter of perception and not physical; and the production of such a perception is for the sake of nourishing their longing— thus has the ultimate limit of the established doctrine of that context been shown.
(88) [172] Thus, through the various distinctions of those respective pastimes, even though it is one, there is a distinction in the manifestation of each respective place, just like the Śrī-vigraha.
Thus it has been said in the Śruti: "The supreme station of Vṛṣṇi shines forth abundantly.
In that [station], however, due to its inclusion within the other pastimes (līlās), no specific space for those other pastimes is generally perceived.
Moreover, even within the manifest pastime (prakaṭa-līlā), a variety of spaces is observed precisely through their non-intermixture.
Just as within the city of Dvārakā, which measures only twelve *yojanas*, there exist objects such as ten million houses measuring two *krośas* each;
and just as in the small pit of Govardhana, there is that—
The entrance of countless cowherd settlements;

just as Brahmā perceived that Vṛndāvana, with its trees, grass, birds, and so forth, possessed space sufficient for itself and yet provided space for infinite objects such as the cosmic eggs and beyond. Just as...
And likewise, in the *Śrī-Nārada-dṛṣṭa-yoga-māyā-vaibhava*, it is stated that at the very same time, the morning, midday, and evening pastimes and so forth occurred simultaneously in Dvārakā.
Thus, regarding Vṛndāvana:
Examples of the different types of manifestations are now illustrated.
Among them, that which follows the unmanifest pastimes is as described in the *Yāmala*, in the dialogue between Rudra and Gaurī:
In every street dwell those who possess sweet speech like the nectar of the lower lip;
among them, some sport in the *santānaka* trees, which are as bright as the rays of ten million rising moons.
And among them, at the end of the night, when Rāma has risen, are others comparable to the ocean illuminated by the splendor of the sun.
Some of those lordly trees possess the luster of mirrors inlaid with gold upon their jewel-like branches.
O fair-faced one, whatever flower is sought after and whatever fruit is desired,
the divine trees of Vṛndāvana produce that very thing at that very moment.
And the meaning is as follows: O Gaurī, whose sweet words are like the honey of the lower lip— O you who possess such speech—
in that Śrī Vṛndāvana, of the rathāṅgas (cakravāka birds) and the santānaka trees...
In their midst, O Rāma, are certain lords of trees, whose rays are as bright as the light of ten million moons;
and among those *santānaka* trees are some that, at the end of the night, resemble the ocean illuminated by the rising sun.
They shine in the Kamadhātu;
some, having transcended those [realms],
shine there— of what nature are they?
"Having the luster of mirrors inlaid with gold":
therein, whenever whatever flower is sought and whenever whatever fruit is sought, at that very moment the divine trees of Vṛndāvana bring them forth.
Thus it is said;
likewise, in the *Brahma-saṃhitā*, within the hymn to Govinda, the Original Person, it is stated:
"The beloveds of Śrī are the trees of plenty, and their beloved is the Supreme Person."
The trees are made of clusters of wish-fulfilling gems, the ground is composed of them, and the water is nectar;
the conversation, the song, the dance, and even the movement of the flute— all these, O dear friend, are the supreme light of consciousness-bliss, which is itself to be tasted.
I worship that Śvetadvīpa, which they here call Goloka, where the milk-ocean flows and where even the great time known as half a *nimeṣa* does not pass.
"Only a few of them, being wise and dwelling in rare intervals of time, know You.

(Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya 5.56). Thus, that which exists there in the form of the sun and other luminaries—which does not perish even during the great dissolution for the sake of the sweetness of worldly play—is the Supreme, consisting of consciousness and bliss, which is to be attained by them in whatever measure it may be.
Moreover, it is the supreme reality itself and not the material (prākṛta);
for the station of the moon and sun therein is described in the Gautamīya-tantra as being distinct, namely, "the moon and sun risen together."
This is a qualification of Vṛndāvana.
Furthermore, there is equality because it consists of the full moon night (rākā-candra) every single night;
"api ca" connects with what follows.
(Page 89) It has been stated that due to the immersion in rasa (*rasāveśa*), the observance of the rule (*samaya*) does not lapse precisely because of that very ignorance [of the rule].
Otherwise, if there were an absence of sequence between preceding and succeeding moments, there would be no such thing as "play" (*līlā*), which consists essentially of purposeful activity.
There would be a loss of its own nature.
"White" means pure and free from defects; "island" means that, like an island, it is devoid of attachment to anything else and is supreme in every respect.
This has been stated by the Śruti: "Just as a lotus stands in a lake, so does it stand upon the earth.
Furthermore, Brahman—
In the *Saṃhitā* itself, at the beginning of its praise of Him, it says: "In palaces made of wish-fulfilling gems and surrounded by millions of *kalpa*-trees" (*BrahmaS* 5.29), and so forth.
Likewise, in the *Nārada-pañcarātra*, in the dialogue between Śruti and Vidyā:
Then, in the four cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, below, and above Śvetamahādvīpa,
there are the lords of the quarters, the waters, and the oceans of milk and nectar.
There is the Great Vṛndāvana, as well as the various pleasure-groves of Vṛndāvana;
its trees are celestial wish-fulfilling trees, and its ground is composed of cintāmaṇi jewels.
There were also hundreds of thousands of play-birds and numerous fragrant flowers,
as well as grounds for the rāsa-maṇḍalas, resplendent with various wonderful and diverse beauties.
Ah, the pleasure-groves and bowers, the sites of various delights,
and the ancient jewel-parasols— the hoods of Śeṣa shine forth!
"Since the splendor of the incomparable radiance of the multitude of crest-jewels belonging to those [gopīs] shines there as Brahman itself, who is capable of describing its form?
Thus, Goloka is indeed the manifestation of Śrī Vṛndāvana that follows its unmanifest pastimes.
This has been explained.
Among the two types of unmanifest pastimes (*aprakaṭa-līlā*) therein, that which consists of the practice of mantra (*mantropāsanāmaya*) is somewhat distinct.
And he is arranged in those respective mantras in specific places of play as they have been shown;
as, for example, in the *Pūrvatāpanīya*.
And as it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa in the words of Śrī Nārada: "In that Vṛndāvana, which is the meritorious abode of Govinda and is crowded with His servants, there alone do I reside."

"O King, on this earth, Govinda-Vaikuṇṭha is located in that Vṛndāvana where the servants headed by Vṛndā reside, longing for Govinda. Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding the manifestation associated with the manifest pastimes (prakaṭa-līlā), it is found in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa, Harivaṃśa, and other texts.

This very manifestation is well-known; at that time, it was seen even by some ordinary people who possessed the arising of a particular fortune, and now a portion of it is seen by us as well. But here—
That which appears as if it were an ordinary region should be understood as being due to the Supreme Goddess’s own will, in that She has voluntarily assumed specific worldly pastimes;
this is because of the Supreme Lord—
Because those abodes have been established as authoritative by both Śruti and Smṛti through qualities such as being entirely beyond conceptual proliferation (prapañca),
it has therefore been stated in the Ādivārāha:

"Those who dwell in Mathurā are indeed the very forms of Viṣṇu; those lacking knowledge do not see them, but those with the eye of wisdom do see them. Thus, even according to this fundamental authority, the manifestation of Śrī Vṛndāvana is associated with the unmanifest pastimes.
And those cowherds, O King, were of such eager minds; this has already been shown in the passage beginning with "Knowing him to be the Lord" (BhP 10.28.11).
As for his engagement in manifest pastimes, it is as follows:
Oh! These [beings], having taken up their own topknots, bow down to your lotus feet— which are worshipped by the best of gods and immortals, and which are worthy of offerings of flowers and fruits.

"Whatever birth as a tree was brought about for the sake of dispelling darkness," and so forth; taking up the worship in the form of flowers and fruit belonging to themselves, they bow with their own crests— that is, by means of those very things.
"This birth as a tree was brought about for the sake of dispelling the darkness of those transmigrating beings who hear and see"—
this is either a *tatpuruṣa* compound with the third case (instrumental), meaning "that which was done by [the tree]."
// 10.15 // The Blessed Lord [spoke] to Śrī Baladeva. [172] [173] And as it happened—
immediately looking all around, he beheld [him] standing before him.
Vṛndāvana is filled with trees that provide sustenance for the people and is dear to all.

"Where even men, wild beasts, and other creatures, who by nature harbor mutual enmity, dwelt together like friends; where anger, thirst, hunger, and the like were quickly overcome as if they were enemies. And so forth.
(Page 90)
It is dear in every respect and in its entirety even to those who delight in the Self (samānām ātmārāmāṇām), as well as to their equal companion, the Blessed Lord (śrī-bhagavataḥ). In this regard,
the presence of any unreal portion is denied.
It has been demonstrated that [it] bestows an excellence of bliss from every perspective.

// 10.13 // Śrī Śuka // 173 // [174] Thus, those very places have been shown as the locus of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes. However, that restriction would be inconsistent given the all-pervading nature (vibhutva) of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
In that regard,

since those places are heard of as being the eternal locus of His pastimes, it is understood that they constitute His own essential manifestation (*svarūpa-vibhūti*) characterized by the power that serves as their substratum— as in the question: "O Blessed One, in what is He established?"
This is because of the Vedic revelation, "In his own majesty" (ChāU 7.24.1),
and because of the scriptural instruction, "The city of Brahma-Gopāla is manifest" (GTU 2.26).
Then, his play occurs right there without any interval;
because others are of a material nature, even direct contact with that [play] is not possible for them, let alone the power to sustain it.

"And by means of a single light, he went to Dvāravatī.

The meaning is that, by the grace of Vāsudeva— manifesting suddenly as a supreme favor— they assumed divine forms and, through the blossoming of their joy, attained an appearance even more wonderful than before. Then, by means of his own chariot, the crest-jewel of celestial vehicles, having first brought her to the southern shore, he secretly established his residence within that very special manifestation of the splendor of Śrī Vṛndāvana— which had previously been shown as Goloka to the illustrious cowherds.

Regarding the phrase "attainment of Vaikuṇṭha": according to the maxim, "If one should find honey near at hand, why go to the mountain?", the indeclinable word *akke* is used in the sense of proximity.

[176] And therefore, because one does not perceive a distinction between the manifest and unmanifest modes of play (*līlā*), there is the state of being unmanifest.

At some time, in accordance with the words of the Blessed One, "The Truthful One, Acyuta, will thus come to Vraja after a very long period" (BhP 10.46.34), and in accordance with the speech of the subjects residing in Dvārakā, "O lotus-eyed one, when will you depart for the Kurus or the Madhus? When I went for the sake of seeing them, they were such that their minds were bound by the subsequent attachment— which brings about the manifestation of a state of great joy— and by the reunion [with Me]; thus being so, they [concealed] their own selves, which are the objects of "mine-ness" (mamatā) and the locus of the ego (ahaṅkāra), as well as this [reality], which was unmanifest.
The meaning is that they did not perceive this either as being considered subordinate to the internal pastimes (*līlā*), or as being considered subordinate to the manifest pastimes (*prakaṭa-līlā*);

The intended meaning is that one does not perceive, as distinct entities, the two-fold manifestation (prakāśa), the two-fold conceit (abhimāna), and the two-fold play (līlā), which are differentiated by way of being manifest and unmanifest.
And thus, name and form [arise] within that very [reality].

The meaning is that they have entered, as it were, into the self of name-and-form (nāma-rūpa), which is a particularity of unmanifest light; yet they have not truly entered, because of their non-difference [from that light].
"Name-and-form" (*nāma-rūpa*) is a collective compound.
In that regard, the illustration for the non-difference between name and form as they exist within manifest and unmanifest pastimes is: "just as sages in meditative absorption."

In this context, "concentration" (samādhi) is understood to mean that the soul is pure. Regarding the non-perception of the distinction between those two *līlās*, the illustration is this: it pertains only to the aspect of making known the ocean of *līlā*, and not to the aspect of knowing everything, as in the case of the principle stated in [PMS] 2.1.33: "But as in the world, there is the uniqueness of the *līlā*. [177]

Because it is the supreme reality that must be resorted to as the substratum of all attributes, and because it persists through those attributes without distinction, there is "Brahman, which is one only, without a second" (ChāU 6.2.1), according to the Śruti.

However, qualifiers such as "supreme" (*param*) and so forth, although non-different from that [reality], serve as differentiators for each individual instance, according to the Śruti: "He becomes one-fold; he becomes two-fold," and so on.
