In this way, the twofold nature is to be understood even in the case of the cows and others. To what did they attain? He says: "Me alone, known by the name Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman in human form."
From the Purāṇa section:
"Among the incarnations, which one will be the most excellent incarnation? How does this incarnation possess the nature of Brahman? [GTU 2.13], and from the Tāpanīya Upaniṣads.

Regarding what kind of relationship they have with you, he says: "the lover, the paramour. The term *ramaṇa* means "husband," but here its etymological sense is set aside by the context, just as the word *nandana* [can mean both "son" and "delighter"].
Just as the son of Mitrā is called "Mitrānandana" (the delighter of Mitrā), but not "Mitrāpati" (the husband of Mitrā);
and even the husband of Mitrā is called "Mitrārāmaṇa" (the lover of Mitrā), but not [otherwise].
Regarding the term "mitrā-putra," this is the meaning: just as in the expression "he makes a beautiful, large, and pleasing mat (bhīṣmam udāram darśanīyam kaṭam karoti)," [the same applies here].

Indeed, an action, while conveying the performance of a particular [object], also conveys its qualifiers, according to the manner of such expressions as "he makes a mat, and that one beautiful. Likewise here too, Brahman is attained.

And they attained that supreme form of the Blessed One— that very form of the Blessed One known as Śrī Kṛṣṇa— by way of such expressions as "I myself. However, because of the specific use of the term "lover" (jāra), there is a particularity in their amorous dalliance.

Thinking that "when [the object] is obtained, the state of being a lover should be even greater," it conveys a superior meaning according to the maxim that "an increase in syllables implies an increase in meaning";
and in that case, the meaning belongs specifically to the additional word.
It culminates through effort, and the state of being a lover arises merely from the perception [of the object], as in the case of the cowherd women and their husbands and so forth;
however, even though [the objects] are common [to all], this is because the Supreme Brahman is the whole of everything.
Because He is the protector of all, He is indeed the Lord (pati).
As it was said by Piṅgalā: "By delighting with the Self" (BhP 11.8.39), and "He rejoiced with Him as Ramā does" (BhP 11.8.34).
And by Lakṣmī-devī as well;
he indeed shall be a husband who has no fear from any quarter,
for he himself protects on all sides the people afflicted by fear.
Thus [it is said in BhP 5.18.20]. Therefore, those who previously perceived him as their paramour later attained him in his very own true form.
Likewise, if he were merely called a "paramour," the ultimate conclusion would not be established.
(Page 98) It is called "Ramaṇa.
If it were merely called "Ramaṇa," his status as the Blessed Lord and his form as Śrī Kṛṣṇa would not be established.

When "me" (mām) is thus spoken, the state of being Brahman and the state of being Bhagavat remain in need of further evidence; therefore, each of those is stated directly. Since [the word] was previously understood as "lover" (jāra), even by the word "delighting" (ramaṇa), only the state of being a lover might be perceived; hence, for the purpose of excluding that, each of those—
And a rearrangement must necessarily be made;

for in these words beginning with "brahma māṃ paramam," since the order of recitation is not intended to be significant and because the state of being a lover (*jāra*) occurs first, the sequence is indeed based on the sense (*ārthika*).
This very [rule] is stronger in all cases;
therefore, the meaning must not be construed by way of reversal.
Furthermore, this is according to the logical principle that "the scripture is purposeful only with respect to what has not [otherwise] been obtained."

Just as in the case of "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*) and similar injunctions, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) applies only to the previously unestablished state of being the Beloved (*ramaṇa*), and not to those already established in succession, beginning from Brahmā and ending with the paramour (*jāra*). This is as expressed in the verse:
"O Goddess, make the son of Nanda-gopa my husband; salutations to you. [BhP 10.22.4] Thus it is established.

If it is argued that for these young girls, the fulfillment of their conception of a husband is required, then the Blessed Lord must certainly bring about the perfection of the resolve of those who are faultless in nature.
And in that very regard:

In passages such as "She went of her own accord" (*svayam aṅgīkṛtaṃ yātābalā*) and so forth, it is established that they were indeed [the gopīs], as indicated by the words "by me" (*mayā*) and "thus" (*iti*).

This is known from the *Sahasranāmastotra*: "He who is the supreme, great Brahman," and also from the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "The auspicious substratum of one's own mind, the all-pervading self, such as it is."

And they attained me, who am such and known as Kṛṣṇa, for the Purāṇic texts state, "The Supreme Brahman is of the form of Kṛṣṇa," and the Śrī Gītā Upaniṣads state, "I am indeed the foundation of Brahman" (Gītā 14.27). Therefore—
The attainment of that very form by themselves was declared by the Blessed Lord Himself in those verses:
"Having fixed your entire mind on Me, with all other mental fluctuations abandoned,
by constantly remembering Me, you shall before long come to Me" (BhP 10.47.36).
"Indeed, devotion to Me leads all beings to immortality;
by good fortune, you have had such affection for Me that it has brought you to Me. Thus [He spoke].
Furthermore, He says that they attained Him in such a way as to be permeated by a particular state of being: "those who desire Me" (mat-kāmāḥ).

Regarding the phrase "the lover, the enjoyer, for one who does not know his true nature," by the word *ramaṇa* (enjoyer) it is specifically the husband who is meant; for the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) of the word *nandana* (delighter) as "son" sets aside its etymological sense (*yaugikatva*).
Just as by the term "Mitrānandana" (the delighter of Mitrā) here only the son of Mitrā is meant, and not the husband of Mitrā,
so it is with the term "Mitrāramaṇa" (the lover of Mitrā).
And [he is] the husband of Mitrā,
but not the son of Mitrā; likewise here as well, according to the opinion of the Kośa, [it is] the lover (ramaṇa).
The word *pati* is conventionally established (*ruḍha*) as referring only to a husband.

Just as there might be pleasure (*ramaṇa*) in the root of a *paṭola* plant, so too the word *ramaṇa* refers to a beloved; and when there is a connection with the class of noble women, the word *priya* denotes only the husband, just like the word *ramaṇa*.

This is because it is well-established in that very way, and because the *Amarakośa* states: "The *dhava*, the *priya*, the *pati*, and the *bhartṛ* [are synonyms for husband]. Furthermore, while in the world *patitva* (the state of being a husband) consists in the acceptance of a maiden through marriage, in the case of the Blessed One, it exists by his very nature as well.
Indeed, the state of being the husband of Mahālakṣmī for the Lord of the Supreme Ether (Paramavyomādhipa) is seen to be established from time immemorial (*anādisiddha*).
For the word *jāra* everywhere denotes only a lover (*upapati*), according to the Amarakośa: "The words *jāra* and *upapati* are synonyms.
And the state of being a lover (*upapatitva*) consists in being perceived [as such] through unrighteousness (*adharmena*).
Just as there is the nature of being a pseudo-property (*upadharma*) and the state of being treated as a property (*dharmīyamānatva*) in what is not a property (*adharma*),
so it is in both cases. (Page 97)
Because it contradicts the Vedas;
for the *Trikāṇḍa-śeṣa* states that "jāra" and "pāpa-pati" (the husband of sin) are synonyms.
Consequently, the state of being a *jāra* does not exist in the act of sexual union.
The state of being a lover does not exist in a paramour,
because their relationship is one of opposition, like that between dharma and adharma or between a master and a thief; this being established, [the phrase] is like "Brahman is my supreme [Self]."

The states of being a paramour (*jāra*) and being a lover (*ramaṇa*) cannot coexist in a single substratum. Therefore, by distinguishing between those women who are eligible [for the practice], he reconciles these two roles through a difference in their qualifications;
for that purpose, he shows that one is real while the other is unreal, stating: "those who desire me are my lovers."

Thus, by these two statements— "for one who does not know the true nature [of the lover]" and "the loverhood [is perceived] there"— the masters have accepted that the state of being a lover (*jāratva*) is merely phenomenal and unreal, and not anything else;
even though it is cognizable through the notion of a lover (*jāra-buddhi*).
Because it has already been stated; and this very point will be established by us later on.
Therefore, the meaning is as follows:
not knowing their own essential nature to be that of an eternally beloved woman for me...

The meaning is that, through the power of the pastimes beginning with their birth, they forgot Me and obtained paramours; even though this was perceived as contrary to dharma, because of their excessive passion, they accepted them as paramours. Furthermore, the phrase "even while obtaining them, they were desirous of Me" refers to the fact that, O dear one, they continued to attend upon their husbands, children, and friends (as described in BhP 11.5.42).
In this manner, how might my particular longing and desire for [anyone] other than Him dissolve like a dream,
so that Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone may manifest as my husband, as if in a waking state? Such is the form [of her prayer].
"For those women, such as they were, have attained me in the very form of their lover"—
it is for this very purpose that,
having set them apart, my two qualifiers are joined with their two qualifiers as "those who desire me."
Regarding the word "rāmaṇam" (delight):
it has been read [in the commentary] as "jāra-svarūpa-vidaḥ" (knowing the nature of the paramour), according to the context;
however, it does not mean that Brahman is my supreme [delight].
Thus, together with these [verses], this has been composed;
and herein, even their own prayer is seen, in order to manifest that state of being his own among their own people.
For, in the verse beginning "Alas! The noble son now stays in the city of Madhu" (BhP 10.47.21), she first reveals her perception of him as her master through the word "his" (*tadīya*);
then, out of wretchedness, she denies that very perception by saying "there among the maidservants" (*kiṅkarīṇām*); and finally, out of longing, she [returns to her former state].

By the verse beginning with "bhujam aguru-sugandham" (BhP 10.47.21), it is clearly understood that Śrī Rādhā-devī has expressed her longing for His acceptance of them as Her own, manifesting this through the very act of claiming Him as Her own. Furthermore, the humility shown here—even in the desire for the status of a wife—is expressed as: "O Śyāmasundara, we are Your maidservants."
This is understood from such statements; moreover, there is a clear prayer for their acceptance [of him], as in:
"Even though you have gone to me alone—who am your beloved and dearest self—with your minds" (BhP 10.46.4).
By the words "these cowherd girls are mine" and "they belong to my very self," it is evident that even in his mind there exists the feeling of ownership toward them;
nevertheless, [the Lord] maintains [them] with great difficulty, and so forth.
His intention was that if we were to come and clearly accept [his view] according to his own perspective, only then would our deliverance occur;
therefore, it was rightly explained by me in that manner.
"Sensual pleasures are delight"—
now let us follow the subject at hand:
[this refers to] attainment through being recognized as a lover and through the state of being one who delights.
"The reason is that they are weak.
For by this word, his innate compassion toward them is manifested;
and by that, his [compassion].

By stating "the cause [is] with Rāma," and so forth, their great love (mahā-prema) has been recalled. Therefore, the meaning is that such great love alone is the cause for attaining Me in that manner.
Thus, although there is attainment in both ways, by the phrase "those who desire Me" (mat-kāmāḥ), it refers specifically to attainment through the state of being His beloved (ramaṇatayā).
The fulfillment has been shown;
for instance, as in "I am dependent on food" (BhP 9.4.63) and "consisting of His own will" (BhP 10.14.2).
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction of the promise [made in Gītā 4.11]: "In whatever way people come to Me.
In that context, the phrase "in whatever way" means "by whichever manner of desire. Therefore—

This follows the logic of the *kratu* sacrifice. Thus, the fulfillment of their desires is established by the principle of "how much more so" (*kaimutya*). Therefore, let it be granted that this applies to them.
Regarding the news of her supreme forms of splendor and beauty,
he says "from association" (saṅgāt), meaning that through association with her, hundreds of thousands of other such qualities also came to me.
In this regard, it must be analyzed as follows: for those who are eternally beloved, the status of being a paramour (*jāra*) toward Him is simply not possible;
for indeed, in the *Śrīmad-daśārṇa* and other such texts, that—

He is designated by name as their husband (*pati*) alone; for although the word *vallabha*—as found in the *Viśvaprakāśa* and other lexicons—has two meanings, namely "beloved" (*dayita*) and "overseer" (*adhyakṣa*), it is his quality of being beloved (*dayitatva*) that applies to them.
Furthermore, in the *Gautamīya-tantra*, in the commentary on that mantra, he is explained specifically as their husband.
It is seen; indeed, having provided two explanations for that name by way of its connection with the state of being Brahmā and Īśvara,
he states the preferred explanation as the final position in the second chapter of the *Gautamīya-tantra*, in the commentary on the ten syllables:
"Or rather, He is the very Lord of the gopīs who have attained perfection through many births;

He is called the Delight of Nanda, the Increaser of the Joy of the Three Worlds. In this context, "attainment of perfection through many births" means having manifested throughout a succession of beginningless kalpas.
It is said thus, as in: "Many births of mine have passed, as well as yours, O Arjuna" (Gītā 4.5);
for there can be no cosmic cycle (*kalpa*) without His manifestation, which is an absolute necessity within the *manvantara* of Vaivasvata.
Because they have attained that worship through the Veda established from time immemorial, their beginninglessness is proven;

and their status as its sole consorts is to be meditated upon in the scriptures concerning the worship of those respective mantras, as they remain devoted to its propitiation without limitation by time.
Because it is being enjoined as such,
and because there is not even a scent of a connection with another husband heard [in the scriptures]; and so it is said in the Brahma-saṃhitā:
He who, being the self of all, dwells in Goloka itself by means of those very digits (kalās) which are manifested from the essence of bliss and consciousness as his own inherent nature.
"I worship that Govinda, the primordial Person" (Brahma Sūtra 5.48).

Thus, according to the manner described as "being served with the agitation of hundreds of thousands of Lakṣmīs," and because the word "that" (tat) is obtained through the invocation, it is made manifest that He dwells in Goloka itself together with those in the form of gopīs.
In the *Līlā*, the elaboration of "belonging to another" (*parakīyatva*) is refuted;

for since [the Lord] is established as His own essential nature (*nija-rūpa*) precisely by virtue of being a *kalā*, the expression "by way of His own essential nature" (*nija-rūpatayā*) remains meaningful in that very sense.

It has been stated in the same way: "Śrī is the beloved, and the Supreme Person (Parama-puruṣa) is the beloved" [Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya 5.56]. Here, he has also shown that it is logical that no illicit sexual union (aupapattya) is possible between Śrī and the Supreme Person.
This refers to the words of Durvāsas addressed to them while they were performing austerities (tapanī).
"Indeed, he is your master" (sa vo hi svāmī). Just as the words *pati*, *ramaṇa*, and *vallabha* are well-known, so too is the word *svāmin*;
for the *Amarakośa* states: "The master's brother-in-law is called *devṛ* or *devara*."

And those words, being employed as referring to a single substratum, exclude mutual difference in meaning, just as in the case of "to Kṛṣṇa, to Vāsudeva, and to the son of Devakī" (BhP 1.8.21). Let alone talk of unmanifest pastimes; even regarding such hidden states, they are manifest—
Even in the context of the *rasa* of divine play (*līlā*), Śrī Śuka himself, out of being overwhelmed by bliss, spoke without concealment:
"They sang of the deeds of Ṛṣabha" (BhP 10.33.7); here, even the Lord [himself] [spoke thus].
The phrase "of the husband Ṛṣabha" has been explained. Furthermore, according to the *Saṅgīta-śāstra*, even Ananta, the husband of Gopī, fell under the power of the sound of the flute.
It is also stated by the words of Śrī Śaṅkarācārya in the *Śrī Yamunā-stava*: "Grant him devotion to the lotus feet of the husband of Rādhikā.
— from the *Śrī Gīta-govinda*.

And by the words of Śrī Jayadeva, "the mind of the husband was nailed down," it is therefore rightly shown by the Blessed One Himself: "to one who does not know the true nature [of her lover], she considers him a paramour; to me, she is my beloved."

Previously, by that very same power of divine play (*līlā-śakti*), for the purpose of manifesting their extreme longing, [the Lord] first concealed their awareness of His own nature as their eternal beloved and made them perceive Śrī Kṛṣṇa as a paramour; and in the future, He will do exactly the same toward Him once again.
The intended meaning is that one performs a contemplation of such a true nature, which produces the wonder of bliss consisting of the manifestation of innate lordship.
Let alone those who are eternally beloved.

News [reached them]. Because of their association with those who had already attained Me, it is established that for the others as well, there was only the state of being My lovers (*ramaṇī*), and not the state of being My paramours (*jārī*). This very point is indicated by the phrase "desirous of Me" (*mat-kāmāḥ*) in the verse: "They have attained Me, the Supreme Brahman."
And by this, because the Supreme Brahman is the partaker of all parts and the enjoyer of all, His absolute sovereignty alone is established, but not His transcendence;
and that being so, He possesses the status of a husband toward those [energies] who desire Him in such a manner.
This is intended to mean that there would otherwise be no state of being a lover (*jāra*).

Thus it was said by Piṅgalā, who— out of a sense of reverence born from her conviction in the excellence of the ultimate distinction between that [Self] and [the world]— delighted herself with the Self, even as she was Dattātreya.

Thus it is said: "He took delight with him as Ramā does" (BhP 11.8.35). Indeed, he would be the husband of the goddess Ramā, free from fear from any quarter; he himself protects on all sides the person who is afflicted by fear. (BhP)
[5.18.20] Thus, since the status of being a fruit (phalatva) ultimately pertains only to a real entity, even when that [entity] is obtained through the notion of it being a lover,
because it is obtained as an object of delight, it results in nothing other than the status of being a husband (patitva).
Thus it has been said:
"Even those who united with that very Supreme Self through the notion of a lover immediately cast off their bodies composed of the gunas, their bonds being utterly destroyed. [BhP 10.29.11]
In this regard, as in the verse, "Even by giving her breast to Hari with the intent to kill, she attained the goal of the righteous" (BhP 10.6.35),
the word "even" (*api*), though connected with the term "intent to kill" (*jighāṃsayā*) which has a contrary meaning, reveals that such an intent should not have been operative there.
Nevertheless, because the human purpose (puruṣārtha) is accomplished, it establishes the very capacity of the object;
likewise, by associating with the word "lover" (jāra), which has a well-known meaning, [it establishes] the state of being a lover through the act of union.
The reality of the object makes that [pleasure] known as such; however, the state of being a lover is not so censured. On the contrary:
"What can be said of the austerity of those women who, with love, served the Teacher of the World with the thought of him as their husband, massaging his feet and so forth? (BhP 10.90.27)

By such statements as these, they have indeed been praised excellently; yet, by such statements as "O, for those who enjoy the dust of their feet" (BhP 10.47.61), even their status as paramours is praised, but rather it is their passion (*rāga*) that is praised. By which—
As for the claim that she was accepted even as a paramour—
that conceptualization of those who call her a paramour, namely that it was done with the thought "she is a paramour," is indeed false.
Because it is inappropriate [to use the word *api*] as it would convey a different meaning even when attached to the word *jāra*;
because it would be harsh (*kaṣṭa*) due to its dependence on the word *saha*; and because of the [presence of the] *upapada*...

This is because of the maxim that "the case-ending denoting the grammatical factor (*kāraka*) is stronger," and because another [factor] must be postulated as the most effective means (*sādhakatama*).
They all attained womanhood and were born in Gokula;
having obtained Hari through desire, they were thereafter liberated from the ocean of worldly existence.
Thus, from hearing the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa, it is concluded that even then these women were indeed not yet possessed of perfected bodies (siddha-deha).
Consequently, by the abandonment of that body and of their husbands, they attained Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
The status of being another's wife is untenable;
how much more so for those who are eternally beloved, though perceived as another's wives through mere illusion?

And in this very way, it has been shown by the Blessed One himself in the passage beginning with "While I was sporting at night" (BhP 10.47.30) and so forth; however, such a word as "paramour" (*jāra*) is used here.

As for the indecorous: how indeed could that which is not even made the object of a reply by women consorting with paramours—rather, [only] words such as "pleasure" (*ramaṇa*) and so forth—are to be designated? How could it possibly be expressed?
It is fit for the fruit.

Thus, having restated [the passage] beginning with "He is indeed a paramour" (*jāra*) and "He is Brahman," it falls within the category of praise; however, because being a paramour consists of delusion and is censured, it is to be abandoned.
As for what was stated— that "delight" (ramaṇam) is the predicate—
this indeed refers to the manifest pastimes, because of the clarity of the former.
Because it has been described, it is well-known to the listener; likewise, because the latter [the unproven] is also well-known by virtue of not having been described, it is established.
Indeed, being well-known and not being well-known are precisely the causes for the engagement with those two.
It is like the expression, "This Brāhmaṇa is a scholar.
Furthermore, it is observed everywhere that one should not state the thing to be enjoined without first stating the restatement (anuvāda).

Because the opposite is observed in the case of the statement, "He whose ladle is made of *parṇa* wood [attains immortality]," and by the maxim that "the scripture is purposeful only where [the result] is not otherwise established," one offers with curds (*dadhi*).
As in such cases, the purport lies solely in the state of being the object of delight (*ramaṇatva*) which was not previously established;

nor is it the case that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which conveys an as-yet-unrealized object, given that [the meanings] from "Brahman-ness" down to "husband-ness" were already well-known in preceding instances.
The elders say:
furthermore, if the state of being a paramour were real, indecorousness would be unavoidable; if it were unreal, there would be inconstancy.

Thus it is; in every respect, it is certainly not subject to that—enough of this excessive detail. Here, when "Brahman" alone is mentioned, [it refers] to the Blessed One, for there is someone who propounds a Brahman devoid of distinctions as heard in scripture.
It was said "supreme" because there might otherwise be doubt;
yet, when "supreme" is said, the fact that he is Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself is not fully realized, and thus it was said "me."
When "me" (mām) is thus uttered, the state of being Brahman and the state of being supreme become dependent upon other means of valid cognition; therefore, that [other] is mentioned.
Likewise, [the word] "lover" (jāra).
When it is stated thus, [the meaning] does not conclude as "it is not established"; therefore, it is said, "it is *ramaṇa*.
When only "*ramaṇa*" is stated, because it has already been previously understood, even by the word "*ramaṇa*" one might somehow imply only the state of being a lover (*jāra*); therefore—
The term "lover" (jāra) is also mentioned as a corroboration for the purpose of negation;
furthermore, because it is the most desired state, "the act of sporting" (ramaṇatva) alone is what is to be enjoined.
But it is not so for the state of being a lover.
Nevertheless, the established tenet (siddhānta) is indeed that in all cases there is the attainment of a desired goal that is free from obstacles through final resolution.
The consensus of both the Rasa and Śāstra traditions is likewise recounted by ancient and modern poets, both worldly and transcendental.

Our venerable predecessors, who are our very source of livelihood, have likewise presented this in the act named *Pūrṇamanoratha* in the *Lalitamādhava*; taking that very work as authoritative, [we describe] the *sambhoga* (enjoyment) which fulfills all aesthetic flavors and is full of abundance, as found in the *Ujjvalanīlamaṇi*.
And this was declared by the Blessed Lord Himself through the passage beginning with "But as for me, O you ladies...
(BhP 10.47.34) and ending with "Those who were sported with by Me during the night... (BhP 10.47.37);
He intended exactly that.
Furthermore, union consisting of the state of being a paramour is always fraught with obstacles;

therefore, it could not be accepted by the various scriptures as the ultimate human goal (*paryavasāna-puruṣārtha*). Thus, [it is said]: "With the petals of the lotuses of Your own feet, for those whose number reaches the highest limit... (*BhP* 10.35.16).

"In the first pair, we did not notice their gait, their disheveled hair, or their soiled garments due to our own agitation"— in such ways, even previously, it was difficult for those women of exalted and great emotions to conceal their inner feelings within Vraja.
"But when this great separation has occurred, what would our family elders and kinsmen not have done had they approached Mādhava to prevent it?
Having cast aside their shame, they wept with loud voices.
"O Govinda, O Dāmodara, O Mādhava," and "Those whose minds are fixed on Me, whose life-breath is Me, who have renounced their physical bodies for My sake."
"When Uddhava, the messenger of Kṛṣṇa, arrived in Vraja,
some women abandoned worldly concerns," and "they were devoid of shame. Thus it is said of a certain woman.

"Having seen the honey-maker," and "She who, having abandoned her kinsmen and the path of the noble which are so difficult to forsake," and "The cowherd women, eager for the sight of Rāma, asked while laughing," [from BhP 10.47.11, 10.47.61, and BhP].
Thus it is said:

It is heard that,
regarding the words "we shall ward him off here" and so forth, he acted exactly as he had intended, casting aside all shame with the words "having abandoned [all hesitation]" and so on.

Indeed, the abandonment of shame on their part would occur only through the manifestation of their internal state, since all the inhabitants of the cowherd settlement are identical in their weeping and so forth; therefore,
it is by means of that manifestation preceded by weeping.
Therefore, even their warding off [of worldly desires] is appropriate.

By some power bestowed by the gods among sages, who were deeply gratified precisely by his multitude of great virtues, he has protected us, disregarding even his own suffering amidst a multitude of calamities, time and again.

He who has thoroughly nourished us with the sweetness woven from his skill in manifesting a hidden friendship through the playful charm of his innate character, loveliness, beauty, and virtues; he who,
by even a slight manifestation of his qualities, has brought about an abundance of joy for us.
Whatever was desired by those like me, even that which had passed away, he—

having made his renowned Yādava lineage known for the protection of all virtuous people— himself, through that very lineage, caused each of those things to be attained as a fragment of his own wondrous and preeminent sweetness.
Moreover, he who set out for the city of the Yadus in order to destroy the hosts of Rājanyas and Asuras, and who,

remaining there for a long time due to the requirements of his mission, repeatedly consoled us— whose minds were tormented by the separation from him— with the help of Uddhava and others; [that very Lord has now departed].

Furthermore, he whom we—our very forms drawn by the pinnacle of longing, having gone to Kurukṣetra under the pretext of visiting sacred fords—attained as the embodiment of the ocean of nectar when we were as if nothing remained but our breath; he whom... [he whom...]

Having thus caused us— who are of such a nature— to dwell in His own presence for several months, He has repeatedly revealed to us a certain hidden seal of affection toward the Yādavas— who have vainly conceived pride because of their supreme kinship with Him— by means of the suggestive implication that "I am Yours alone."
Thus he has kindled us from all sides—
he who, having firmly determined that Śrī Vṛndāvana alone is our own supreme desire even above himself, by means of oaths and the like, [has acted] with his own sudden...
Having placed his full trust in our arrival, he insistently sent us right here; yet now, alas,

even before he has completed the remainder of his duties, he has suddenly come to Gokula himself out of apprehension for us, who had begun the endeavor to liberate millions of lives without his own presence.
Having drawn [his beloved] out from the mouth of the serpent that is the time of separation from her, He remains as if sprinkling her with a flood of the nectar of His own glance;
and therein, at every moment, with a certain affection that is ever renewed and unique to Him alone—
By means of his own unique nature consisting solely of the essence of aesthetic sentiment (*rasa*), and therein by the accumulation of the overflowing stream of the nectar of his own supreme beauty,
and therein further by various ornaments such as flowers and the like—
By means of the enjoyment of its portions,
therein by the imposition of a particular weight of the sweetness of grace, and therein also by the diversion of knowledge through the wonder of the manifestation of a multitude of diverse qualities.
Even there, by means of the playful diversions such as tending cows, assuming the form of a calf, playing childhood games, and mimicking the enchanting sound of the flute;
even there, by means of the grand display of sweetness and skill in pastimes such as departing from and entering Gokula; even there—
He remains constantly fondling us with an excess of affection manifested through various special pastimes and acts of gratification suited to each of his friends;
because of this, alas, we are not even able to attend to the passing of time or our coming and going.

Following this account, the exclusive devotees of Vraja explain that when Śrī Kṛṣṇa returned from Dvārakā, certain residents of Vraja uttered words of ecstatic joy at that time— such as "Victory to the Abode of Living Beings" (BhP 10.90.48)— which manifested from the mouth of Śrī Śuka.
For the manifestation of specific meanings occurs without any difficulty;
moreover, it is possible for the Śrī Bhāgavata to possess a manifold range of meanings.
Because he is the form of the wish-fulfilling cow for the learned;
for thus [it is said]: "He triumphs," and so forth.
He is this certain one, our most beloved throughout millions of lifetimes, who by his universal manifestation—Śrī...

Victorious is He who exists with supreme excellence as the destroyer of that sorrow arising from separation from Him, which specifically affects both the stationary and moving beings of Vṛndāvana itself.
By implication, this refers specifically to Śrī Vṛndāvana;
for the state of even the stationary entities within Śrī Vṛndāvana has indeed been described.
By the words "with a purely loving disposition" and so forth—
by what is she distinguished?
By her glorious face with its beautiful smile.
By this, it is revealed that he is eternally of the singular essence of bliss and is always perfectly gracious toward his own people.
What is he doing? [He is gazing upon] those women who belong to that city which is Vraja in form.

Having engendered passion in those noble wives, he increased their God of Love— whom they regarded as a deity because he shines preeminently above all joys of love— and who possesses a most divine form.
But surely they say, "This is the son of the illustrious Devakī";
how then can you have the conceit of ownership toward him here?
Regarding that, he says: "He whose worldly renown is the report that his birth was in Devakī is indeed false.
Then, raising the doubt as to how he has the name Vāsudeva, he says: "The abode of people" (jananivāsa).

The meaning is that it is designated as such because it is the dwelling place or the refuge for people, specifically for our own kin; or alternatively, because we, who are one's own kin, have made our abode there. Consequently, [the suffix] is used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) or the agent (*kartṛ*).
The term *vāsudeva* is derived from the *vauṇādika* suffix;

its analysis (*vigraha*) is "he who sports and plays" (*divyati krīḍati*), and thus he is a *deva*. Furthermore, the statement by Śrī Garga beginning with "Previously this was Vāsudeva" (BhP 10.8.14) does not appear convincing to us either.
This is the underlying intention (*bhāva*). To address the doubt as to why this discourse on the birth from Devakī occurred, he says:
"In such a way that the best of the Yadus were present as members of the assembly and assistants, by means of their own arms..."
He was casting away that abundant unrighteousness and that wicked lineage by means of Arjuna and others who were almost like his own arms,

in order to destroy it; for according to the rule regarding the suffix *śatṛ* (present participle), it is remembered that this suffix denotes both a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and a cause (*hetu*) of the action.

The meaning is: "Having reflected thus, [He thought], 'When my own birth is announced, those various associates will become [my allies]'"—as it was said by Śrī Kṛṣṇa to the Lord of Vraja after the killing of Kaṃsa: "O kinsmen, yours..."

"We shall go to see Him, having brought happiness to our friends" (BhP 10.45.23). Here, by means of the adjective alone, the substantive word "the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa" is evoked, just as in the expression: "Here rises the one who breaks the seal of the lotus plants."
it has also been stated that for them, due to that supreme bliss, there is no concern even with the observance of rules: "Indeed, one does not go even to where there is a rule" (Brahma Sūtra 5.56).
Therefore, for those who are intoxicated with the supreme bliss of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s arrival, the thought "He has come this very day" remains constantly in their hearts; [as Vṛndāvana-dāsa adds here:
just as that very state exists within the unmanifest, natural mood directed toward the manifest pastimes.
Likewise, entry into those forms of its majesty consisting of the worship of mantras should be understood as an entry into one's own respective prior state of being [toward them],
just as the state of being of the Gaṅgā exists within its series of pools.
Thus, in both places, He is shown to be exactly the same:
"O Govinda, Lord of the beloved Gopīs, where the slayer of Kaṃsa sports in the company of the cows, cowherds, and gopīs" (from the Pātāla-khaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa).
By these two [names], "Slayer of the demon Kaṃsa" and so forth,

it is heard that just as [he possesses] the nature of the Delight of Nanda (Nandanaṇdana) in his natural state, so too does he follow that same nature even in his mantra-form: "The auspiciousness of all the worlds, Nanda..."
Regarding the statement "the son of Gopā is the deity," it is stated as "the delighter of Nanda" in the second chapter of the *Gautamīya-tantra*, and likewise in this [text].
[End of Vṛtti addition.]

Thus, by the entry of one who possesses specific moods pertaining to manifest pastimes into the unmanifest pastimes, the oneness of the second [pastime], namely the pastime of external disappearance, has been described. In that regard, although even previously...
Although such a disposition has persisted among them from time immemorial, it should be understood that the Lord descends again and again to renew and kindle that very disposition.
Thus, the fact that Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the Supreme Lord Himself has been demonstrated.
Even there, in Śrī Gokula, a supreme manifestation of that [divine light] is seen; and that, pertaining to His sovereignty, consists of the essence of truth, knowledge, infinity, and bliss.
Upon beholding the Lord of millions of universes in His singular form,
He was moved by compassion even to grant the state of being a mother directly to Pūtanā.
And his sweetness is such that the women of Vraja, the Pulindya forest-dwellers, the grasses and creepers,
and even the cows long for the touch of his feet as he tends them.
"Of the Great-Souled One" (BhP 10.83.43), as stated in the prayers of the illustrious Queen Paṭṭamahiṣī and others.
Even while remaining here, for those women who possess a love superior to all else, there is the good fortune of the touch of His feet.
Such a statement is consistent only with the intention of highlighting the excellence of the preeminent manifestation of that sweetness;
and it has been said accordingly:
"Beholding this form, which is the good fortune of the three worlds..."
In passages such as, "The cows, birds, trees, and deer bore horripilation...
and so forth, He is praised as being engaged in *līlā*. Furthermore, in passages such as, "His parents did not obtain the benefit of Kṛṣṇa’s noble childhood...
and so forth, the excellence of His devotees is also stated, beginning with Vṛndāvana.
In the beginning, [Kṛṣṇa says], "I shall behold Govardhana and the sands of the Yamunā" (BhP 10.11.36);
then, regarding His attendants, "Oh, what fortune! Oh, what fortune! (BhP 10.14.32), and so forth; and likewise, "Thus for the virtuous... (BhP 10.12.11), and so on.

In the passage beginning with "What did Nanda do? (BhP 10.8.43), in the passage beginning with "These [gopīs], moreover... (BhP 10.47.51), and in the passage beginning with "What austerity did the gopīs perform? (BhP 10.44.14).
In the beginning, and also in such passages as "There too, he shone exceedingly with them" (BhP 10.33.6), the ultimate limit of the excellence of their radiance is shown;
therefore, He was surely propitiated by all of them.

It should be understood that this applies even more so in the case of Śrī Rādhikā, who is renowned for the excellence of her love, as indicated by such passages as "The Blessed Lord Hari is the Sovereign" (BhP 10.30.28).
And here is the essential point:
in the second section, having indeed described the Blessed Lord as the Supreme, His two-fold potency was described.
In that regard, the first [form] is the Śrī-Bhagavatī who is worshipped by the Śrī-Vaiṣṇavas; she is His very own essential nature (svarūpa-bhūtā), for His divinity indeed resides in her alone.
And now, the second...
For them, Māyā— characterized by illusion— is to be viewed with indifference like the world,
since its nature as the world exists only in Me. In that regard, the word "Lakṣmī" refers to the prior power (śakti), just as the word "Bhagavat" refers to the possessor of power (śaktimat).
That he "applies himself" (prayujyate) has also been shown in the second [chapter] alone.
Therefore, since it has been determined in this context that the Blessed Lord is indeed named Śrī Kṛṣṇa, what is the name of His own essential power (svarūpa-śakti)?
It is to be determined:
therein, among both cities, that which is called Śrī-Mahī is to be known as being in Mathurā.
Even though the name of Rukmiṇī is well-known in the Śruti regarding the unmanifest pastimes, it serves as an indication for the others;

that the illustrious queens are the internal potency (svarūpa-śakti) of His very nature is seen in the Skanda Purāṇa, Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, in the dialogue between Śrī Śiva and Gaurī, within the *Gopyāditya-māhātmya*.
Long ago, when the immensely radiant Kṛṣṇa arrived at Prabhāsa accompanied by all the Yādavas, numbering fifty-six crores.
Sixteen thousand gopīs gathered there;
likewise, O beloved, these one hundred and sixty thousand are the sons of Kṛṣṇa.
Having begun thus, [it continues]:
"Then, O Great Goddess, sixteen Vidyās are recorded.
I shall tell you their names; listen to them with one-pointed mind."
Lambinī, Candrikā, Kāntā, Krūrā, Śāntā, Mahodayā,
Bhīṣaṇī, Nandinī, Śokā, Supūrvavimalā, and Kṣayā.
These arts of the *haṃsa*—namely *śubhadā*, *śobhanā*, and *puṇyā*—are [the letters] in sequence;
indeed, the *haṃsa* is considered to be Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self, Janārdana.
O Goddess, these powers of his are proclaimed to be exactly sixteen;
Kṛṣṇa is considered to be the form of the moon, while they are remembered as being the forms of its digits (kalās).
Among them, Mālinī is the sixteenth digit (kalā) with its full orb;
beginning from the lunar day of the first (pratipad), the moon moves through these [digits].
O fair-faced one, those sixteen digits which exist in the form of the gopīs are each individually multiplied by a thousand.
"Thus, O Goddess, this secret born of knowledge has been told to you.
The man who knows this should indeed be known as a Vaiṣṇava by the wise. (108.5–8, 10–16).
Here, "gopyaḥ" means "the queens."
According to the *Nāma-liṅgānuśāsana*, the word *gopa* can also mean "king.
*Lambinī* is the power of descent (*avatāra-śakti*). *Suvimalā* means "exceedingly pure" (*su-pūrva-vimalā*).
Regarding the phrase "haṃsaśīta," he states what is intended by the expression "haṃsaya" that was obtained there: namely, "the haṃsa itself.
And that [haṃsa] is of the nature of the moon—the moon—...
The meaning is "by means of an illustration.

The phrase "having the form of digits" (kalā-rūpā) means that those powers (śaktayaḥ) are to be illustrated by the example of the digits (kalā) of the moon, such as Amṛtā and so forth; this is the meaning.
He speaks of the final, great power (*mahā-śakti*) not previously mentioned with the word "complete" (*sampūrṇā*);
this indeed is [as follows] on page 109.
She is to be known as the aggregate form of all the digits (*kalā*).
To provide an illustrative example, he states that the moon is likewise; "on the first day" (*pratipad*) refers to those [days] which are equal to this.

Regarding the arts (*kalās*), he states what is intended: "only sixteen," because these sixteen alone possess the nature of knowledge (*vidyā*). This is because the secret of the possibility of such knowledge lies in this very instruction; for that knowledge is the inferential mark of being a Vaiṣṇava.
And because of its being an indicative mark (*liṅga*):

even though cruelty, terror, and grief are indeed of the very nature of the Blessed Lord, they constitute the hardness of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, just as in the verse: "He was like a thunderbolt to the Mallas" (BhP 10.47.17).
Because he causes [the truth] to be understood;
because he terrifies the wicked, like the death of the lord of the Bhojas; and because he is the teacher of the unrighteous.

And because they are indeed the causes of his grief, their respective etymologies are thus justified; just as the light of the sun, though its sole nature is radiance, manifests as darkness and so forth for owls. Therefore, it is perfectly clear that Kṛṣṇa is considered to be the form of the moon, while those [energies] are remembered as being the forms of its digits (kalās).
The state of being their very nature has been demonstrated.
Thus, since they constitute her essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*), their status as Lakṣmīs is indeed established. Intending this very point, he speaks of their status as Lakṣmīs:
In their homes— which were free from the need for servants and beyond all conceptualization— He remained, transcending all equality and superiority;
overflowing with His own desire, He took delight in the company of the goddesses of fortune.
"Just as another [person], while performing the domestic sacrifices (gārhapatya-medha), [is accompanied by others];
and the commentary states: "By the Ramās, who are portions (aṃśa) of Lakṣmī"—this is because they are indeed her own essential power (svarūpa-śakti).
It has been stated that he "rejoices.

For this very reason, he is "overflowing," meaning pervaded by *kāma*, which is a specific form of love (*prema*) consisting of the arising of a particular modification of the power of supreme bliss (*paramānanda-śakti-vṛtti-viśeṣa*), and which is his own, belonging to himself.
by the very principle of *kaimutya* (a fortiori), the fact that the eight illustrious principal queens (*paṭṭa-mahiṣī*) are indeed His own essential powers (*svarūpa-śakti*) is established.
In this regard, the fact that Śrī Satyabhāmā is the embodiment of the Earth-power (bhū-śakti) is well known from the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa and other sources;
likewise, Śrī Yamunā is the embodiment of the Mercy-power (kṛpā-śakti).
One should investigate such matters in the *Skanda-yamunā-māhātmya* and other texts; however,

since Satyabhāmā’s extraordinary good fortune is well-known in the *Śrī-harivaṃśa* and other works, she should be understood as possessing an abundance of the power of love (*prema-śakti*) and the power of the earth (*bhū-śakti*).
Śrī Rukmiṇī herself was indeed Lakṣmī;
O King, there was great joy among the inhabitants of the city upon seeing Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī, united with his beloved Rukmiṇī in Dvārakā.
Since she is well-known as such in these and other passages in great abundance,
he himself states her mutual suitability by way of her being Lakṣmī herself:
Rukmiṇī alone is worthy to be his wife, and no other;
he too, being of faultless nature, is the fitting husband for the daughter of Bhīṣmaka.
This is clear.

// 10.53 // The inhabitants of the city of Vidarbha [spoke] to one another // 184 // [185] Thus, regarding Rukmiṇī as Śrī and so forth, [it is said]: "She who, assuming a body through her divine play (līlā), possessed a form corresponding [to His]" (BhP 10.60.9).
This is clear.

Therefore, by virtue of being a fitting counterpart to the Lord Himself, her status as Lakṣmī herself is indeed established. For this very reason, in the passage [BhP 10.52.16], "the daughter of Bhīṣmaka, Vaidarbhī, who is the measure (mātrā) of Śrī, at the svayaṃvara," the word *mātrā*— derived from the root *mā* with the suffix *traṅ*— is used in the locative sense (of receptacle) due to its abundance, meaning "she in whom [Śrī] is contained."
This is to be understood; [the suffix] *mātra* is used here in the sense of totality or restriction, as in the word *mātram*.
Consequently, since she is the locus for the inclusion of Lakṣmī as she is renowned in Vaikuṇṭha, the meaning is that she alone is completely perfect in every respect.
But as for what [you said]:
"Indeed, O lotus-eyed one, it is so;
you are indeed the incomparable manifestation of the all-pervading Blessed One."
"Where is the Blessed Lord, the sovereign of the three worlds, who delights in His own glory; and where am I, whose nature is composed of the *guṇas*, whose feet are grasped by the ignorant?"—
this was spoken by her [the Earth] herself, having considered herself to be merely a reflection of His own portion (*nijāṃśābhāsa*) due to her state of wretchedness.
It should be understood thus; or else,
it means that its nature (prakṛti), which is secondary (gauṇī) in its qualities (guṇa), is its inherent essence (svabhāva), and thus it is of an inferior form.
As it is said in that very same place:
"May Your foot be my refuge as I wander through the cycles of rebirth"— this was spoken by her alone, due to her firm conviction in the descent of the Lord as a human being.
This is an expression of wretchedness (*dainyokti*).
Here, the actual meaning impelled by fate is this:
"O lotus-eyed one, I am incomparable to you, the Blessed One. (Page 110)
As for what you said— "Is it not certain that it is precisely of the kind about to be described, and not of any other kind?"—
he says the same thing himself: "In his own [work]..."
The Blessed One is delighted in His own essential majesty, such as sovereignty and the like; where else, then, could He be?
Likewise, I am one whose very nature (prakṛti) or essential form consists of those same qualities, such as sovereignty and so forth; where else, then, could I be?

But "not elsewhere" means that their existence is in one and the same essential nature (*svarūpa*). Therefore, because there is no absolute difference between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*), I am one whose feet are grasped and served by both the ignorant and those who know the truth of You, O Śrī Viṣṇu.
The intended meaning is that, due to the absence of the relationship between the standard of comparison (upamāna) and the object of comparison (upameya), there is an absence of similarity.
Likewise, in the phrase "wandering by means of the paths," the actual meaning is indeed "by means of your own paths. As it has been said:
"In the state of divinity, she possesses a divine body, and in the state of humanity, she is human" (ViP 1.9.143).
In this very way— O lotus-eyed one, let there be for me devotion to your feet.
When you, who see no difference between yourself and me, look upon me with eyes filled with passion for the sake of my growth— that indeed is the supreme compassion shown toward us.

Thus, here too, her status as the *prakṛti* (primordial nature) is to be explained solely through the metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) with dejection. Alternatively, he is one by whom the excessive passion (*rajas*) pertaining to this householder state has been fully accepted and embraced, characterized by an excellence in pleasing all living beings.
The actual meaning, however, is as follows: regarding what was said, "We are indifferent," and so forth,
the Blessed Lord replied therein, "Let it be so."
O lotus-eyed one, may I have devotion for Your feet, You who delight in Yourself and in me;
and as it has been said that You delight in me, so may I also [delight in You].

The meaning is that, with his mind fixed on her, he could not find sleep at night; this is implied by the word "himself" (svayam eva). Now, one might ask: "How can there be delight in you for me, who am delighted in the Self? To this he replies: "because my vision is not distinct" (anatirikta-dṛṣṭeḥ).
This means that my vision is not distinct—that is, devoid of any sense of separateness—between the empowered Self and myself, who am His power.

The sense is that because the power and the possessor of power are not separate entities, or because both are understood as being mutually distinguished, it is indeed appropriate to have love even for me. Thus,
while such love exists naturally, it is especially so—
When you, having taken up an excess of *rajas*— that is, one by whom there is an intensity of passion (*rāga*) for the sake of increasing this state known as *rati*—
look upon me with such feeling, then he [the Lord] is directed toward us.
"Supreme compassion indeed"—
the sense is that my conviction is very firm: "Your indifference toward anyone other than those directly related to me is exactly so."
Therefore, it has been rightly stated by the verse beginning with "yā līlayā dhṛta-tanoḥ" (BhP 10.60.9) that Śrī Rukmiṇī-devī herself is Lakṣmī.
regarding the manifestations of His own essential power (svarūpa-śakti) within Vṛndāvana, who are the divine ladies of Vraja;
as it is said in the Brahma-saṃhitā:
He who, being the self of all, dwells in Goloka itself by means of those very potencies (kalās) which are manifested from the essence of bliss and consciousness as His own inherent nature.
"I worship that Govinda, the primordial Person"—thus [it is said].
By the use of the word "that" (tat) in the mantra along with those Śrī-gopīs, [he is indicated as being one with them] through their parts (kalābhiḥ), that is, their powers (śaktibhiḥ). His own...
In their nature as form— that is, as their own essential nature—
and by virtue of the previously mentioned excellence, even all those [energies] which have manifested in a supremely perfect manner possess nothing but the state of being Lakṣmī herself.
Thus it is said in that very same place:
"served with the agitation of hundreds and thousands of Lakṣmīs," meaning he is the beloved of the Śrīs (the goddesses of fortune) and their beloved.

And [He is called] the Supreme Person (parama-puruṣa). Having this very intention in mind, even in the Svāyambhuva Āgama, that triad of His special beloveds is taught by means of the words Śrī, Bhū, and Līlā.
Therefore, their excellence is described as being even greater than that of Lakṣmī (p. 111), who resides in the supreme heaven and other realms, by virtue of that very name.
It should be understood that this is intended to express their superiority over other forms of Lakṣmī;
for these very ones are the true glories of Śrī Vṛndāvana.
In the same way, in passages such as "with the placement of feet and the waving of arms" (BhP 10.33.7), it is stated that these belong to the wives of Kṛṣṇa;
for this very reason, it is said here: "the impeller of the ignorant portion of the Gopī-folk" (GTU 1.8).

In the *Tāpanī-vākya*, regarding the etymological explanation (*nirukti*) of the name situated within the illustrious *Daśākṣara-mantra*, those who are the "people of the gopīs" (*gopī-jana*) should be explained as follows: they are those who have attained (*ā*) perfectly (*sam*) that which is knowledge (*vidyā*) in the form of supreme love (*parama-prema*), and whose function (*vṛtti*) is its very essence (*kalā*).
This is understood from the context of the *Śrī-gītā* passages such as "the royal knowledge, the royal secret" (*rāja-vidyā rāja-guhyam*, Gītā 9.2). [Avidyā...]
By the word *kalā*, it is explained that she is indeed the power of love (*prema-śakti*) who causes the delusion of all the senses, whose activity (*vṛtti*) is ignorance (*avidyā*) itself;
for in another interpretation, there is no connection with ignorance in the Blessed Lady.
Thus it has been said:
"The Lord (Īśvara) is Being-Consciousness-Bliss embraced by the consciousness of Hlādinī;
the individual soul (jīva), enveloped by its own ignorance, is a mine of a multitude of afflictions."
Thus it is stated in the *Svāmī-sūkta*:
"In you, the refuge of all, the powers of bliss (*hlādinī*), existence (*sandhinī*), and consciousness (*saṃvit*) are one;
but in you, who are devoid of material qualities (*guṇa-varjita*), there is no mixed power that causes both joy and suffering."
Thus it is stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (1.12.69). Alternatively, for those who know only the mere majesty [of the Lord], this etymology of the word "gopījana" is like the meditation on the Virāṭ form.
As it is stated in that very same work, the *Gopālapadanirukti*, that [the Self] "revolves" until the end of creation;
therein, by the term *avidyā-kalā*, it is precisely *māyā* that is being denoted.

Therefore, since He is their impeller and the one who sets them forth in their respective sports, He is indeed identical in meaning with the term *vallabha* (the Beloved).
